Foreword

Enrico Franconi, by Dr., Professor of Computer Science at the Free University of Bozen-Bolzano, Italy, Director of the KRDB Research Centre for Knowledge and Data.

It is with great enthusiasm and profound honour that I contribute to the foreword of the third edition of this exceptional book, a comprehensive and illuminating guide to information modeling and relational databases, underscoring its profound importance in the realm of enterprise modeling and data management. Even more in this new edition, one cannot help but acknowledge the sheer breadth and depth of knowledge included within its pages.

This book serves as an indispensable resource for comprehending the object-role modeling (ORM) language and its fact-oriented modeling methodology. ORM stands as a beacon in the realm of data modeling, offering a rigorous and yet user-friendly approach. This book meticulously dissects the semantic complexity of enterprises with strict attention to detail. The authors' dedication to exploring and evaluating various conceptual modeling notations against ORM sets this book apart, providing readers with a panoramic view of the landscape of data modeling paradigms while presenting an accurate understanding of conceptual modeling and evidence of the advantages of ORM.

The chapters clarify the nuances of conceptual modeling, emphasizing the necessary precision of a modeling language. As someone from a logic-based knowledge representation and reasoning background, I greatly appreciate the formal rigor of the ORM notation, where ambiguities and sloppiness find no place, unlike many other (widely known) conceptual modeling notations. Furthermore, the book doesn’t merely describe the precise meaning of the modeling constructs but also elucidates why these constructs exist in the language. A meticulous analysis of their use cases and a methodology for their design hold equal importance in the book.

I find it fascinating how ORM offers a powerful and precise yet understandable conceptual modeling approach, and of course also how ORM is presented in this book in a precise yet understandable manner. As expected, the fact-oriented modeling methodology associated with ORM is thoroughly detailed in a clear way and serves as another key pillar of this book. It guides the understanding of data semantics and the design of data structures that authentically and correctly mirror the business reality and needs. The book focuses also quite a lot on the relationship between a conceptual model and its implementation in some database structure, emphasizing correctness and effectiveness while not forgetting the intricacies of real-world SQL.

The fact-oriented modeling methodology as explained in the previous editions of the book has influenced a lot of my research. Indeed, it was after a first reading of this book that I started working on the intersection between classical logic-based knowledge representation and ORM with its fact-oriented modeling methodology. I was also influenced by the textual version of the ORM language (FORML), also discussed in this book. I met Terry Halpin to discuss the outcome of my research, only to realize that there was much more for me to learn beforehand! Terry is a humble scientist who, after every discussion, always seems to be right.

The lifelong dedication of Terry Halpin and Tony Morgan to developing enterprise modeling concepts substantiates the significance of this work. The updated and expanded coverage, along with a plethora of exercises embedded in the chapters, enhance the book's value. The book stays current with the latest versions and trends, ensuring readers have access to the most recent developments in the field. The content encompassing ORM, ER, UML, SQL, and OWL has undergone comprehensive updates, incorporating their most recent iterations. Additional chapters addressing NoSQL technologies, such as key-value, column-oriented, and graph databases, have been integrated in this edition of the book. A chapter covering contemporary popular data file formats, such as XML and JSON, has been added. Extensive revisions have been made to all other chapters, enhancing the depth of coverage for numerous topics.

Finally, I want to emphasize the book's relevance to a diverse audience, including data modelers, data engineers, data analysts, enterprise architects, and programmers, highlighting its inclusivity and accessibility. The incorporation of exercises throughout the book offers readers an interactive and immersive learning experience, fostering a deeper understanding of conceptual modeling.

Foreword

Herman Balsters, by Dr., Partner at NorthChain, Groningen, The Netherlands.

I first became acquainted with ORM in 2005 at an ORM Workshop in Cyprus as part of the OTM Confederated International Workshops and Conference. I had just presented a paper on data federations at the OODB conference and out of pure curiosity, I paid a short visit to the ORM Workshop to learn a bit more about the ORM language. When I wandered in, Terry Halpin was offering a presentation. I was amazed with the lively discussions that went on during this presentation, and was surprised not only by the enthusiasm of the workshop participants but also by the high quality of comments and questions. Instead of paying only a short visit, I stayed at the ORM Workshop during the complete remainder of my stay in Cyprus, and I have been a great fan of ORM ever since.

During my work as a researcher and associate professor at the University of Groningen, I was heavily involved with languages such as unified modeling language (UML) and business process model and notation (BPMN), trying to capture the essence of information modeling. I had a constant struggle with these languages, which were considered state of the art, because I just could not get a full grasp of what models written in these languages really meant. I have a background in pure mathematics (in particular, mathematical logic) and computer science, and I wanted to have a clear idea of the semantics and completeness of the data and process models that I was trying to specify. I also wanted to see a clear connection between a model and how that model is implemented. In both aspects, I felt uncomfortable with the prevailing modeling languages of that time. And it was not only in research that I felt this lack of precision and completeness, but also in teaching. Nothing is harder to explain to students than something that you as a teacher do not completely understand.

All that changed the day I entered that ORM Workshop in Cyprus. It took me a while to master all the details of ORM, but after that, I was able to actually write models with complete understanding and with such precision that the models could directly be tied to implementations. Even today, I still use ORM with deep respect and satisfaction.

ORM is a so-called fact-oriented data modeling language. In ORM, you write facts about the world surrounding us. This means that you specify objects and relations between these objects, resulting in certain statements about the world. ORM does this in such a way that even nontechnical domain experts will be able to model facts about their domain of expertise. This has to do with the close resemblance that ORM has with natural language specifications about the world surrounding us. Yet ORM also does that in such a way that you can model facts with an extremely high level of detail and (mathematical) precision. ORM is a graphical language, with an intuitively understandable notation. ORM is also equipped with a powerful tool (NORMA) that allows for the graphical editing of ORM models, and validation checks. Another appealing aspect of ORM is the possibility of compiling ORM models directly into the relational data model, and after that, compilation to SQL. Hence, in ORM you can go from modeling directly to an implementation.

In 2008, authors Terry Halpin and Tony Morgan released the second edition of this wonderful book. I have used it ever since. Over the years, I have taught ORM to hundreds of students, and have supervised both Masters and Ph.D. students in their research involving ORM. The book excels in its simple and clear writing, covering almost every topic in information modeling. Also, the abundance of examples explaining the theory and practice of modeling using ORM makes this book essential for anyone wanting to understand all the details pertaining to information modeling.

This book is both technical and philosophical. It is technical because it provides for an abundance of material concerning theories, notations, examples, and tools to tackle almost anything that is thrown to an information modeler. As a bonus, we are shown how to technically implement those models as a relational database. But in a sense, the book is also philosophical because it takes you into an arena of challenging problems concerning the representation of the world surrounding us. ORM is all about using language to capture that world, and what the best language to do that job should look like.

As a university professor, I had the pleasure of using ORM to teach modeling to students, to write research papers, and to supervise Masters and PhD students in information modeling. Since leaving academia in 2018, I have been involved in information modeling on a more industrial level, where I have been confronted with some extremely challenging modeling problems in actual practice. Also in these complex situations involving modeling issues pertaining to data, business rules, and business processes, ORM provided solutions that I am sure I would otherwise not have had.

Terry Halpin is the world’s leading expert on ORM, and there is no better book than this one to get an understanding of ORM and how to tackle information modeling. I therefore fully recommend the third edition of this book to anyone interested in information modeling.

Foreword

Gordon C. Everest, by Dr., Professor Emeritus of MIS and “Data” Modeling Carlson School of Management, University of Minnesota, USA.

I am delighted and honored to again write a foreword, this time to the third edition of this book. It gives me another opportunity to convince those in the world of data modeling that there is a better way. I am absolutely convinced that object-role modeling (ORM) is a better way to do data modeling. My goal here is to sufficiently perk your interest to seriously study ORM. This book is the best resource available.

The Greek philosopher Socrates advised “Know thyself” to live a worthwhile life. Similarly, we can say “Know your world”, the reality in which you live, operate, and make decisions. Because it is impossible for any one person to know everything about their world, we need a representation of that world, a model that captures information about the things, relationships, activities/processes, and rules in that world. This representation consists of two parts: the definition of the structure and format, called the schema, and the actual data stored consistent with its definition. A collection of “databases” of information becomes an important surrogate for that world.

We make decisions in and about our world based on the surrogate databases we build. That is an awesome responsibility and thus demands a high degree of integrity, quality, and availability of our data stores. That requires a data modeling scheme that can capture a rich set of semantics, and ORM is the best of anything out there today.

The use of the term “data modeling” is often misleading. It suggests we are modeling data, when we are really modeling the things and relationships (objects and roles in relationships) in some user domain of interest—modeling in data, using data constructs, which eventually becomes a “data” model after the model is populated with data.

Data modeling is the foundation of information systems development—if you don't get the database design “right”, then the systems you build will be like a house of cards, collapsing under the weight of inevitable future forces for enhancement, integration, and quality improvement. Thus, we need a scheme to guide our data modeling efforts to produce data models that clearly and accurately represent the users’ domain of discourse and facilitate human communication, a shared understanding, and validation for quality control. The people who live in and know the user domain must be directly involved in the modeling process, supported by data modeling specialists who understand the design methodology.

This book is a must for anyone who is serious about data modeling, but with a caution: you must devote enough time and effort to really understand ORM. Fortunately, I had my students as a captive audience for a whole semester—long enough for them to learn and practice ORM and become convinced that it is a better way. With ORM, you can raise your data modeling skills to a whole new level.

This book also examines record-based modeling schemes: UML, SQL based on Ted Codd's relational model, and Peter Chen's entity relationship (ER) diagrams with many variations—Barker as in Oracle, Finkelstein's information engineering (IE), and IDEF1X (as in ERwin), with new material on the data structure representations in XML, JSON, and NoSQL. Viewing these familiar modeling approaches from an ORM perspective provides an enriched understanding of their underlying nature.

Record-based modeling schemes use three constructs: entity, attribute, and relationship. They can directly represent only at most binary, one-to-many relationships. But it is the clustering of attributes into entity records that is the root of many of our problems in data modeling. Normalization is the test to see if we clustered too much, and record decomposition is the remedy to correct a violation of the normal forms.

Normalization is the Achilles heel of data modeling. Oh, to be able to avoid normalization altogether? The mere suggestion is intriguing to students and practitioners of data modeling. Well, with ORM you can. The problem stems from the lack of a clear and complete definition of relationships when we throw stuff (attributes) into an entity record or table, so that the intrarecord structure is implicitly defined or assumed. ORM forces you to separately consider and explicitly define all relevant relationships and constraints among the object domains in your universe.

ORM is based on only two constructs: objects and relationships (which correspond to the concepts of nouns as subject or object and verbs as predicates in sentences). Both entities and attributes (in the relational modeling scheme) are based on objects (not to be confused with objects in object-oriented technology) and roles in ORM. Objects play roles in relationships with other objects. Thus, objects implicitly have attributes (descriptors or properties) by virtue of the roles they play in relationships with other objects.

In record-based modeling, there are two kinds of relationships: interrecord (defined explicitly and represented using foreign keys), and intrarecord among attributes (without explicitly defining the characteristics of any of the relationships, which is why we need to enforce the normalization rules). In ORM, all relationships are represented the same way with a single construct. When the ORM model is a valid representation of the world being modeled, the functional and multivalued dependencies are explicitly defined, and hence, the generation of “records” (in a relational table) can be automated and can guarantee that the result will be normalized (to 5NF). That’s good news for data modelers.

ORM does not supplant ER diagrams or relational database designs; rather, it is a stage before. It can enable, enlighten, and inform our development and understanding of ER/relational data models. We build records more for system efficiency than for human convenience or comprehension. The premature notion of a record (a cluster of attribute domains along with an identifier to represent an entity) gets in the way of good data modeling. ORM does not involve records, tables, or attributes. So consequently, we don't get bogged down in “TABLE THINK” (see https://tdan.com/recognizing-and-treating-tableitis/26060). With ORM, there is no need for an explicit normalization process.

This third edition is even more focused on the centrality of data in information systems, and on the importance of semantics. Starting with the realization that users (collectively) know more than we could ever capture in a data model, we must use a data modeling scheme that captures the widest possible range of semantics and expresses this meaning graphically. Semantics is paramount, and ORM goes way beyond any record-based modeling scheme in graphically depicting semantics.

Well, is that sufficient to pique your interest in learning more about ORM? If you are a would-be student of ORM and you take data modeling seriously, I encourage you to invest some time in reading this book. You won't regret it. You will grow to appreciate ORM and will become a better data modeler for it—just ask any of my thousands of former students. To develop effective and maintainable information systems, we need good data models, and for that we need a good data modeling scheme or methodology. ORM allows us to develop database designs at the highest conceptual level, unencumbered by things that are not of primary concern to user domain specialists. My deep desire is to see more and more database designers using ORM. The systems we build and the world we live in will be better for it. Join me in this journey and enjoy the adventure.

Preface

This book is about information systems, focusing on information modeling and database systems (especially relational database systems, but also covering nonrelational systems). It is written primarily for data modelers and database practitioners as well as students of computer science or information management. It should also be useful to anyone wishing to formulate the information structure of business domains in a way that can be readily understood by humans yet easily implemented on computers. In addition, it provides a simple conceptual framework for understanding what database systems really are as well as a thorough introduction to SQL and other key topics in data management.

A major part of this book deals with fact-oriented modeling, a conceptual modeling approach that views the world in terms of simple facts about objects and the roles they play. Originating in Europe, fact orientation is today used worldwide and comes in many flavors, including the Semantics of Business Vocabulary and Business Rules (SBVR). The version of fact orientation described in this book is second-generation Object-Role Modeling (ORM 2), and is based on extensions to the Natural-Language Information Analysis Method (NIAM).

Two other popular notations for information modeling are Entity-Relationship (ER) diagrams and Unified Modeling Language (UML) class diagrams. For conceptual information analysis, the ORM method has several advantages over the ER and UML approaches. For example, ORM models can be easily verbalized and populated for validation with domain experts, they are more stable under changes to the business domain, and they typically capture more business rules in diagram form.

However, ER diagrams and UML class diagrams are good for compact summaries, and their structures are closer to the final implementation, so they also have value. Hence, the coverage includes chapters on data modeling in ER and UML, and indicates how ER and UML data models can be easily generated from ORM models.

To make the text more approachable to the general reader with an interest in databases, the language is kept simple, and a formalized, mathematical treatment is mostly avoided. Where necessary, relevant concepts from elementary logic and set theory are discussed prior to their application. Most of the material in this book has been class tested in courses for both industry and academia, and the basic ORM method has been taught successfully even at the high school level. The content is modularized, so that instructors wishing to omit some material may make an appropriate selection for their courses.

The first chapter motivates the study of conceptual modeling, and briefly compares the ORM, ER, and UML approaches. It also includes a historical and structural overview of information systems. Chapter 2 provides a structural background, explaining the conceptual architecture of, and development frameworks for, information systems. It introduces a number of key concepts that are dealt with more thoroughly in later chapters, and should be read in full by the reader with little or no database experience.

Chapter 3 is fundamental. Following an overview of conceptual modeling language criteria and the ORM Conceptual Schema Design Procedure (CSDP), this chapter covers the first three steps of the CSDP. The first step (verbalizing familiar examples in terms of elementary facts) may seem trivial, but it should not be rushed, as it provides the foundation for the model. The rest of this chapter covers the basic graphical notation for fact types, and then offers guidance on how to classify objects into types and identify information that can be arithmetically derived.

Chapter 4 begins the task of specifying constraints on the populations of fact types. The most important kind of constraint (the uniqueness constraint) is considered in detail. Then some checks on the elementarity of the fact types are discussed. This chapter also introduces the join and projection operations at the conceptual level; the relational version of these operations is important in the later work on relational databases.

Chapter 5 covers mandatory role constraints, including a check for detecting information that can be logically derived. Reference schemes are then examined in some depth. Some of the more complex reference schemes considered here could be skipped in a short course. The CSDP steps covered so far are then reviewed by applying them in a case study, and the logical derivation check is then considered.

Chapter 6 covers value, set comparison (subset, equality, and exclusion), and subtyping constraints. Section 6.6 deals with advanced aspects of subtyping. Though important in practice, the material in this section could be skimmed over in a first reading.

Chapter 7 deals with the final step of the CSDP. Less-common constraints are considered (e.g., frequency constraints and ring constraints), and final checks are made on the design. Sections 7.3–7.5 are somewhat advanced, and could be skipped in a short course.

Chapter 8 discusses the ER approach, starting with Chen’s original notation then moving on to the three most popular notations in current use: the Barker ER notation, the Information Engineering notation, and the IDEF1X notation (actually a hybrid of ER and relational notations). Comparisons with ORM are included along the way.

Chapter 9 examines the use of UML class diagrams for data modeling, including a detailed comparison with ORM. Business rule constructs in ORM with no graphic counterpart in UML are identified and then captured in UML using user-defined constraints or notes.

Chapter 10 considers several advanced aspects of information modeling, such as join constraints, historical fact types, collection types, open/closed world semantics, and higher-order types. The discussion of deontic rules and nominalization is fundamental to understanding the SBVR flavor of fact orientation. This chapter is technically the most challenging in the book, and it could be skipped in an introductory course.

Chapter 11 describes how a conceptual model may be implemented in a relational database system. The first three sections are fundamental to understanding how a conceptual schema may be mapped to a relational schema. Section 11.4 considers advanced relational mapping aspects, and it could be omitted in a short course.

Chapter 12 provides a foundational introduction to relational databases and SQL queries. Section 12.1 covers relational algebra; although not used as a practical query language, the algebra is important for understanding the basic relational operations supported by SQL. Section 12.2 provides an overview of how the relational model of data compares with data models adopted by some relational database management systems. Sections 12.3–12.14 cover the main features of SQL, focusing on versions of Standard SQL as specified by the International Standards Organization, with some attention also paid to commercial SQL systems.

Chapter 13 discusses further aspects of SQL (e.g., data definition, triggers, and stored procedures), and introduces some practical issues such as security, metadata, and concurrency.

Chapter 14 discusses how and when to transform one schema into another schema at the same level (conceptual or logical). Sections 14.1–14.4 examine the notion of conceptual schema equivalence, and ways in which conceptual schemas may be reshaped. As one application of this theory, Section 14.5 specifies a procedure for optimizing a database design by performing conceptual transformations before mapping. Section 14.6 provides concise coverage of normalization theory, including some new insights. Section 14.7 briefly considers denormalization and low-level optimization. Sections 14.8 and 14.9 illustrate the role of conceptual optimization in database reengineering, and conclude with a discussion of data migration and query transformation. Sections 14.4, 14.5, and 14.7–14.9 are of an advanced nature and may be skipped in a short course. In a very short course, the whole chapter could be skipped.

Chapter 15 broadens the treatment of information systems analysis by examining behavioral aspects of business using process and state models. The two main approaches of process modeling and state modeling are analyzed using their representations in UML. Detailed coverage of process modeling using the BPMN standard is provided, together with a methodology for linking process models and information models.

Chapter 16 examines various data file formats, including CSV, XML, JSON, YAML, and some other markup languages. In addition to their use for data interchange, XML and JSON are now fully incorporated into the SQL standard as data types. Examples of their use are provided together with a discussion on their mapping from ORM.

Chapter 17 reviews alternatives to the dominant relational database paradigm, in particular, “NoSQL” databases. The motivations for such systems are discussed and the major database types are described individually. Methods for mapping from an information model to each of these database types are introduced. The chapter concludes with some further ideas on future evolution, including the potential impact of artificial intelligence.

Chapter 18 examines other modeling aspects and trends. Topics covered include data warehousing, conceptual query languages, schema abstraction mechanisms, further design aspects, ontologies and the semantic web, and metamodeling. Though these topics are important and interesting, they could be omitted in a short course.

In line with the ORM method, this text adopts a “cookbook” approach, with plenty of diagrams and examples. Each chapter begins with a brief overview and ends with a chapter summary of the major points covered, with chapter notes to provide fine points and further references.

One of the major features of the book is its large number of exercises, which have been thoroughly class-tested. A bibliography of all cited references is included at the end of the book, where you will also find glossaries of technical symbols and terms for ORM, ER, and UML (class diagrams only). A comprehensive index provides easy access to explanations of technical topics.

For readers familiar with the second edition of this book, the major differences are now summarized. The coverage of ORM, ER, UML, SQL, OWL, and BPMN has been thoroughly updated to cover their latest versions. A significant amount of new material has been added. Various data file formats such as CSV, XML, JSON, YAML, and some other markup languages are now covered, and a more thorough treatment is provided for nonrelational databases, especially NoSQL. All previous chapters have been substantially revised, with several topics covered in greater depth. The new content has led to a larger book.

US spelling is used throughout the book, except for two forewords by European authors. US punctuation rules have also been used, except for quoted items, where item separators and sentence terminators (e.g., commas and periods) appear after, rather than just before, closing quotes.

Online resources

To reduce the size and cost of the book, supplementary material is available at the website https://www.elsevier.com/books-and-journals/book-companion/9780443237904 for downloading. There are five appendices.

Appendix A provides an overview of the evolution of computer hardware and software. Appendix B discusses two kinds of subtype matrix to determine subtype graphs from significant populations. Appendix C discusses set-comparison queries in SQL. Appendix D discusses ranking and extrema queries in SQL. Appendix E discusses ways to implement derivation rules in SQL using triggers, generated columns, stored procedures, views, user-defined functions, and common table expressions. Other appendices may be added as the need arises.

The answers to the exercises are contained in two files, one for the odd-numbered questions and one for the even-numbered questions. The answers to the odd-numbered questions are openly accessible, but the answers to the even-numbered questions are password protected to provide classroom instructors with a range of exercises for classroom discussion. Additional material on ORM and other topics is available via the Useful Websites section at the back of the book.

Further exercises and related pedagogic material are included in supplementary online resources that are available to instructors using this book as a course text. These resources and a password for exercise answers are available to classroom instructors at https://inspectioncopy.elsevier.com/.

ORM software

ORM is supported by a variety of modeling tools. At the time of writing, the Natural ORM Architect (NORMA) tool provides the most complete support for the ORM 2 notation discussed in this book. A free version of NORMA is available as an open source plug-in to Microsoft Visual Studio and may be downloaded from https://ormsolutions.com/ or https://sourceforge.net/projects/orm. For details on installing and using NORMA, see the NORMA labs downloadable from the Resources page at www.orm.net. The free, community version of Visual Studio is downloadable from https://visualstudio.microsoft.com/vs/community/.

NORMA Professional (NORMA Pro) has additional features such as multipage relational schemas and formal support for derivation rules. For details on how to get a licence for the professional version of NORMA, contact Matt Curland at mcurland@live.com.

Other tools supporting different flavors of fact-oriented modeling include CaseTalk, CogNIAM tools, ActiveFacts, and Boston. Links to these tools may be found in the Useful Websites section that is included at the back of this book.
