Potentially, this provides a point at which references to an ORM model could be stored, but these would only be visible in the BPMN tool being used to manage the process model and not to anyone viewing the graphical representation of the process from a business perspective. Such attributes are intended to facilitate process automation and have little relevance to modeling at a conceptual level.

An alternative approach is to introduce an intermediate stage between the BPMN model and the ORM model, forming a Process-Information Bridge (PIB). The Data Store reference can then be to a PIB element containing the relevant ORM linkage. One data item can be used in multiple activities in a process, so this also provides a location to resolve the one-to-many relationship. Fig. 15.37 shows the relevant diagram notation.

Next, we can turn to the ORM end of the relationship. In ORM (as opposed to an Entity-Attribute model), the attributes (properties) of the entity are unbundled and can be addressed in terms of separate fact types. “Entities” are formed from collections of fact types in a mapping process that produces a new model of a type defined by the mapping (for example, a relational model).

Although the unbundling of entities in ORM potentially offers a finer-grained definition of a relationship between activity and information, it is not necessarily convenient for cross-referencing of the kind we are considering. An activity is likely to require all information about an entity to be treated together rather than as isolated facts. For example, an agent updating stored data about personnel would probably expect to see all relevant information about a particular employee to be displayed at the same time. Instead of referring to individual fact types, it would be much simpler if the fact types were arranged in convenient bundles related to major entity types.

A straightforward way of achieving this is to group fact types into relations, in the sense originally expressed by Codd. Facilities already exist in ORM to produce normalized relations from an ORM model with the Rmap procedure. In a conceptual model, there is no prior commitment to a relational database solution, but this does not matter because normalized relations can be realized in other types of data structures such as XML and JSON; see Chapter 16 for more details.

A convenient data reference to a group of fact types in an information model can therefore be made by simply using the (unique) name of the relation. Accessing a particular data item during the execution of a process would require the relation name plus a key value that is unique within the relation. The same activity may access different instances of the relation in different instances (executions) of the process. However, only the relation’s name is necessary to define the linkage between a process model and an information model.

This approach would create a set of hierarchical links between the process model and the information model, as outlined in Fig. 15.38.

Each PIBRef will contain the following:

  • • An indicator showing the type of CRUD access intended in this case. The usual access will be either Read-only, where the activity is not expected to change the data, or Full, where the activity can view the data and possibly also change it. These can be indicated by a single letter (R or F, where F is a shorthand for CRUD). In the unlikely event of more specificity being necessary, then the individual letters of CRUD can be used.
  • • The identification of the ORM elements involved in this case, using relation names. More than one relation could be used in the same PIBRef. For example, an activity might involve reading from one relation and updating another.

Each set of PIBRef access/relation values is likely to appear in one PIBRef only—the same PIBRef can be reused in the process model so there would be no need to repeat it. However, if duplication is accidentally introduced, it would not be harmful, merely slightly wasteful. The general scheme is summarized in Fig. 15.39.

To illustrate some of these points, we can look at an example process model. Fig. 15.40 illustrates a simple complaints process using BPMN. After recording the complaint, the client is contacted to acknowledge receipt and the relevant department is contacted to assess the complaint. After assessment, the client is either compensated in some way or a standard letter is sent to explain the resolution. Details of the case are filed in case of any future query, and the process terminates.

To provide a concrete example of the relationship between process and information, we’ll look at the SendStandardLetter activity; a corresponding picture could be drawn for any of the other activities. We will assume that appropriate resources and manual services are available to the activity, such as printing, envelope stuffing, and franking, and focus on the information usage. Fig. 15.41 shows a fragment of an information model, including the types of facts that might be relevant to the SendStandardLetter activity.

We are assuming here that the letter consists mainly of “boilerplate” text with the client information, the case reference, and dates inserted at the appropriate points. To identify the relevant facts, the activity requires two primary objects to be identified: a Case and a LetterType. From the Case, we can uniquely identify the Client and hence the Client’s Title, Name, and Address. From the LetterType, we can identify the appropriate text to form the body of the letter. The current date is assumed to be available from the activity’s environment. This information is sufficient for the activity to create and send the standard letter.

Fig. 15.42 shows a relational view of the information. This can be used as the basis for defining the necessary bridge between process and information.

From the process perspective, the necessary link is provided by the SendLetter Data Store reference in the process model of Fig. 15.40. The SendStandardLetter activity requires Read access (R) to the LetterType, Client, and Case relations but full access (F) to the ClientWasSentLetterTypeOnDate relation. The associated PIB can be defined in a suitable editing tool, as illustrated in Fig. 15.43. This shows the four relations, with the last relation being expanded to show its attributes. This specific tool also allows the use of alternative names in the process context.

A PIB file of this kind (probably expressed in XML or JSON) is a useful resource in its own right. It provides traceability between process and information at a conceptual level. The structure can be used to answer queries such as which activities rely on a given relation, or which activities create instances of a given fact type. This can help to ensure that systems designs are coherent before embarking on implementation.

15.10 Decision Model and Notation

Simple decisions can be defined in BPMN using appropriate gateway constructs, but this becomes infeasible for more complex decisions, such as evaluating the many factors influencing the approval of a loan application. To address this need, a new standard called Decision Model and Notation (DMN) was created by OMG. The first version of the standard was proposed in 2015, but it has undergone several revisions and is expected to evolve further over time. DMN is intended to be used in conjunction with BPMN in processes involving complex decisions.

The basis of a decision is the evaluation of some given input data against predefined business logic. A decision involving many factors may be broken down into a set of subdecisions combined to give the final result. DMN provides a graphical notation to show the linking of data (including intermediate results) and decision logic blocks. Here, diagrams only show how the logic is organized for human convenience. The real definition of the decision lies in the business logic contained in the blocks. DMN provides two means of expressing this logic: decision tables and a special expression language.

A decision table shows a list of input/output conditions indicating the output that results from a specific set of inputs. The table contains all possible combinations of input values. A row of the table contains columns for input values, corresponding outputs, and optional annotations. If more convenient, the orientation of the table can be changed by switching rows and columns.

As an alternative, DMN provides a language for defining business logic called Friendly Enough Expression Language (FEEL). This is claimed to be “friendly enough” for nontechnical business people to understand. It provides a collection of operators and functions that can be used to specify how a conclusion can be reached from a combination of input data. These are organized into “boxed expressions” that can be nested in complex cases.

The decision logic is invoked from BPMN through a special “Business Rule” activity type. Although the logic may be complex, the result is often very simple, for example, just a “yes” or “no” value. Activities that follow later in the process can use the decision result to influence the path taken, possibly using an appropriate gateway element.

Because DMN is an adjunct to BPMN, it requires no additional treatment from a conceptual modeling perspective. A general approach to combining ORM, BPMN, and DMN is outlined in Fig. 15.44.

Broadly speaking, the relevant information from an ORM model is marshaled together using the Process-Information bridge approach discussed above. A Business Rule activity invokes the decision at the appropriate point in the process. The decision logic to be applied at that point is expressed in DMN, referring to the available information used as inputs to the decision and defining the decision outcome (which may or may not be stored persistently). DMN is still a relatively young standard, and further revisions can be expected in the future.

15.11 Summary

ORM provides a powerful methodology and notation for capturing the structure of information at a conceptual (i.e., implementation-free) level. From an ORM model, one can infer some partial ordering on the dynamics of the information. For example, information on mandatory fact types associated with a primary object type must be available no later than the time at which that object type is instantiated. References between primary fact types must be ordered in a way that maintains referential integrity—in a database system, these typically appear as foreign key references.

However, these limited constraints fall far short of a definition of a process. Some other forms of expression are necessary to define explicitly the intentions of a business in executing its activities. Business process models provide one way of doing this; state models provide another. Nor does ORM provide any way of expressing other aspects of process elements, such as the resources involved. This is not a criticism of ORM: it’s just that a description of a business involves many aspects in addition to the structure of the information it uses.

Clearly, it may be appropriate to consider a business from many different perspectives, but these different points of view must be reconciled because they are ultimately an expression of the same business system. Trying to model these different perspectives with ORM alone would be like trying to model an object-oriented system in UML and being limited to using only class diagrams. This implies a multi-viewpoint approach to business modeling. However, combining different perspectives does not mean using independent models, as we are really talking about different views onto one common model.

Both process models and state models can be used to express behavioral aspects. The techniques that they embody have evolved in similar ways because they have responded to the same pressures, such as the need to deal with large, complex sets of activities. UML includes both activity and state modeling, but its use in business modeling is compromised by its primary orientation toward defining software artifacts.

Standards are becoming more important in process modeling. Informal standards, such as the popularly quoted workflow patterns, have helped establish a better understanding of important features of business processes. Standards of a more official kind, such as BPMN and DMN, are helping facilitate the uptake of process modeling by businesses of all kinds.

Chapter Notes

Rummler and Brache (1995), Burlton (2001), and many others have described methodologies for capturing business process definitions, and Hammer (1997) and others have emphasized the restructuring of businesses around processes. Havey (2005) gives a broad summary of several business process modeling approaches. A good introduction to Workflow is given by van der Aalst and van Hee (2004). Many valuable contributions to state modeling have been made by David Harel; see for example Harel and Politi (1998). The systematic modeling of business processes remains an area of great interest in information technology. Several standardization initiatives continue within organizations such as the Object Management Group (OMG) and the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C), including the Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN), Business Process Definition Metamodel (BPDM), Business Process Maturity Model (BPMM), Decision Model and Notation (DMN), the Business Motivation Model (BMM), and many others, including related initiatives in the area of web services. The latest public information on OMG standards (BPMN, DMN, etc., and UML) can be found at www.omg.org. Members of OMG also have access to the latest work in progress on each of the standards. The relevant W3C standards relating to process orchestration and process choreography can be accessed at www.w3c.org. The use of UML for business modeling is discussed by Eriksson and Penker (2000). Lassen and van der Aalst (2006) and Ouyang et al. (2006) discuss techniques for translating workflow processes to BPEL. Many papers have used the “classic” workflow patterns defined by van der Aalst, ter Hofstede, and others, and there is a workflow patterns website (www.workflowpatterns.com). This provides detailed descriptions with a Petri-net orientation. Additional discussion of state modeling and ORM is given in Morgan (2006).

16 Data File Formats

Abstract

This chapter covers various data file formats including CSV, XML, JSON, YAML, and some other markup languages. In addition to their use for data interchange, XML and JSON have been incorporated into the structured query language standard as data types. Examples of their use are provided together with a discussion on their mapping from object-role modeling.

Keywords

CSV; XML; JSON; YAML; Markup; SQL/XML; SQL/JSON

16.1 External Data Structures

Previous chapters have made the implicit assumption that data will be stored in a database system of some kind, such as a relational database. In this chapter, we consider how data can be represented in a way that's independent of a particular type of data store. This may be necessary when we need to transfer data between different systems. If the transfer takes place between two systems of the same kind, we can make use of any functionality built into the system. As examples, we can use a server-to-server replication mechanism, or restore a backup made on one server onto a different server. But these approaches will not usually work between two unlike systems, even if they are of the same general kind. For instance, a backup copy made on SQL Server cannot be restored on an Oracle system. We also need to be aware of possible interchange between different kinds of systems, such as a database management system and a spreadsheet.

A widely used and long-established approach is to use comma-separated values, typically referred to as a “CSV file”. This is a simple file format used to store tabular data in a plain text format. In a CSV file, each line of text represents a record, with the fields in each record being separated by commas. This structure is roughly equivalent to the values in a single table in a relational database. Tab-separated values are a close cousin; as the name suggests, the separator between fields here is a tab character instead of a comma. If the data itself contains delimiter characters (comma, tab, newline), additional measures such as quoting or escaping are needed.

The main advantage of a CSV file is its simplicity. The file can be opened and edited with any text editor, and the structure is easy to understand, just rows and columns (though the columns may not be obvious because of different field lengths in different rows). CSV files are widely supported by a variety of applications, including spreadsheets, programming languages, and databases. They are quite compact because they consist mainly of data with only a minimal set of delimiter characters. Because they contain no information about how the data might be stored, they are a popular choice for straightforward data transfer between different kinds of systems. Text files of this kind can also be used as simple databases when partnered with an appropriate query facility, such as the venerable AWK language found in the UNIX environment.

However, this same lack of structure limits the expressiveness of the format. There's no built-in way to include metadata about the data or the file itself. There's no way of defining data types. Most important of all, there's no way of expressing even moderately complex structures or relationships.

The need to address these issues has promoted interest in more sophisticated representations. Two major alternatives have emerged: the eXtensible Markup Language (XML) and JavaScript Object Notation (JSON). Both are in widespread use, especially for the transfer of structured data between systems, though they can both be used as information stores in their own right. They share some common features.

  1. 1. They are text-based. Like CSV files, XML and JSON files can be opened and edited with a simple text editor. However, the complexity of the structure can make this a daunting task. It's very easy to make editing errors that render the structure invalid, and it's difficult to visualize the structure unless it is laid out appropriately. For this reason, it's common to use special editors that are sensitive to the conventions of the notation. The result, though, is still just text, which can be stored and retrieved using standard facilities.
  2. 2. They are hierarchical. Elements can contain other elements (recursively), which results in the data being contained in a tree-like structure. This is the case even when the original data is not a natural hierarchy. An inevitable consequence is the possibility of data duplication, which will need to be managed, either in a data store or in applications that use the data.
  3. 3. They use a “bracketed” notation. Data elements are contained within a matching pair of opening and closing delimiters such as < x >, ( x ), [ x ], or { x }. Nested elements must be wholly contained, so < x < y >> may be valid, but <x < > y > is definitely not.
  4. 4. They are nondeterminative, in the sense that the same data structure could be represented in different, but equally valid, ways. For example, in XML a data item could appear as the value of an attribute or the content of an element. The choice between these can be guided by some high-level nonspecific policies or by the intended use of the data, but this is not enforced by any language constraints or tools. This is different from the application of normalization rules in a relational scenario.

Although both XML and JSON are text-based, in structured query language (SQL) terms, they can also be considered as complex data types alongside BLOB, DATETIME, etc., and both have been adopted as such within the SQL standard. XML was added as a data type in SQL:2003. JSON was introduced through text operations in SQL:2016, and as a data type in SQL:2023. Using a built-in data type instead of text has some advantages. Validation is simpler, some operations are more efficient, and the overhead of conversion can be avoided when the input or output is required to be in XML or JSON form. In this chapter, we will focus mainly on how XML and JSON can be used for the representation of structured data.

16.2 XML

XML is a key member of a family of standards produced by the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C). Version 1.0 first appeared in 1998, with Version 1.1 following in 2004. Several subsequent revisions have corrected errata and provided clarifications. The growth of WWW systems using HTML (itself introduced in 1993) exposed the need for a language that provided a stronger way of representing structured data to support seamless data exchange, transformation, and interoperability across different systems and platforms, and also to allow for extensions to customize the language for specific applications.

There are several other standards relating to XML. In addition to XML itself (and its relationship to SQL), we will limit our main discussion in this chapter to the following:

XPath. This is an expression language that provides a means of hierarchic addressing of the nodes in an XML tree. As well as modeling the tree structure of XML, the data model also includes atomic values, function items, and sequences.

XQuery. This is a query language designed to be broadly applicable across many types of XML data sources, including structured and semistructured documents, relational databases, and object repositories. XQuery uses the structure of XML intelligently to express queries across all these kinds of data, whether physically stored in XML or viewed as XML via middleware.

These both depend in turn on the XQuery and XPath Data Model. This defines the information contained in the input to a query processor and all permissible values of expressions in the XQuery and XPath languages. Both languages have been extended to provide support for JSON as well as XML.

The data structure for a particular universe of discourse (UoD) can be defined by a schema. The XML Schema standard provides a means of defining the structure, content, and semantics of XML documents. It replaces the earlier document type definitions (DTDs) used to define structure. An XML document can be validated against a schema to ensure that its structure is consistent. Like SQL, XML defines a variety of data types, although these do not correspond exactly. The SQL specification (part 14) defines a mapping between XML Schema and SQL datatypes, but XML Schema is a complex topic, and we will not examine it in detail in this chapter.

XML Structure

The crucial distinction between relational and XML data is that XML structure is inherently hierarchical. This is a consequence of the expression of the structure as items embedded within other items. Fig. 16.1 illustrates this with a simple list of items. XML has a more complex syntax, but the principle is the same. As the figure shows, a natural interpretation of embedding one item within another is that a contained item becomes a child of the containing item.

Interestingly, early hierarchical database systems were commercially successful—with IBM’s IMS being a prominent example—before they became overtaken by later developments. The rigidity of these earlier hierarchical systems proved to be uncompetitive against alternatives (especially the relational model) and so they became obsolete. XML does not set out to imitate these earlier systems, but there seems to be something compelling about the hierarchical notion that just won’t go away. Some differences in structure between relational and XML structure are summarized in Table 16.1.

Table 16.1

Some differences between relational and XML structured data.

The directory structure of most operating systems provides a familiar example of a hierarchy. Even in a graphical interface, we have become used to a system of “folders” that can contain a combination of other “folders” and leaf nodes called “files”. The file system analogy is particularly relevant here because the XPath/XQuery expressions used to navigate the XML structures resemble the textual commands used to navigate directory structures in environments that aren’t based on a graphical user interface (GUI). The basic hierarchy concepts are shown in Fig. 16.2.

We’re going to be navigating from node Q, which provides the “context” for our path expression. Node Q might be at the top of the hierarchy we’re considering, in which case it can be taken to represent the whole of our XML document. Apart from that special case, we can always go up one level from Q to the node P, the parent of Q. If Q has siblings (nodes that also have the parent P), we can navigate sideways. If Q has children, then we can navigate down. Some combination of up/sideways/down movements can take us to a new node. Once we get there, the newly selected node can become the context for some other navigation.

Most of the time, we’re going to be concerned with relationships between XML elements, so, for example, we might want to know about all elements that are “contained in” element Q (i.e., they are descendent nodes of the node Q). But we might also want to know about all elements that have some specific attribute, all elements related to some specific namespace, and so on. All these possible dimensions are known in XPath/XQuery as axes, and the languages provide a sophisticated notation for the precise definition of navigation along various combinations of axes. Unfortunately, the full notation is a little cumbersome. Fortunately, there are short-form notations that cover the main possibilities, and we’ll concentrate on those.

Nodes or “Elements” are identified in XML with a pair of named tags (opening and closing). Nodes can have zero or more attributes, which are listed in the opening tag. Each opened tag must ultimately be closed after all the content of the tag has been listed. The following XML expression shows an example:

       <movie movieNr=“1”> <title> Cosmology </title> </movie>

Here, we have a tag named “movie” with one attribute, movieNr, that contains data. It contains another tag named title, which itself contains some data. The closing tag repeats the tag name preceded by a solidus or slash character. Optionally, elements that contain no other elements can be closed with just a single solidus character following any attributes, as in the following.

       <movie movieNr=“1” />

The guidelines for choosing between attribute or element content as the location for data are a little vague. Broadly speaking, attributes are supposed to be for intrinsic properties of the node, but this is open to interpretation. It's certainly true that the following representation is just as valid, syntactically, as the first.

       <movie title=“Cosmology”> <movieNr> 1 </movieNr> </movie>

In many cases, finding a path to the relevant node or nodes is all that's necessary to extract relevant data from XML. The required path can be specified using an XPath expression. To provide some concrete examples, we’ll return to the Movies example from Chapter 1. There, we saw how the content of a report could be captured as relational tables. Listing 16.1 shows similar information (with slightly different data from the example in Chapter 1). The initial tag simply identifies this as an XML document. This listing is a lot more verbose than an equivalent rendering in, say, a CSV file, but that's the price that must be paid to achieve the expressiveness necessary to represent complex data structures.

Navigation is relative to a given node in an XPath sequence. The basic navigational notation resembles that of a conventional file system. A period or full stop “ . ” means “the current node”, “ .. ” means “the parent of the current node”. A slash or solidus character “ / ” without further qualification means “go down one level”; “ // ” means go down any number of levels. Names are taken to refer to elements unless prefixed with “@”, in which case they refer to attributes. At any step in the path, a predicate can be introduced in square brackets. This will filter the resulting nodes, so only those for which the predicate is “True” will be included. Table 16.2 shows some typical expressions that use these concepts.

Table 16.2

Example path expressions.

Now that we have some idea of how to move around an XML hierarchy, we can consider how to query XML data. In simple cases, the result of the path expression may be sufficient, but in general, we will need more powerful expressions. This need is met by XQuery, a language for manipulating XML values. Roughly speaking, XQuery is partnered with XML data in the same way that SQL is partnered with relational data. Like SQL, XQuery is declarative. It expresses the data sources and the processing rules to be applied, but it does not specify the explicit procedure by which the results should be produced.

XQuery is a functional language, so we must specify what we want to do in functional terms. Most software developers are familiar with the concept of a function. A function has a name, zero or more input parameters, and a body that computes some result to be returned. From a functional programming perspective, the arguments to a function can be constants, or the results produced by other functions (i.e., a parameter can be a call to another function). Now, we have another hierarchy: functions that provide results to functions that provide … and so on. This function hierarchy may be established dynamically and may bear no direct relationship to the data hierarchy. The top level of the function hierarchy computes the result we are seeking; the lower-level functions provide results to their parents to (ultimately) enable the top-level computation. XQuery defines more than a hundred built-in functions, but commercial systems may not yet implement all of these.

XQuery allows information to be combined from multiple sources and restructured to produce a new result. The most common expressions of this kind in XQuery are called FLWOR expressions, from the first letter of the types of clauses that may appear in the expression: for, let, where, order by, and return. FLWOR expressions are the XQuery equivalent of select statements in SQL.

The clauses in a FLWOR expression are defined in terms of tuples. The tuples are created by binding variables to values in for and/or let clauses, so every FLWOR expression must have at least one for or let clause. The difference between the two is that for iterates over the items in an expression, producing a tuple for each, and let produces one tuple for the entire result of an expression. As a simple example, the following FLWOR expression produces the same result as the last path example in Table 16.2. The dollar sign “$” indicates a variable in XQuery.

for $m in moviewhere $m/star = “Tom Hanks”return $m/released

As a slightly more complex example, let’s assume that we want to invert the hierarchy of the source XML. For our Movies XML fragment, we could list the movies in which an actor starred under each actor, instead of listing the stars under each movie. An expression in XQuery to do this might look like the following:

for $s in distinct-values ( movie/star )order by $s descendingreturn   <starring>      <actor> { $s } </actor>      <movies> { for $m in movie where $m/star = $s return $m/title } </movies>   </starring>

Here, we’ve used the distinct-values ( ) function to make sure that each actor only appears once and sorted the result in descending order of actor name. The query contains constructors, indicated by braces around an inner expression, which are used to build element content. Evaluating the query produces the result:

 <starring>    <actor>Tom Hanks</actor>    <movies>      <title>The Da Vinci Code</title>      <title>Cast Away</title>    </movies> </starring> <starring>    <actor>Stephen Chow</actor>    <movies>      <title>Kung Fu Hustle</title>    </movies> </starring> …etc.

Of course, we’re not limited to using a single XML document or fragment. Let’s say we have some XML data containing reviews of the movies, like the example shown in Listing 16.2.

The reviews are related to the movies by the unique movieNr reference. In standard SQL, if we wanted to show the movie titles along with the rating scores for each movie, we could use a join. We can do the same kind of thing in XQuery.

Here’s one way of doing the equivalent of an inner join.

  • for $m in movie
  • where some $r in review satisfies( $m/@movieNr = $r/movieNr )
  • return
  •    <reviewscore>
  •           { $m/title, $m/released }
  •           { for $r in review where $m/@movieNr = $r/movieNr return $r/rating }
  •    </reviewscore>

The query includes the release year as well as the title to avoid ambiguities between movies with the same name. The “where some … satisfies (…)” construct is an existential quantifier test so that we only get results for movies that have had a review. The query produces the following result:

 <reviewscore>   <title>The Secret Garden</title>   <released>1993</released>   <rating>4</rating> </reviewscore> <reviewscore>   <title>The Da Vinci Code</title>   <released>2006</released>   <rating>4</rating>   <rating>5</rating>   <rating>1</rating> </reviewscore>

To get the equivalent of an outer join, which would also include the movies with no reviews, we would simply need to omit the existential quantifier test in the second line of the query.

As a final XQuery example, we’ll show the equivalents of the aggregate or bag functions in SQL, which include sum( ), count( ), avg( ), max( ), and min( ). Let’s suppose we want to produce a summary element for each movie, showing the total number of reviews and the average score as attributes. The following query would be one way of producing the required result.

for $m in moviereturn <reviewsummary total = “{ count ( review [ movieNr = $m/@movieNr ] ) }”   avg = “{ avg ( review [ movieNr = $m/@movieNr]/rating ) }” >  { $m/title, $m/released } </reviewsummary>

Here, we’ve used the XQuery functions count( ) and avg( ), which operate in a similar way to their SQL counterparts. For an empty list of elements (in this case, movies that have no reviews), the count( ) function returns zero and the avg( ) function returns an empty result. Running the query produces the following XML fragment:

 <reviewsummary total=“0” avg=“”>   <title>Cosmology</title>   <released>2006</released> </reviewsummary> <reviewsummary total=“0” avg=“”>   <title>Kung Fu Hustle</title>   <released>2004</released> </reviewsummary> <reviewsummary total=“0” avg=“”>   <title>The Secret Garden</title>   <released>1987</released> </reviewsummary> <reviewsummary total=“1” avg=“4”>   <title>The Secret Garden</title>   <released>1993</released> </reviewsummary> <reviewsummary total=“3” avg=“3.33333333333333”>   <title>The Da Vinci Code</title>   <released>2006</released> </reviewsummary> <reviewsummary total=“0” avg=“”>   <title>Cast Away</title>   <released>2000</released> </reviewsummary>

XQuery has many other features, and a more complete description would require a book in its own right. Some references to further information sources are included in the chapter notes.

We can also work with XML values using a standard programming language. Library functions are available for most languages to allow an XML processor to be incorporated into a program. Two types are available. The first, usually known as a DOM processor, loads the complete Document Object Model into an internal program structure. From there, various functions can be used to navigate through the model to extract tags and attributes as individual items or lists within the program. Because the whole DOM is in memory, this is convenient and reasonably efficient, but there is going to be some upper limit on the size of the XML file that can be loaded.

The alternative is usually referred to as a SAX processor (Simple API for XML). This uses a different event-based strategy to process an XML file. As the XML document is read, each significant item (such as a start tag) is sent to the program where it can be stored for later use or processed immediately. The important distinction is that the entire document does not need to be stored in memory, and so there is no upper limit on document size. The disadvantage is that it is more difficult to carry out operations that require references back and forth between various parts of the model.

SQL/XML

SQL:2003 introduced XML as a new built-in data type. XML data is strongly typed, as XML values are assumed to be tree-like data structures that are distinct from their representation in the form of a text string. The XML type can be used wherever other SQL types are allowed, such as in table columns, as parameters of a routine, as variables, and so on. Although relational data and XML data are both structured, there are some significant differences between them. Table 16.3 (repeated from Table 16.1) identifies some key points.

Table 16.3

Some differences between relational and XML structured data.

XML data can be stored in a database either in a text column (i.e., char, varchar, or clob) or in a column of data type xml. A textual representation might be preferred if it is important to retain the textual fidelity of a document (which may include text that has no relevance to the data structure) or if the XML is always entered and retrieved as a complete document. However, storing the data in an XML column allows efficient processing of the XML data in the database, rather than in a middle-tier application.

In addition to the XML data type, the SQL:2003 standard also introduced some related features, such as new XML operators, functions, and rules for mapping between SQL concepts and XML concepts. Most vendors broadly support these features or their equivalents, but the need to integrate the additional XML features into different preexisting frameworks has inevitably resulted in some differences in syntactic detail. The fact that XML support is an area of keen competition for vendors is also likely to produce a variety of nonstandard extensions. The picture is further complicated by the need for interoperability with other standards, such as XQuery. Fortunately, this competition is limited to the variety of operators, functions, and so on that are provided to integrate XML with SQL. The standards governing the structure of XML data are defined outside SQL, and so the XML values themselves are reasonably consistent from one database system to another.

In 2006, the part of the SQL standard dealing with XML (Part 14) was revised and extended to consolidate the features of SQL/XML, as it has come to be called. (The standard is sometimes referred to as SQL:2006, although this is a little misleading because only the XML part was revised in 2006.) Here, we will use SQL/XML:2006 to specifically distinguish the more recent version where necessary.

In SQL/XML:2006, the xml data type is based on the XQuery data model.17

A sequence containing exactly one document node is termed XML content, with the type modifier xml(content). A special type of content is where the document node contains exactly one element node (plus, possibly comment and processing instruction nodes), and this is termed an XML document, with the type modifier xml(document).

A secondary modifier can be added for xml(content) and xml(document) to indicate whether the content or document can contain both typed and untyped elements (any), only untyped elements (untyped), or elements defined by a schema (schema name). If a schema is defined, the element and attribute nodes are guaranteed to be valid according to the schema. These distinctions are summarized in Fig. 16.3. If the type xml is specified without a modifier, any default assumption about these more specialized subtypes is implementation-dependent.

The SQL:2003 standard introduced the predicate is document to test whether an XML expression is a document. The basic syntax is:

   xmlexpression is [ not ] document

Although the syntax of the predicate remained unchanged from SQL:2003, the meaning shifted somewhat because of the realignment of SQL/XML:2006 with the XQuery data model. Three more predicates were added: is content, xmlexists, and is valid. The is content predicate tests whether an XML expression is legitimate XML content, using the syntax:

   xmlexpression is [ not ] content

To test whether an expression contains valid XML, the xmlexists predicate can be used. The syntax, simplified a little, is as follows:

xmlexists ( XQuery-expression  [ passing value-expression  [ as identifier ] [ { by ref | by value } ] ] [,…] )

If the XQuery evaluation is of a value that turns out to be null (perhaps passed as an argument from SQL), then the predicate result is unknown. For nonnull values, if the XQuery evaluation returns an empty sequence, the predicate’s value is false; otherwise, the result is true. The following example shows the use of xmlexists in a select statement to retrieve “id” values for customers in a given city, with the customer details being stored in a column of the xml type.

select c.custId from customer as cwhere xmlexists ( ‘ $d/*:customerinfo/*:addr [ *:city = “Salt Lake City” ] ’passing info as “d” )

The is valid predicate checks to see if an XML value is valid according to a given XML schema. The details of validity assessment are a little complex and are not covered here. The simplified syntax is:

 xml-value-expression is [ not ] valid   [ identity-constraint-option ]   [ according to xmlschema { uri | registered-name } ]   [ valid-element-clause ]

The xml-value-expression is checked according to the schema identified by the choice of namespace. If none is specified, each element is validated according to the schema associated with its namespace. If specified, the schema can be identified either by URI or by its registered name. The optional identity-constraint-option and valid-element-clause parameters provide for a more detailed specification of exactly how schema checking should be done.

Several built-in XML operators were introduced in the SQL:2003 standard. One of the operators, xmlroot, could be used to modify the version and standalone properties of an XML expression, but this was removed in SQL/XML:2006 so we don’t cover it here.

The first two SQL/XML operations we’ll look at, xmlparse and xmlserialize, convert back and forth between structured and string representations of XML. The xmlparse operation takes an SQL string expression and produces the equivalent XML structure. A parameter defines whether the string expression is expected to represent a document or content. The basic syntax has remained consistent since SQL:2003.

xmlparse ( { document | content } stringexpression [ { preserve | strip } whitespace ] )

The result of the operation could be assigned to a variable of type xml or stored in an xml column. The precise way in which whitespace is handled is by xmlparse, which is subject to detailed rules that are not considered here.

The xmlserialize operation performs the inverse of xmlparse, producing a string version of a given XML expression. The SQL standard does not mandate the precise format of the resulting string, but does require that a subsequent xmlparse of a string produced by xmlserialize should reproduce the original XML expression. In other words, given an XML document called myXmlData, the following construct:

xmlparse ( document ( xmlserialize ( document myXmlData as varchar ( max ) ) ) )

should produce a result equal to myXmlData. The original SQL:2003 syntax of xmlserialize was extended in SQL/XML:2006.

xmlserialize ( { document | content } xmlexpression as SQLdatatype   [ version string ]   [ including xmldeclaration | excluding xmldeclaration ] )

The SQL datatype for the result could be any SQL string type (such as char, varchar), but serialized XML tends to be lengthy, so a character large object (clob) type is likely to be a common choice. Optionally, including xmldeclaration prepends the XML declaration “< ?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"? >” to the result; the default is excluding xmldeclaration. The XML version can also be separately specified; at present, this will be limited to “1.0”.

The xmlconcat operation introduced in SQL:2003 was retained in SQL:2006. It simply concatenates a list of XML expressions, producing a new XML expression.

xmlconcat ( xmlexpression [, …]  [ returning { content | sequence } ] )

The optional returning clause was added in SQL/XML:2006. If this is omitted, it is implementation-defined whether returning content or sequence is implicit.

The SQL:2003 standard defined several “publishing” functions to generate XML expressions from SQL expressions. These were extended in SQL/XML:2006, and new functions were added. Here, we cover only the SQL/XML:2006 definitions of the functions.

The xmlelement function is used to create an XML element from a given set of parameters. Recall that an XML element has the basic form:

   <tagname optionalAttributes>  optionalElementContent </tagname>

So, for example, an element representing a customer might look something like:

   <cust custid = “1234”> Widgets Inc </cust>

If required, the tagname can be further qualified by prefixing it with a namespace, in which case the namespace URI must also be specified. The xmlelement function constructs an individual XML element from the parameters provided and returns it as an xml value. The basic syntax for character strings is shown here. There is also a variant for binary strings that we won’t consider.

The embedded xmlnamespaces and xmlattributes functions are optionally used in the context of a given element to add any required namespace declarations or attributes to the element. The element content is defined by a list of expressions that is optional, so it’s possible to create an empty element. Also optional is the returning clause, which we’ve already seen.

xmlelement ( name xmlelementname   [ , xmlnamespaces (namespace-declaration-item [,…] ) ]   [ , xmlattributes ( attributevalue [as attributename ] [,…] )  [ , elementcontent [,…]  [ option { null on null | empty on null | absent on null | nil on null | nil on no content } ] ]  [ returning { content | sequence } ] )

The content option requires a little more explanation. In SQL, a missing optional value is explicitly marked as null. This is not a value recognized in XML, although null is legitimate for the SQL xml data type. Depending on the desired result, a missing value could be indicated in XML by simply omitting the relevant element or by including the element begin/end tags with no contained value. If an explicit indicator equivalent to null is required, a further option is the “nil” mechanism specified in the “XML Schema For Instances” namespace. The namespace is typically introduced with a declaration such as:

  •    xmlns:xsi = “http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance”

The xsi prefix is used by convention, but some other prefix could be substituted. Once this is defined, the nil attribute defined in XMLSchema-instance can be set to True.

   <myElement xsi:nil = “true”></myElement>

An element attributed in this way may not have any element content but may still carry other attributes. The SQL:2003 standard acknowledged the xsi:nil option, but did not prescribe how this should be specified in conjunction with operations such as xmlelement. SQL/XML:2006 provided close control over these choices, as summarized in Table 16.4.

Table 16.4

Options for handling null and nil.

As a simple example of the use of xmlelement, consider a Customers table that is purely relational (it contains no XML). We could produce a result table containing a mixture of relational data and XML representing selected customer information in the following way:

select c.id,xmlelement( name “cust”, xmlattributes (c.id as “custid”), custName) as Xcustfrom Customers as c where custid = 1234

which would produce a result such as:

where the data contained in the Xcust column is of type xml. Calls to xmlelement can be nested so that elements can be created within elements, producing the characteristic hierarchical structure of XML.

The xmlforest function is a convenient way of applying xmlconcat to a sequence of xmlelement results: it produces a sequence of elements from a list of expressions. The elements can be named explicitly or implicitly. As with xmlelement, calls to xmlforest can also be nested. The basic syntax is as follows:

xmlforest ( [ xmlnamespaces (namespace-declaration-item , ), ]elementvalue [ as elementname ] [,…] [ option { null on null | empty on null | absent on null | nil on null | nil on no content } ] ] [ returning { content | sequence } ] )

The parameters are used in the same way as xmlelement. For example,

select o.orderId, xmlelement ( name “order”,  xmlforest ( o.custName as “customer”, o.date ) ) as Xorderfrom Orders as o        where orderid > 9800

would produce a result such as:

If preservation of the case in SQL names is important, they should be aliased as delimited identifiers. Regular identifiers are likely to be mapped to all uppercase in some implementations. For example, the date element in the example just given could appear as <DATE> … </DATE> instead of <date> … </date>.

An equivalent result table could be produced in SQL Server as follows:

select o.orderId, (select o,custName ‘customer', o.date 'date'from orders as ofor xml path (‘order'), type) as Xorderfrom orders as owhere orderid > 9800

SQL Server uses various for xml … constructs to convert relational data to XML. The for xml path variant gives full control over how the XML structure is to be generated on a column-by-column basis. The type parameter specifies that the result should be of type xml, as opposed to its string equivalent.

Returning to SQL/XML, the xmlagg function is an aggregate function, similar to SQL’s sum, avg, etc. It returns a single value from a given bag of values, which must be the result of an xml type expression. The resulting xml values are concatenated to produce a single xml value. Optionally, an order by clause can be used to order the results before concatenating, using a similar syntax to SQL. Any null produced is dropped before concatenating. If all the results of the expression are null, or the bag is empty, the result of the xmlagg function is the null value. The basic syntax is as follows:

xmlagg ( XML-value-expression [ order by sort-specification ] [ returning { content | sequence } ] )

As an example of the xmlagg function, suppose we have an “Orders” table and want to group by customer, showing, for each customer, an element for each order placed by that customer. For simplicity, we’ll just assume that both orders and customers are represented by a simple ID value. We could construct the result as follows:

select xmlelement  ( name “Customer”, xmlattributes ( o.custId as “customerId” ),xmlagg ( xmlelement ( name “order”, o.orderId )order by o.orderId ) ) as XcustOrdersfrom Orders as ogroup by o.custId

which would give a result resembling:

The xmlpi function generates a single XQuery processing instruction node, as follows:

xmlpi ( name target [ , string-expression ] [  returning { content | sequence } ] )

The target identifier (name) cannot be ‘xml’ (in any case combination) and the string expression cannot contain the substring ‘?>’. The xmlcomment and xmltext functions are also straightforward, each simply producing a node of the appropriate type. Here are some examples of the use of these functions.

  •    xmlpi ( name “Warning”, “Turn off now” )          produces          <?Warning Turn off now?>
  •    xmlcomment ( “This is my comment” )               produces                 <!-- This is my comment -->
  •    xmltext ( “Here is my text” )                                produces          Here is my text

The xmldocument function returns a document node (as defined by the XQuery data model) that has the given XML value as its content. This is useful for converting an arbitrary XQuery sequence into an XML document.

xmldocument ( xmlvalue [  returning { content | sequence } ] )

A separate casting function, xmlcast, is provided for casting to and from XML values. This works in the same way as the standard SQL cast function, except that at least one of the data types involved must be xml. It’s also possible to cast between the subtypes of xml, subject to certain rules that we won’t go into here. Note that casting backward and forward between XML values and strings is not the same as using the xmlparse and xmlserialize functions.

Like the valid predicate, the xmlvalidate function ensures that a given XML expression is valid according to the related schema definitions. As with the valid predicate, schemas can optionally be explicitly specified. However, unlike the valid predicate, the xmlvalidate function also persistently annotates the XML expression with type information. The syntax is:

xmlvalidate( { document | content | sequence } xmlexpression [ according to xmlschema { uri | registered-name } ] [ valid-element-clause ] )

We saw earlier how the xmlnamespaces function could be used in the context of xmlelement and xmlforest functions. A more complete syntax for xmlnamespaces is:

xmlnamespaces ( { XML-namespace-URI as namespace-prefix |default XML-namespace-URI | no default } [,…] )

The default option applies the namespace definition to any nested elements, unless overridden by a lower-level no default. Similarly, the no default option can be overridden by a lower-level default. The default and the no default options can be specified at most once in an xmlnamespaces argument list.

The SQL:2003 standard introduced an extensive set of mapping rules to define how SQL entities map from SQL to XML (and the reverse). The specification of the rules is quite extensive, and some aspects are implementation-dependent, so we won’t cover all the details here. Broadly speaking, SQL data types are mapped to the closest equivalent type defined in XML Schema. XML Schema facets and annotations can be used to indicate distinctions in certain areas, For example, basic XML Schema does not distinguish between character varying and character large object, which are distinct types in SQL. Delimited identifiers in SQL are mapped as defined, preserving the upper/lower case of characters. Case is not guaranteed to be preserved for regular identifiers.

Some special treatment is given to characters that would result in illegal names in XML. The general technique is to replace the character by _xNNNN_ or _xNNNNNN_, where N is a hexadecimal digit and NNNN or NNNNNN is the Unicode representation of the character. There are two variants of the identifier mapping: partially escaped and fully escaped. The key differences between these are in the treatment of noninitial colons and identifiers beginning with the letters “xml” (in any combination of uppercase or lowercase). The differences are summarized in the examples in Table 16.5.

Table 16.5

Mapping SQL identifiers to XML.

Using XQuery

One of the most important aspects introduced in SQL/XML:2006 was the ability to integrate XQuery into the established relational database framework–a key motivator in moving SQL/XML to the XQuery data model. One point of caution: if you have a background in SQL, you will need to remember that, unlike SQL, XQuery is case-sensitive, and so care is needed in specifying expressions. It’s also important to keep in mind that in SQL/XML, we will be operating on XML values and not their serialized representations. So, for example, we’re not trying to textually process “angle brackets”, although these may be useful in denoting structures for human readability.

Finally, we’ll look at some mechanisms provided in SQL/XML that help integrate XQuery into the relational framework. The most important of these is the xmlquery function, which allows an XQuery expression to be evaluated from within an SQL context. SQL alone cannot operate on parts of an XML document: the whole document is treated as a single value. With the xmlquery function, it’s possible to query inside an XML document so that XML data can participate in SQL queries and SQL processing can be applied to returned XML values (for instance, using order by to order the results). The basic syntax of xmlquery is as follows. The arguments are used in a similar way to the equivalents we have already seen in other functions.

xmlquery ( XQuery-expression [ passing [ { by ref | by value } ] XML-query-argument [,…] ] [ returning { content | sequence } ] [ { by ref | by value } ] [ { null on empty | empty on empty } ] )

Another function, xmltable, provides a useful way to integrate XQuery results back into SQL. Normally, an XQuery expression would return a sequence, but by using xmltable, we can execute an XQuery expression and return values as a table instead. The returned table can contain columns of any SQL data type, including XML, although values inserted into xml columns in xmltable must be well-formed with a single root node. The basic syntax is:

xmltable ( [ xmlnamespaces ( namespace-declaration-item [,…] ), ] row-pattern [ passing [ { by ref | by value } ] XMLquery-argument [,…] ]columns { { colname for ordinality | colname datatype [ by ref | by value ] path column-pattern} [,…] } )

The row-pattern defines an expression that produces a sequence of elements. Each element in this sequence will become a row in the resulting table. The columns clause lists the column definitions and the path expression used to find the column value within each element of the row-pattern. The for ordinality option creates a column with an automatic ordinal reference to the row, so the first row is 1, the second row 2, and so on. An example is shown here. This assumes that we have an xml value called movieXML, the contents of which are similar to the examples we used when discussing XQuery. If this xmltable function call is contained in a select statement, the value being passed could be selected from a suitable xml column in a table.

xmltable (‘//movies'passing movieXMLcolumns “Seqno” for ordinality, “MovieNr” int path ‘@movieNr', “Movie Name” varchar (50) path ‘title', “Release Year” char(4) path ‘released' “Director” varchar(50) path ‘director' )

The resulting table would have the following form, and could be aliased and so on, in the same way as a table produced by other means.

In this case, values in the automatically generated SeqNo column and the retrieved MovieNr column are coincidentally the same. Had the XML data been in a different order, the SeqNo column would remain unchanged, but the MovieNr column (and the other retrieved columns) would reflect the XML element ordering.

Exercise 16.2

The following schema shows part of a database that holds information about repair technicians and the types of assemblies that they are competent to repair. Different technicians may be competent at repairing different assemblies.

  1. 1. Using the facilities provided in a modern database system, turn the contents of the repair database into three XML documents, that is, one XML document per table.
  2. 2. Use XPath and XQuery expressions to produce the following results, using one or more of the Technician, Competence, and Assembly XML documents. Produce the results either as an XML document or as an XML fragment.
    1. (a) List all supervisors and under each supervisor all technicians that report to them. The Supervisor and Technician elements should have empNr as an attribute and the concatenation of ‘firstName' || ‘ ' || ‘lastName' as the element content.
    2. (b) List the assemblies in a hierarchic form (i.e., the top-level assemblies will have subassemblies, which will have their own subassemblies, etc.). Show the assemblyCode as the content of each element.
    3. (c) List all the assemblies with a complexity code of 5 or higher that have a report. Order the list by complexityNr (descending) and assemblyCode (ascending).
    4. (d) For each technician, list the types of assembly that they are competent to repair. Include each assembly’s complexityNr as an attribute.
    5. (e) List all technicians with a certificationRefs element under each technician. Use xsi:nil = “true” in cases where the technician has no certificationRef. For each certificationRef that does exist, show the related assemblyCode.
    6. (f) List all assemblies that no technician is competent to repair.
  3. 3. Using the facilities provided in a modern database system, turn each XML result from the queries in Question 2 into a relational table.

16.3 JSON

JSON stands for JavaScript Object Notation, which describes its origin and function very clearly. Like XML, JSON is a text-based format that makes it very easy to interchange data between different systems. Each system can store the data in its own internal form for efficient processing, but these internal representations do not need to be the same. JSON was first defined by Douglas Crockford in the early 2000s as a format for data interchange, but it subsequently became widely adopted as a convenient way of expressing data structure and is supported in most programming languages. An early “informational” standard (Crockford, 2006) was followed by the first international standard (ECMA-404) in 2013.

The syntax of JSON is very simple and is a slightly modified version of JavaScript syntax. There are two main structural elements.

  1. 1. Sets of key-value pairs. A colon character separates the key and the value, as in:
 “givenName” : “Alan”, “familyName” : “Turing”

The key is enclosed in double quotes. Successive items are separated by a comma character and the set is enclosed in braces. The order of items in the set is not significant. Such sets are termed “objects” from their JavaScript origins.

  1. 2. Arrays containing an ordered collection of values. Values are separated by comma characters. An array is enclosed in square brackets.

Whitespace characters (space, tab, newline, …) outside quoted values are ignored. Values can be a string, a number, a Boolean, the special value null, or either of the structured types (objects and arrays). The broad guidelines are that arrays are used for collections of similar items and objects are used for collections of properties for an individual item.

The JSON syntax is slightly different to JavaScript, which does not require quoted keys and allows other possible values, such as functions, but the general style is similar. This makes JSON processing in JavaScript very straightforward, and the language has built-in functions for handling JSON text. JSON.parse() converts a text representation into a JavaScript object structure and JSON.stringify() converts a JavaScript object structure into text. Similar functionality is provided in other object-oriented languages. One noticeable absence from JSON is any capability for expressing comments. This was a deliberate choice made by its designers but has been a source of frustration for many users.

This straightforward processing is a distinct advantage over XML, which requires a more complex parser to process text into an internal representation and provides only indirect access to data values.

The nesting of entities (e.g., objects containing objects) produces a hierarchical structure in much the same way as XML, but JSON also provides arrays, which have no direct equivalent in XML. Like XML, a JSON file can be opened and edited with nothing more than a simple text editor. Human readability can be helped by sensible use of whitespace characters, but dedicated editors, sensitive to JSON structure, are also available. JSON files are generally more compact than the equivalent XML representation of the same data.

Another difference between XML and JSON is the approach to data typing. XML, like SQL, has an extensive range of data types that can be specified in a schema. JavaScript is a dynamically typed language, and this is carried over into JSON, which has only three scalar data types: string, number, and Boolean (plus null, which, like SQL, indicates the absence of a value). Numbers can be integer or floating point, and Booleans have the value true or false.

JSON support is available in many languages, not just JavaScript. Once a JSON file is loaded into the language of choice, the standard facilities of that language can be used to carry out operations on the data in the usual way, such as iterating over the members of a collection. Extracting data from the object structure created by loading the JSON file requires code in JavaScript, Python, C#, or whatever host language is being used. Strictly speaking, JSON refers to the text format, so once it has been loaded, it is no longer JSON but a structure of the kind appropriate to the language. The syntax may vary by language, there may be different conventions for single versus double quotes, and so on. Data operations are normally carried out on this internal structure, not on the JSON text. Each language will also provide some function to carry out the reverse process to output a textual representation of the inner structure. Different languages may change the format slightly by introducing extra whitespace characters into the output. This does not change the data, but it means that results may not be identical if moving from one programming language to another.

Like XML, a JSON file can be described precisely with a schema. The JSON Schema specification describes the structure, constraints, and validation rules for JSON documents. JSON Schema is itself written in a JSON format. It uses JSON objects to describe the structure of the data it validates. This means that JSON Schema documents themselves can be validated. The expected properties of an object can be defined, each property with its own validation rules and data types. This includes maximum and minimum values for numeric properties, maximum and minimum and lengths for strings, regular expression patterns, and special formats such as email or URL. Array properties can be specified with data types and maximum and minimum numbers of items. JSON Schema includes many other features that we will not cover here. The specification is constantly reviewed and updated and is freely available. There are many tools available for validation of JSON against a specific schema, generating a JSON schema, generating code from a schema, and so on. As with XML Schema, we will not delve into the full details here.

To illustrate the general features of JSON, we can use the Movies information previously covered as an XML example in Listing 16.1. Listing 16.3 shows the same information in JSON format. The movies object contains an array (a list) of individual movies. Array items are accessed by index, so the first movie is movies[0] (array indexes are zero-based). Each movie item in the array is an object containing properties such as title, director, etc. A property can itself be an object or an array, as in the case of the stars property, which contains a list of star objects. Object properties can be accessed via the name of the key.

Unlike XML and XQuery, JSON has no special query language. Instead, the general features of a host programming language are used to process data. We need to bear in mind that once a JSON file is loaded it is no longer JSON, but instead is a structure that is meaningful in the context of the host language. To provide some concrete examples of extracting required data values, we can use the same queries as in the previous XML example, shown in Table 16.2. Here we will use Python to express the queries, but other languages follow a similar approach. The first step is to load the JSON file into a Python dictionary with the aid of a presupplied json library.

import json# Open JSON file  theFile = open(‘movies.json’)# load JSON object into Python dictionary  data = json.load(theFile)
# Iterate over the json object for item in data[‘movies’]:# code fragment goes here

Now we can iterate over the content of the dictionary to extract (and in this case print) the required data. The code fragments in Table 16.6 are assumed to directly follow the Python code above.

Table 16.6

Example Python code fragments.

In some respects, a JSON file (and a corresponding program to load and process the file) could be considered a small database in its own right, though perhaps lacking many features expected in a complete database system such as transactions, concurrency, and so on. However, the JSON format has proved so useful that it has been used as the basis for full database systems, commonly referred to as Document Databases. These are usually classified as a type of “NoSQL” database and are discussed in more detail in Chapter 17.

SQL/JSON

Given the widespread use of JSON, the SQL standard needed to be extended to accommodate it in the same way that it had previously accommodated XML. SQL:2016 provided support for JSON stored as text in a character-based column (typically varchar). Time pressures did not allow the full definition of JSON as a data type, but this was completed in SQL:2023, so data can be stored in a column of data type json. This had already been anticipated by several vendors, but their solutions are not necessarily compatible with each other or with the SQL:2023 standard. However, all vendors consistently adhere to the standard definition of JSON. There are two immediate advantages of a json data type.

  1. 1. Values can be automatically validated as correctly formed JSON. A data type such as varchar has no intrinsic understanding of JSON structure, so an additional function is required for text to establish that it represents a valid JSON value.
  2. 2. Values can be processed more efficiently by converting JSON text into a binary form for internal operations, avoiding relatively expensive string processing. The binary versions also require less storage.

The SQL/JSON data model covers SQL/JSON items and SQL/JSON sequences. A sequence is an ordered list of items. An item is any of the following:

  • • An SQL/JSON object: an unordered collection of members, where each member is a key-value pair, the value component being an SQL/JSON item.
  • • An SQL/JSON array: an ordered list of elements, where each element is an SQL/JSON item.
  • • An SQL/JSON scalar: a nonnull value with a type that is one of the standard JSON types (character string, numeric, or Boolean) or datetime.
  • • An SQL/JSON null (different from an SQL null).

Because the structural items (object and array) can be nested, JSON text can represent data with any required degree of complexity.

Values can be inserted into a json column in the usual way. Assume we have the following table definition:

create table movies ( movienr int primary key moviedata json )

The primary key column here is included simply as a convenience. We could enter JSON data using one row for each movie in a similar way to any other SQL data type.

  • insert into movies values (3,
  •         '{ “title”: “The Secret Garden”,
  •              “released”: “1987”,
  •              “director”: “Alan Grint”,
  •              “stars”: [
  •                    { “name”: “Gennie James”, “gender”: “F” },
  •                   { “name”: “Barret Oliver”, “gender”: “M” }
  •              ]
  •         }')

However, we don't necessarily have to split data up in this way. For example, all the movie data in Listing 16.2 could be entered as a single value in a json column.

SQL:2023 provides several functions to work with JSON values. These fall into two categories. SQL/JSON retrieval functions operate on SQL/JSON data and return values either as SQL data or SQL/JSON data. SQL/JSON construction functions return SQL/JSON values from either SQL data or SQL/JSON data.

Although JSON support was added to SQL:2016, it did not include the json data type until SQL:2023. During the intervening period, several vendors introduced individual interpretations of the data type and the corresponding functions to work with it. The result was some variance between different systems, including the following:

  1. 1. Certain SQL/JSON functions are missing completely, though it may be possible to obtain similar results in a more roundabout way.
  2. 2. Functions are provided with the same names as SQL/JSON functions but with different syntax.
  3. 3. Functions have the same main syntax as the SQL/JSON definitions but do not support some optional clauses defined in SQL:2023.

Hopefully, this situation will normalize in the future. The main SQL/JSON query functions in SQL:2023 are summarized in Table 16.7.

Table 16.7

SQL/JSON query functions.

Some systems may provide alternatives such as json_extract(), which offers similar functionality to json_query(), and json_contains(), which may be used as a replacement for json_exists().

These query operators locate relevant parts of the JSON data using a path language. This is similar in principle to using XPath with XML data, but the JSON path language has a syntax closer to JavaScript.

A path starts from the root of the relevant JSON text. This will be an object or an array and is represented as a “dollar” symbol ($). The path shows the steps from the root to the required element (or elements) within the JSON text using accessors: square brackets ([ ]) for elements in an array and a period or “dot” (.) for members of an object. The ECMAScript Language Specification for JSONpath also allows bracket notation for object members, but this is not supported in SQL/JSON. An asterisk (*) is used as a wildcard character to indicate all elements in an array or all members of an object. To illustrate these concepts, assume we have the JSON text of Listing 16.3 stored in a movie column of a table called videos.

This text contains a single object called movies. The value of this object is a list of six elements. Each element of the list is an object with members such as “title”, “director”, and so on. We can use the following query to get a list of all movie names.

select json_query(movie, ‘$.movies[*].title') from videos

To build the path from the root, we first add the movies member (the only member at this level). Next, we add a wildcard specification for all elements of the movies array. Finally, we add the title member from each of the array elements. All path expressions work in this way, though they can be much more complex.

JSON path expressions can be used in two modes: lax and strict. Lax mode is the default, and it provides automatic handling of some structural problems. If an object accessor in a path expression finds an array instead of an object, the array is converted to a sequence and the object accessor is then applied to each element of the sequence. If an array accessor finds a value that is not an array, the value is converted to a single-element array. If an error cannot be handled by these mechanisms, an empty SQL/JSON sequence is returned.

In strict mode, a structural error is reported without any attempt at correction. This is useful for identifying why a path expression is returning unexpected results.

The purpose of json_query is to return an extract from the JSON text. This will be a structural item (an array or an object) containing other items. To return a scalar value, json_value is used. This has a similar syntax to json_query, but the path must identify a single item. Consider the following two queries:

select json_query(movie, ‘$.movies[*].movieNr') from videosselect json_value(movie, ‘$.movies[*].movieNr') from videos

The first will return a list of movie numbers, but the second will return null because the result is not a scalar value. It's possible to cast a scalar returned by json_value into an appropriate SQL data type. For example:

select json_value(movie, ‘$.movies[0].movieNr returning decimal(5,2)') from videos

returns a scalar value (because this query specifies only the first array item) with a cast to the designated SQL type. If no cast is specified, the type of the return value is a system default (typically varchar).

If a null is returned, we might want to know the reason. There are three possibilities: the null may have been retrieved from the JSON text being queried, the specified value does not exist, or some error has occurred. The default for all these cases is to return null, but we can distinguish between them with optional clauses to deal with the “on empty” and “on error” cases. For example, the following query will return the text "Not found" because we have specified an array index that does not exist in the data. Such optional clauses are not supported in all systems.

select json_value(movie, ‘$.movies[8].movieNr' default 'Not found' on empty) from videos

We can use json_exists to check whether a specific item is present or not. In this case, the return value is 1 if the item exists and 0 if it does not. For example:

select json_exists(movie, ‘$.movies[*].director') from videos

will return 1 indicating that at least one occurrence of the specified item has been found, but:

select json_exists(movie, ‘$.movies[*].producer') from videos

returns 0 because our movie objects do not contain a producer member.

One useful application of json_exists is in the creation of check constraints to ensure that JSON data contains some mandatory elements. Further predicates can be used to check whether an item is (or is not) a JSON value, array, object, or scalar, but we won't go into the details of these here.

Although json_query can return results from JSON documents, the results remain in a JSON format. To be consistent with other operations, we may prefer results in the form of a standard SQL table. This is the functionality provided by json_table, which extracts data from a JSON document and returns it as a relational table. Here's a simple example, based on our usual movie data.

select jt.Title, jt.Director from videos as v,json_table (v.movies, ‘$.movies[*]' columns(   Title varchar(20) path '$.title',   Director varchar(20) path ‘$.director'  )) as jt

The select statement identifies columns from the aliased JSON table (“jt”) created by the json_table function. The first argument to the function specifies the JSON source, in this case the movies column of the videos table. The second argument defines the starting point in the JSON text, in this case the movies array. The column list defines the column name, the SQL data type, and the path in the current context (in this case, the starting point defined previously). The result is a straightforward SQL table.

It's possible to include data from different levels of the JSON text by using “nested” columns. In our data, the names of any stars of a movie are at a level below the title of the movie. The following example shows how these levels can be combined.

select jt.* from videos as v,json_table (v.movies, ‘$.movies[*]' columns(   Title varchar(20) path ‘$.title',   Released int path ‘$.released',nested path ‘$.stars[*]'columns (      Starring varchar(20) path ‘$.name')  )) as jtorder by Released

Again, this produces a standard SQL result table.

Tables produced in this way can participate in all the usual table operations such as join operations with other (non-JSON) tables in the database. A possible use of json_table is to create views that allow the JSON origins of the data to be hidden from SQL developers.
