There is one more SQL/JSON retrieval function, and that is json_serialize. This takes a JSON value as input and returns JSON text in one of the SQL character data types (typically varchar). This is useful if the “raw” JSON value is in a binary form, which is not intended for human readability. Some implementations may also include a “pretty” option to produce nicely formatted text.

The operations we have considered so far assume that we have some JSON value stored in the database and want to extract some or all of it, in various ways. SQL/JSON also defines construction functions that build SQL/JSON items from non-SQL/JSON values.

The most obvious of these is json_parse, which takes a text input and converts it to a JSON sequence. This is essentially the reverse operation to json_serialize. If the input text is not well-formed JSON, an error will be returned. The json_scalar function is simple: it creates a JSON value from a non-JSON value. For example, an SQL value of data type int would be converted to a JSON number.

More interesting are the functions to construct JSON structural elements, objects and arrays. The constructors can be nested, so we can build JSON values of arbitrary complexity. These functions are summarized in Table 16.8.

Table 16.8

SQL/JSON structural construction functions.

These functions have many options, and we'll explore some of these with examples. The relational tables in Fig. 16.4 show some data about agents and their allocation to projects. The SQL data types are int for employee numbers and rate and varchar for other columns. Blank spaces represent SQL null. We'll assume that we ultimately want to create a single JSON object containing an individual object for each agent, including any project allocation(s) that they may have.

Creating objects is straightforward. The following query defines an object structure with members for employee number and office, which is then applied to each row of the Agent table.

  • select json_object('empNr' value nr, 'office' value office) from Agent
  •    Result:
  •    {“empNr”: 101, “office”: “Boston”}
  •    {“empNr”: 232, “office”: “Portland”}
  •    {“empNr”: 397, “office”: “Durham”}
  •    {“empNr”: 468, “office”: null}

Some implementations of json_object replace the value keyword with a comma. An ugly feature of the result is the null in the last object. A more natural JSON representation would omit this member entirely. SQL/JSON defines an optional absent on null clause to effect this, but it's not supported in all implementations. We may be able to find a workaround by providing something more meaningful based on domain knowledge. For instance, if we know that the reason for Dave Dunk having no office recorded is that he is mobile, so his office varies, we can replace the null.

  • select json_object(‘empNr' , nr,
  •                             ‘office', case when office is not null then office else ‘varies' end)
  • from Agent
  •    Result:
  •    {“empNr”: 101, “office”: “Boston”}
  •    {“empNr”: 232, “office”: “Portland”}
  •    {“empNr”: 397, “office”: “Durham”}
  •    {“empNr”: 468, “office”: “varies”}

It's obvious how this query could be extended to include separate members for givenName and familyName, but an alternative would be to create a name member containing objects for each of the name components. This can be done by nesting additional json_object constructors within the name member.

Phone information is a little more complex because the member is not single-valued. We'll assume that a list of numbers is required, each represented by an object. This can be produced by nesting object constructors inside an array constructor in the following way.

  • select json_array(     json_object(‘type' value ‘home', ‘number' value homePhone
  • json_object(‘type' value ‘work', ‘number' value workPhone) )
  • from Agent
  •    Result:
  •    [{“type”: “home”, “number”: “222-9876”}, {“type”: “work”, “number”: “222-1234”}]
  •    [{“type”: “home”, “number”: null}, {“type”: “work”, “number”: “555-6789”}]
  •    [{“type”: “home”, “number”: “777-6789”}, {“type”: “work”, “number”: “777-4321”}]
  •    [{“type”: “home”, “number”: null}, {“type”: “work”, “number”: null}]

To integrate this information, we can introduce a phones member into our earlier object, with the array construct above nested inside it. We have the same issue as before with nulls. If the absent on empty clause is not available, we could create a more complex SQL query to remove the null members from the JSON result, but for our current purposes, we'll just accept the nulls.

The functions not covered so far are the object aggregate and array aggregate constructors. We can illustrate these with the Project table. The json_objectagg function requires a key-value pair, as in the following example:

  • select empNr, json_objectagg(projName, rate)
  • from Project group by empNr
  •   Result:
  •   101     {“Grebe”: 2, “Mallard”: 1}
  •   232     {“Grebe”: 3, “Plover”: 1, “Bittern”: 2}

Here, the resulting object for each group has a member for each item in the group. This differs from json_object, which would give a separate object for each item.

Creating an aggregating array works similarly but requires only the identification of the value to be listed. This gives an array with an element for each item in the group.

  • select empNr, json_arrayagg(projName)
  • from Project group by empNr
  •  Result:
  •   101     [“Mallard”, “Grebe”]
  •   232     [“Grebe”, “Plover”, “Bittern”]

To meet our aim of a comprehensive Agent object, the json_arrayagg constructor looks the most appropriate. This can be integrated into the larger query by nesting it within a projects member of the main object structure.

To create the required final JSON structure, the rows containing the above elements can be aggregated together to form a list of agents within an enveloping object, as shown in the following query.

select json_object (‘Agents', json_arrayagg(json_object(       ‘empNr' value nr,     ‘name', json_object(‘given' value givenName, 'family' value familyName),     ‘phone', json_array(json_object(‘work' value workPhone),json_object(‘home' value homePhone)),     ‘office', case when office is not null then office else ‘varies' end,     ‘projects', (select json_arrayagg(projName)from Project p where p.empNr = a.nr group by p.empNr))))from Agent a

The following listing shows the combined result, formatted slightly to make the structure more obvious.

 {“Agents”: [  {“empNr”: 101,  “name”: {“given”: “Alice”, “family”: “Andrews”},  “phone”: [{“work”: “222-1234”}, {“home”: “222-9876”}],  “office”: “Boston”,  “projects”: [“Mallard”, “Grebe”]  },  {“empNr”: 232,  “name”: {“given”: “Bob”, “family”: “Brown”},  “phone”: [{“work”: “555-6789”}, {“home”: null}],  “office”: “Portland”,  “projects”: [“Grebe”, “Plover”, “Bittern”]
  },  {“empNr”: 397,  “name”: {“given”: “Carol”, “family”: "Codd”},  “phone”: [{“work”: “777-4321”}, {“home”: “777-6789”}],  “office”: “Durham”,  “projects”: null  },  {“empNr”: 468,  “name”: {“given”: “Dave”, “family”: “Dunk”},  “phone”: [{“work”: null}, {“home”: null}],  “office”: “varies”,  “projects”: null  } ] }

16.4 Other Markup Languages

As the name suggests, markup languages, like XML, work by adding additional markings of some kind to the original information to indicate its function or purpose. Historically, the leading application for markup was in the publishing industry, where it was (and still is) used to show the treatment to be applied to the author's text to turn it into a properly formatted layout for printing. In a database context, we might consider markup as metadata.

A language close in spirit to JSON is YAML. This originally stood for “Yet Another Markup Language”, but other interpretations of the name have emerged subsequently. YAML is a superset of JSON with some additional features, and utilities are available to convert back and forth between YAML and JSON. The main motivation for YAML was to provide a more “human-readable” format than JSON, especially avoiding extensive use of brackets (rounded, square, or curly). Nesting can be indicated by indenting items in a similar way to the Python language using spaces. This reduces the possibility of common keyboard errors.

Some brief features of YAML include the following:

  • • Items are nested by indenting child nodes below their parent.
  • • Key-value pairs are separated by a colon, but quotes are not required.
  • • New items in a list are indicated by a hyphen.
  • • Scalar values including strings, numbers, and Booleans can be used freely.
  • • Quotes are not needed for strings but can be used if needed (for example, if a number is required to be treated as a string).
  • • Comments can be indicated by a hash character (comments are stripped out when converted to JSON).
  • • Additional commands are provided to control the layout of text in output (e.g., suppressing newlines).

The following shows an abbreviated version of our movie data example expressed in YAML.

 --- # This is a YAML document movies:  - movieNr: 1     title: Cosmology     released: ‘2006'     director: Lee Lafferty  - movieNr: 2     title: Kung Fu Hustle     released: ‘2004'     director: Stephen Chow    stars:     - name: Stephen Chow      gender: M  - movieNr: 5     title: The Da Vinci Code     released: ‘2006'     director: Ron Howard    stars:     - name: Tom Hanks      gender: M     - name: Ian McKellen      gender: M     - name: Audrey Tautou      gender: F …

YAML is a popular choice for relatively short documents where data structure needs to be explicitly represented. Two examples are configuration files containing application data and the interchange of structured messages. It is not widely used for large data collections. Its ease of use is partly due to automated decisions about the intention behind a data value, which can lead to unexpected consequences. For example, some parsers may interpret the unquoted value No as the Boolean value false, which may not have been the original intention.

The most familiar markup language is probably HTML, used to define the structure of web pages. Unlike XML, the tags in HTML are predefined and have specific meanings defined in the HTML standard. In the early days of web usage, HTML was also used as a rather weak method of identifying some aspects of data structure, but this was clearly unsatisfactory. Like XML, HTML can seem clumsy and awkward for authors, and several alternatives have been developed. Some examples include the following.

  • • The cutely named Markdown is a lightweight language that is used to add formatting indicators to textual documents. The marked document can be used in various applications to generate publishing formats such as PDF and convert to other formats such as a complete static website. However, it is obviously limited in its capability to express data structures.
  • • AsciiDoc is a plain text equivalent to the XML-based DocBook format used for structured documents. Documents can be created simply using a text editor and then rendered to a desired final format, such as PDF, HTML, and many others.
  • • MediaWiki is another lightweight language designed for ease of use. As the name suggests, it was developed for the creation of Wiki pages and is the basis for Wikipedia. As with other languages of this type, its documents can be re-processed into many other formats, including HTML.

The main purpose of most of these languages is to define the structure of documents, not the structure of data. Although there is a certain amount of overlap, there is no pressing need to use these languages for data description when better alternatives are available. We will therefore not explore them any further in this chapter.

16.5 XML, JSON, and ORM

A question worth considering is whether object-role modeling (ORM) can be used to design an XML schema or a JSON schema, in much the same way that it can be used to design a relational schema. The answer is certainly “Yes”, but there are some additional considerations that are not relevant in the relational case.

As already mentioned, an ORM model can be represented in XML, and this indeed is the default file format used by the NORMA tool. The general structure can be outlined as follows:

 <ORMModel>  <Objects>   <Object id = 123 …> </ObjectType>   <Object id = 456 …> </ObjectType>   …    </Objects>  <Facts>   <Fact id = 321 …>   <FactRole id = 789 …> </FactRole>     <FactRole id = 987 …> </FactRole>   </Fact>   …  </Facts>  <Constraints> … </Constraints>  …  <ORMDiagram> … </ORMDiagram> </ORMModel>

Each item has a unique identifier (UUID), and these are used to relate items together. For example, the object playing a fact role can be referenced from the role entity using its UUID.

Although this structure captures all the ORM model details, it does not provide a good template for a data model. Some of the content, such as the diagram information, has no relevance in defining a data structure, and items in the *.orm file such as object types and fact types are represented in ways that are intended to facilitate modeling operations, not data transfer. Instead, what is required is a mapping from the ORM model to an XML schema that accommodates the relevant data.

Mapping from an ORM model to a relational schema was discussed in Chapter 11. There are only a few possible options in the Rmap procedure, such as how to treat subtypes. The procedure is largely automatic, and two different developers mapping the same ORM model will generally produce the same relational schema. However, the situation is different for XML.

The first issue is that XML obliges us to represent the data as a hierarchy, even if no natural hierarchy exists in the ORM model. This is a consequence of the nesting of elements within elements, which is intrinsic to XML. Consider the tiny ORM model shown in Fig. 16.5.

One option would be to nest Courses under Students.

 <Model>     <Student name = “Alice” …>         <Course id = “CS101” …> …</Course>         <Course id = “CS104” …> …</Course>     </Student>     <Student name = “Bob” …>        <Course id = “CS101” …> …</Course>     </Student> </Model>

But nesting of Students under Courses could be equally valid.

 <Model>  <Course id = “CS101" …>   <Student name = “Alice” …> … </Student>   <Student name = “Bob” …>… </Student>  </Course>  <Course id = “CS104” …>   <Student name = “Alice” …> … </Student>  </Course> </Model>

We could also consider something closer to a relational style, with a Student list, a Course list, and a list of linking Enrolment elements.

 <Model>  <Students>   <Student name = “Alice” …> … </Student>   <Student name = “Bob" …>… </Student>  </Students>  <Courses>   <Course id = “CS101” …> …</Course>   <Course id = “CS104” …> …</Course>  </Courses>  <Enrolments>   <Enrolment student = “Alice” course = “CS101”> … </Enrolment>   <Enrolment student = “Alice” course = “CS104”> … </Enrolment>   <Enrolment student = “Bob” course = “CS101”> … </Enrolment>  </Enrolments> </Model>

Which of these would be preferable cannot be inferred from the ORM model because the choice depends on external factors such as the intended use of the data and patterns of access.

A second issue is that XML provides two options for storing data: as the value of an element attribute or as the content of an element. The examples above show student name as an attribute, but the following would be an equally valid alternative:

 <Student>  <Name>Alice</Name>  … </Student>

There is no firm rule for deciding between these options, although various guidelines have been suggested, such as reserving attributes for metadata only. Attributes have some limitations that would make elements preferable in some cases, for instance, data that is multivalued or has some inner structure, but for straightforward scalar values either approach could be used.

Although we have been describing the situation with XML, similar issues arise with JSON, which also offers choices about how to represent the data. What all this means is that two different developers mapping the same ORM model may produce very different XML schemas (or JSON schemas).

To produce an XML rendering of a relational structure, we can follow a systematic procedure that is straightforward to automate.

Each relational table will map to an element type in XML, which can have a plural tag name (e.g., <Employees>). Each of these major element types will be nested under a suitably named root node. These major elements will contain a list of subelements of the relevant type.

Rows in a table will map to subelements with a singular tag name (e.g., <Employee>). nested under their parent element (e.g., <Employees>). Relational columns map to attributes of their related subelements. A UUID attribute can be added to each subelement for easy identification and cross-referencing.

The result is an XML file similar to the “relational” style in the examples above. Even if this is not the preferred format, it may still be a good first step. Once we have an XML file, it can be transformed into alternative XML structures using appropriate code, perhaps using the XML Stylesheet Language for Transforms (XSLT).

If we need to produce an XML file directly from an ORM schema, we can adapt the approach above by adding some extra steps. First, we follow the Rmap procedure to identify the relational structure corresponding to the ORM schema. Next, we apply the procedure above to this relational structure to define the XML schema elements. Finally, we need to add any required constraints from the ORM schema to the XML schema. This last step is not necessary when producing a data transfer file from a database because we can assume that the appropriate constraints will already have been applied to the data.

Mapping to a JSON schema can follow a similar procedure. Tables become JSON objects, rows become lists of nested objects within the parent types, and column values appear as key-value pairs within the nested object.

16.6 Summary

XML is a member of a family of markup languages based on the Standard Generalized Markup Language (SGML). Other languages based on SGML include HTML, though this has now diverged somewhat from its original basis. XML was designed to be easy to parse, initially in the context of web applications, but it is now well established as a general-purpose tool for describing data structure independent of any specific data container. It has become a built-in feature of many applications, though its presence may not be immediately obvious. As examples, the current formats of Microsoft Office files (such as *.docx, *.pptx, and *.xlsx) are based on XML, and the NORMA tool used to create and manage object relational models uses XML in its *.orm file format.

A key feature of XML is its extensibility. Unlike HTML, it does not assume predefined tag names, so a schema can be designed to meet any required scenario. If warranted, the schema can be documented in machine-readable form so that an XML document can be validated against the schema definition to ensure that it is consistent. The original schema definition method, inherited from SGML, used DTDs, which are expressed in their own language. Modern usage has moved to the expression of the schema in XML itself, using XML Schema Definition (XSD) or the simpler alternative Relax NG.

The XML definition is controlled by the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C). Several other W3C standards exist within the XML family. In addition to XML Schema, we have already discussed XPath and XQuery in some depth. These allow XML data to be queried in a way that corresponds roughly to the way that the select statement is used in querying SQL tables. Other W3C standards include the following:

XSLT (Extensible Stylesheet Language Transformations) is an XML-based language used to convert an XML document into a different XML schema or into a completely different format such as PDF.

XLink (XML Linking Language) provides methods for creating internal and external links within XML documents and associating metadata with the links.

XPointer is based on XPath and supports addressing into the internal structures of XML documents. This can be used to create something equivalent to a foreign key in a relational database.

XHTML is a somewhat stricter version of HTML with a syntax conforming to XML.

SVG (Scalable Vector Graphics) is a language for describing two-dimensional vector graphics that allows smooth scaling to different display resolutions.

There are many other XML-based standards produced by W3C and other bodies, perhaps running into hundreds of examples, as well as an uncountable number of private applications. This makes XML probably the most well-established method of defining structured data outside of a database system.

XML is a text format, and although it can be manipulated using text processing operations, it is more effective to use processing operations that are sensitive to the data structure being expressed. Database systems first started using XML as a text format, but recognition of its value led to its incorporation as a native data type in the SQL standard. Most database vendors have added features to store XML data, operate on XML data, and convert backward and forward between XML and relational table structures, sometimes including proprietary extensions that are not part of the official SQL standard.

JSON is a slightly younger language than XML. It was originally developed as a relatively lightweight communication language between web servers and browsers, using standard browser facilities instead of auxiliary plug-ins. This made JavaScript an obvious starting point for the definition of a markup language, and so JavaScript objects became the basis for the notation.

A major factor in the popularity of JSON is its simplicity and ease of processing compared to XML. It is a more compact format that reduces the bandwidth required for the transmission of data; this is an important factor given the reasons for its creation. It is also a better fit with web-related technology in general, relevant, for example, in application development. Against that, it is somewhat less expressive than XML. It has no support for namespaces, and it is unsuitable in applications where precise definition of data types is important. However, its adoption as the primary structuring principle in document databases and its incorporation into SQL as a native data type show that it is sufficiently robust to meet the demands of a wide range of real-world scenarios.

XML and JSON will continue to coexist for the foreseeable future because one is not a direct replacement for the other. It's tempting to caricature XML as heavyweight and JSON as lightweight solutions to data structuring outside of a data store, but this blurs some of the important features of each. It's certainly true that there is a large middle ground where either could be employed effectively, and any choice between them would be made on factors other than their data structuring capabilities.

Chapter Notes

The SQL standard has been adopted by the International Standards Organization (ISO) as ISO/IEC 9075. Copies can be ordered from ISO or via national standards organizations such as ANSI. Because of its size (several thousand pages in total), the standard is split into several parts. Part 2 (Foundations) and Part 14 (SQL/XML) are the most relevant to this chapter.

The relevant XML standards are being progressed through the W3C. Full details, including the current versions of the standards themselves, can be found at www.w3c.org. The standards documents are not particularly easy to read, but a large amount of more readable tutorial information is available. XQuery especially is still relatively unfamiliar to many database practitioners, but it seems likely to become progressively more important in utilizing heterogeneous data. Useful introductions can be found in Walmsley (2015) and Melton and Buxton (2006).

JSON arrived as a data format later than XML, but it is now established as an essential component in data management. A short introduction to JSON can be found in Basset (2015). Because of its origins in JavaScript, its standardization falls under ECMA, the same body responsible for the specification of the JavaScript language (now sometimes referred to as ECMAScript). A comprehensive description of JavaScript is given in Flanagan (2020). Copies of standards and further details can be found at www.ecma-international.org. JavaScript and JSON are covered in standards ECMA-262 and ECMA-404, respectively. The latter has also been adopted as an ISO standard (ISO/IEC 21778). JSON Schema is still a work in progress, but the latest status can be found at www.json-schema.org. For further details on JSONPath, see Gössner and Bormann (2021).

XML and JSON functionality is now included in major relational databases but because of variations between different implementations, the vendor’s documentation is often the most useful resource. Most commercial systems provide online help that can be searched in various ways.

References18

  • Crockford D. The Application/JSON Media Type for JavaScript Object Notation (JSON). Available at: https://www.ietf.org/rfc/rfc4627.txt. 2006.

17 NoSQL and Other Nonrelational Databases

Abstract

This chapter reviews alternatives to the dominant relational database paradigm. The motivations for such systems are discussed and the major database types are described individually. Methods for mapping from an information model to each of these database types are introduced. Some further ideas on future evolution are considered, including the potential impact of artificial intelligence.

Keywords

NoSQL; Key-value database; Document database; Column-oriented database; Graph database; Logic database; AI

Chapter Outline

  • 17.1 The Growth of the NoSQL Movement
  • 17.2 Key-Value Stores
  • 17.3 Column-Oriented Databases
  • 17.4 Document Databases
  • 17.5 Graph Databases
  • 17.6 Other Nonrelational Databases
  • 17.7 Summary

17.1 The Growth of the NoSQL Movement

Following the publication of E.F. Codd’s ground-breaking relational paper in 1970 (Codd, 1970), it was not until the 1980s that commercial relational database systems became widely available. Since that time, they have become the dominant data storage model. Other data resources are used at smaller scales, such as spreadsheets, text files, and so on, but for large-scale data, relational systems have reigned supreme.

The NoSQL movement started to emerge in the 2010s in response to perceived shortcomings in the relational approach (Leavitt, 2010). It’s worth noting straight away that “NoSQL” is not a particularly good choice of name. The crucial point is not really an issue with the structured query language (SQL). In fact, some NoSQL vendors try very hard to provide languages that are as similar as possible to SQL. Instead, NoSQL approaches rely on data models that are nonrelational to provide their distinctive features. There are some suggestions that “NoSQL” should be interpreted as “Not Only SQL”, but this would include every kind of database, rendering it completely meaningless.

The driving forces behind the movement did not result from a failure of the relational model as such but from new challenges and opportunities exposed by the general evolution of technology. The following trends are especially relevant:

  • • The cost of data storage has fallen dramatically. In the 1980s, there was a preoccupation with minimizing storage requirements because of the expense of the hardware involved. Today, consumers are commonly offered services that include gigabytes of free data storage space, which would have been unthinkable in earlier times. The decreasing incentives to minimize storage have contributed to the continual increase in database sizes.
  • • There is now a much greater understanding of the value of data. Even something as simple as a validated relationship between a person and their email address has a cash value. This has motivated organizations to collect as much data as possible, even if there appears to be no immediate use for the information.
  • • Relational databases evolved at a time when “client-server” was the dominant information system architecture. This naturally led to databases that served a limited internal pool of interests. Most organizations now recognize the advantages of being able to transfer data between disparate systems, both internally within the organization and externally with customers, suppliers, partners, and so on. This has been facilitated by interchange formats such as eXtensible Markup Language (XML) and JavaScript Object Notation (JSON), as discussed in Chapter 16.
  • • Since its public appearance in 1990, the Internet has grown by several orders of magnitude. Fast and reliable network connections are now widespread, and connectivity is taken for granted in most of the world. Many websites (and the databases that support them) have millions of users rather than the hundreds that would be considered a large user population in the 1980s.
  • • The day-to-day operations of most organizations are now reliant on some kind of information technology (IT) platform that facilitates data exchange within and without the organization. Growth in general data usage has been explosive. To a large extent, this has been fueled by today’s extensive use of smartphones. In other words, most people carry a computer and communication device with them all the time and do not need to be tethered to a static business system. For example, the publication of street maps has virtually collapsed because most people will now get the relevant map (accessing a remote database) via their phone.

As these trends have evolved, they have exposed database systems to new challenges and opportunities. Rising to these has raised questions about the best way to organize data resources, perhaps by deviating from the relational model that has been the standard for so long.

Before diving into more detail about NoSQL, it will be useful to review some selected database characteristics to provide a context for discussion to follow. For this chapter, we’ll assume that some important factors that might be relevant to choosing a database solution are equally balanced among all candidates. These include features such as security, ease of installation, documentation, vendor reputation, support, and so on. Our focus here will be on aspects that are important in discussing the distinction between relational and nonrelational databases.

The Relational Model

The obvious place to start is with the relational model. Many NoSQL proponents describe this as defining a particular type of database system, but that’s not quite correct. What is being modeled is the structure of information, not the structure of a system. Relational databases evolved to meet the needs of relational structures, not the other way around. A relational model captures relationships within a collection of information in a natural and logical way, as explained in detail in earlier chapters of this book. The expression of a relational model is usually referred to as the relational schema.

One feature deserves special attention. A relational schema captures the intrinsic structure of the information but has nothing to say about how the information will be (or can be) used. The neutral standpoint guides attention to what the information is, rather than what it does. Depending on the point of view, this can be seen as either a strength or a weakness.

If we assume that the schema has been properly normalized, then we can be sure that unnecessary duplication has been avoided, as each piece of information occurs only once. This provides the maximum flexibility when we consider how the information might be used because it is not optimized in a direction that favors any specific type of usage. We might subsequently choose to depart from a pure normalized model to optimize performance in a certain direction. Sadly though, optimizing one factor in a given situation normally deoptimizes other factors, so having a neutral position is a useful starting point.

The most common reason for denormalizing a relational schema is to improve performance in a specified usage scenario. Values from different relations can be combined to give any desired result, but this involves join operations that are relatively expensive in computational terms. The joins can be avoided by combining the relations involved, in effect prejoining them rather than waiting for a query. However, although this reduces the cost of queries, it makes updates more expensive because of the need to manage duplicate information that the denormalization has introduced.

Determining the best policy requires knowledge of the anticipated data traffic. To take some examples, an online catalogue might have infrequent updates but large numbers of queries, whereas a logging application might have many updates but only rare queries. Concerns about performance figure largely in NoSQL databases, as we will see later.

Many NoSQL platforms announce the lack of a schema as a major benefit. Defining a database schema of any kind may indeed involve a considerable amount of work, such as identifying the data to be accommodated, understanding its relevance to the business, arbitrating between competing demands, and so on. The websites of NoSQL vendors often include examples that show how easy it can be to create arbitrary data structures without thinking about these kinds of issues.

However, the same could be true for relational databases. We could create a database, and then add as many tables as we like containing whatever columns we like without any reference to a schema. The standard approach (get the schema right before proceeding) reflects some hard-won experience in building real-world systems.

There are several reasons why defining a data schema might be important for a potential enterprise system. Defining what should or should not fall within the remit of the system may require accommodations between points of view within the enterprise. It is better to resolve these kinds of issues in advance before investing time and effort that may turn out to be wasted.

Applications using the database will always need to know how the information is structured. The idea of writing an application that can handle its required data in absolutely any structure or format is completely unrealistic. In the real world, application programs must be written to work with some defined structure.

A schema also has value as a convenient summary of the information deemed important by the enterprise. This makes it easier to form a shared culture among those responsible for the database and its applications.

Distributed Databases

Distributed systems play an essential role in modern computing. A distributed database system stores its data on more than just a single node, using multiple physical or virtual machines at the same time. The distributed machines have one shared state and operate concurrently.

Distributed systems offer three important features: scalability, availability, and fault tolerance. There is some overlap between these concerns, as we will see shortly, but scalability especially is one of the key motivators for the NoSQL movement.

The two main approaches to scalability can be summarized as scale-up or scale-out. The first of these uses progressively more powerful servers as demands increase. The second splits the database into different parts that can be mounted on an increasing number of servers as demands increase.

One way of scaling up is to migrate the database to a more powerful machine, but there are obvious limits to this. An alternative is to use a cluster of servers that shares a common data store. This obviously introduces additional complications and will sooner or later also come to a point where further extension is not feasible.

NoSQL databases focus more on the scale-out strategy, which can cope with databases far larger than would be possible by scaling-up. The key step is to identify a suitable method of partitioning the database. Partitioning could be done in two ways, vertically or horizontally. Consider the example shown in Fig. 17.1.

Vertical partitioning effectively assigns different table columns to different servers. This can provide some advantages. First, relatively slow-moving data can be separated from more dynamic data. Slow-moving data is a good candidate for an application to cache in a lower-performance store. Second, sensitive data can be stored in a separate partition with additional security controls. Finally, vertical partitioning can reduce the amount of concurrent access that’s needed. A possible outcome is shown in Fig. 17.2.

Vertical partitioning can be used within the same server. Horizontal partitioning (also known as sharding) is used to split data over several servers. This introduces an additional difficulty because applications now need to know which server contains the relevant partition. This can be done in several ways, for example:

  • • By range: Each server contains a known range of key values.
  • • By lookup: An auxiliary table contains a cross-reference between keys and servers.
  • • By hash: A hashing function is used on the key to identify the relevant server.

The distribution strategy may also consider other factors such as geography. If data traffic is primarily driven by localized concerns, it can be directed to servers that are physically close to where the information is created or consumed. Fig. 17.3 shows a simple horizontal partitioning, splitting the data over two servers.

The CAP Theorem

The CAP theorem was first introduced by Brewer in 2000 and is a widely used concept in distributed systems design (Gilbert and Lynch, 2002). At its core, the CAP theorem is about understanding the trade-offs that must be made when building distributed systems. Specifically, it states that it is impossible for a distributed system to simultaneously provide all three of the following guarantees:

  • • Consistency: Every node in a distributed system sees the same data at the same time, implying that every read operation must return the value of the most recent write of the data.
  • • Availability: Every request made to the system will receive a response in a reasonable time frame, regardless of whether a node in the system has failed or is experiencing issues.
  • • Partition tolerance: A distributed system should continue to function even when network partitions occur, due to nodes in the system becoming separated from each other due to network failures or other issues.

In other words, the CAP theorem proposes that it’s only possible to have two of the three guarantees at any given time. This means that a highly available and partition-tolerant system must sacrifice consistency; a highly consistent and partition-tolerant system must sacrifice availability; and a system with high availability and consistency must sacrifice partition tolerance.

If the database is not partitioned, then it can be both consistent and available (sometimes known as a CA database). This is exactly the case in the traditional database with a large central server (i.e., a single-node system). If the database is partitioned, then it can prioritize consistency (CP) or prioritize availability (AP). Consider a distributed system, as shown in Fig. 17.4; just two nodes are sufficient to make the point.

Updates made on one node can be transferred to the other node, with some latency, over the network connection. Both sets of users can eventually see consistent data. But if there is a failure, such as a loss of the network connection between Node 1 and Node 2, then there are two possibilities:

  1. (a) Prevent access to one node. This assures consistency on the working node but removes availability for users on the other node (the CP option).
  2. (b) Allow access to both nodes. The system remains available for all users, but updates on one node cannot reach the other, thus losing consistency (the AP option).

This example is obviously trivial, but it illustrates the balance that must be considered in a distributed system. There is no single right answer, as the choice depends on the purpose that the application is intended to serve. A financial system may prefer consistency, but a social media platform may prefer availability. Different distributed systems may explore different compromises in trading off some loss of consistency against some loss of availability.

ACID and BASE

Traditional databases usually conform to a set of principles known by the acronym ACID from the terms Atomic, Consistent, Isolated, and Durable (Gray and Reuter, 1993).

  • • Atomic: All operations in a transaction must either be completed successfully or not at all. If any operation fails during the execution of a transaction, the entire transaction is aborted and rolled back to its previous state.
  • • Consistent: The database must transition from one consistent state to another after each successful transaction. All data integrity constraints must be maintained before and after each transaction.
  • • Isolated: Concurrent transactions do not interfere with each other’s execution. Each transaction should appear as if it is being executed independently without affecting other ongoing transactions.
  • • Durable: Once a transaction has completed successfully (“committed”), any changes made to the database should persist even in the event of a system failure.

The ACID viewpoint strongly values consistency, making it well-suited for traditional transactional database systems where reliable data is crucial. The rise of distributed systems has promoted interest in a different perspective, known by the acronym BASE, from the terms Basically Available, Soft state, and Eventually consistent (Pritchett, 2008).

  • • Basically available means that the system should always be available for requests, even if the system is experiencing some sort of failure or outage.
  • • Soft state refers to the fact that different copies of the data do not need to be in a completely consistent state at all times.
  • • Eventually consistent means that differences in data will eventually become reconciled, given enough time.

The BASE viewpoint strongly values availability over consistency by allowing temporary inconsistencies between replicas of the data. This is obviously a looser requirement than ACID, but it is more relevant for distributed systems.

Databases can ensure consistency by employing various techniques and mechanisms to synchronize data across multiple nodes in a distributed system. Some common methods used by CP databases include the following:

  • • Consensus protocols: CP databases often utilize consensus protocols, such as Paxos or Raft, to achieve agreement among nodes about the order and validity of data updates. These protocols ensure that all nodes in the system reach a consistent state by requiring a majority or unanimous agreement before committing changes.
  • • Two-phase commit: In a distributed transaction, a two-phase commit protocol can be used to coordinate the commit or rollback of changes across multiple nodes. It ensures that all participating nodes agree to commit the transaction or abort it, guaranteeing consistency across the system.
  • • Quorums and replicas: CP databases typically use replication to maintain multiple copies of data across different nodes. Quorums are used to determine the minimum number of nodes that need to agree on a read or write operation to ensure consistency. By requiring a certain number of replicas to participate in operations, CP databases can ensure that all replicas are consistent before returning a result.
  • • Synchronization and locking: CP databases may use synchronization mechanisms, such as distributed locks or optimistic concurrency control, to prevent concurrent access and modifications to shared data. These techniques ensure that conflicting changes are serialized and applied in a consistent order.
  • • Data versioning and conflict resolution: CP databases often employ data versioning or timestamping to track changes and resolve conflicts when concurrent updates occur. By assigning unique versions or timestamps to data, conflicts can be detected and resolved based on predefined rules or policies.

Of course, achieving consistency can introduce latency and may reduce availability, especially during network partitions or failures. The specific mechanisms and trade-offs employed by a CP database depend on its design and the level of consistency required by the application.

Availability

Availability in distributed systems refers to the ability of the system to respond to client requests, even when some parts of the system have failed. This is important because one of the main reasons for using a distributed architecture is to increase availability and fault tolerance.

In a distributed database, several methods can be employed to provide high availability, ensuring that the system remains operational and accessible even in the presence of failures or network partitions. Here are some common techniques used to achieve high availability:

  • • Replication, which involves creating multiple copies of data across different nodes in the distributed database. By having replicas in different locations, the system can continue serving read and write requests even if some nodes fail. Replication also improves fault tolerance, as a copy of the data is available even if one or more nodes become unavailable.
  • • Data partitioning, or sharding, involves dividing the dataset into smaller subsets and distributing them across multiple nodes. Each node is responsible for a specific partition of the data. By distributing the data, the system can handle a larger volume of requests in parallel, improving availability and scalability.
  • • Load balancing techniques distribute incoming requests across multiple nodes in a distributed database, ensuring that the workload is evenly distributed. This helps prevent any single node from becoming overwhelmed with requests, improving availability by avoiding bottlenecks and optimizing resource utilization.
  • • Failure detection and recovery mechanisms are crucial for high availability. Nodes can periodically check the health of other nodes and detect failures. Upon failure detection, the system can take appropriate actions, such as promoting replicas to replace failed nodes or redistributing the data. Automatic failure detection and recovery minimize downtime and ensure continuous availability.
  • • Redundancy and Failover: Redundancy involves having multiple nodes or components that can serve the same function. In case of a failure, failover mechanisms can redirect requests to healthy nodes or activate standby replicas. Redundancy and failover strategies provide fault tolerance and improve availability by minimizing the impact of failures on system operations.

By combining these techniques, distributed databases can achieve high availability by ensuring continuous access to data and uninterrupted operation, even in the face of failures or network disruptions. The specific methods used depend on the database system’s design, requirements, and the desired level of availability.

NoSQL Benefits

When comparing relational database systems from various suppliers, it’s clear that they have many commonalities. This is hardly surprising given that they are all based on the same fundamental logical concept. The same cannot be said for NoSQL databases. Each NoSQL database is designed to fill a specific niche, resulting in a wide range of variations among different systems. As we will see later, these can be classified into broad families, but they all share a common set of motivations for their existence. These fall into three main categories: coping with large amounts of data, improving performance, and enabling a more agile database development process.

As we’ve already noted, there is a consistent trend toward ever-bigger databases. For practical reasons, this means implementing a “scale-out” policy to support the database on multiple computers, raising all the distributed system issues discussed above.

Distribution is not so easy with a relational database, and many of the NoSQL approaches are aimed at providing ways of scaling using relatively cheap commodity hardware, usually by partitioning the database in some way. This also makes a cloud computing architecture a good fit for Big Data systems, and all cloud service providers offer managed NoSQL solutions.

NoSQL systems usually provide options for adjusting the trade-off boundary between consistency and availability, so that the system is as consistent as possible and as available as possible within the conditions of the intended type of application. A particular application area may offer special features that can be exploited to improve either consistency or availability within that given context.

Although the falling cost of hardware has made minimizing storage space less important, it can still become significant with very large volumes of data. Some NoSQL approaches provide ways of compressing data and storing sparse data in an efficient way, both to reduce storage space and to increase performance. However, this must be set against the increased storage required for the duplicate data that inevitably arises without normalization.

Dealing with large databases also raises issues of performance. This is always a concern with any kind of database, but an approach that might give an acceptable performance with a small database may be totally unacceptable in a larger system. The need to scale out in a distributed system also provides opportunities for improving performance. For example, the load on a server can be reduced by directing a proportion of the queries to other servers that hold copies of the same data.

In relational systems, it’s quite common to denormalize the database to increase performance for specific types of queries, principally by avoiding the penalty of joins between tables. In most NoSQL systems, this is a standard feature, although it would be misleading to call the structure “denormalized” because it may never have been normalized in the first place.

Of course, knowledge of anticipated traffic is essential to maximizing performance, especially the relative frequency of reading from the database versus writing to the database. NoSQL systems are typically aimed at scenarios with a large proportion of reads but few writes. Database records may be entered with some form of bulk loading of relatively static data. This also eases the problems of consistency: if there are no writes there is no way for the database to become inconsistent!

Another efficiency bonus claimed for NoSQL databases is the simplification (and reduced cost) of system management. This can be due to built-in automation of various administrative tasks that traditionally required special expertise and complex manual procedures. Examples include automated sharding, data distribution and replication, easier deployment, and easier system configuration.

Agile development methodologies have gained popularity in all areas of system development. They promise rapid delivery of an initial working system, the ability to respond promptly to changes as they occur during development, and risk reduction through the early identification of problems.

Some NoSQL products define a database schema as a burdensome overhead and promote the lack of a schema as a major agility benefit. The usual example quoted is the ad hoc addition of new data elements to an existing database. However, this is not as distinctive as it may seem. It’s also straightforward to extend a relational database using commands such as:

  •    create table MyNewTable …, and
  •    alter table MyOldTable add myNewColumn …

The situation is more difficult when we consider deleting or modifying an existing structure. The impact of this depends on whether the database is intended to support a single application (such as a mobile phone app) or multiple applications (sometimes called an integration database).

The latter case is more typical of business systems. The two styles are illustrated in Fig. 17.5.

In an application database, the developer of the application and the developer of the database are typically the same person. This makes it easy for changes in the application to be reflected in corresponding changes to the database structure and vice versa. However, things may not be so simple for an integration database because database changes to suit one application may require changes to other applications. Without some kind of schema, it becomes very difficult to manage database integrity. The lack of any authoritative reference to the data structure can also make general application development unnecessarily difficult and error prone.

NoSQL databases often store data in a form that directly matches its external usage, for example using the structure of a business document. This is typically encoded in the same way as the interchange formats described in Chapter 16, with JSON being a common choice. Interfacing between object-oriented application code and a relational database is usually accomplished through some kind of object-relational mapping layer, and it’s possible to eliminate this so-called “impedance mismatch” in some NoSQL systems.

The definition of a relational table requires that a specific data type is allocated to each column. NoSQL databases are often considered in situations involving unstructured or ad hoc data or where data has high variability, and so dynamic typing may be preferable.

Potential Drawbacks of NoSQL Databases

NoSQL databases have gained popularity due to their flexibility and scalability for certain use cases. However, they also have some drawbacks that need to be considered. Here are some common drawbacks associated with NoSQL databases:

  • • Lack of a standardized query language: Unlike relational databases that use SQL as a standardized query language, each NoSQL database has its own unique query language or application programming interface (API). This can make it difficult to switch between different NoSQL databases or integrate them with existing systems. The lack of standardization leads to smaller user communities compared to SQL databases, which may make it more challenging to find support and resources.
  • • Data duplication and denormalization: NoSQL databases typically denormalize data to improve performance and enable horizontal scalability. This means that data may be duplicated across multiple records or collections, leading to increased storage requirements. More importantly, maintaining data consistency across denormalized structures can involve extra complexity.
  • • Lack of data integrity constraints: Unlike relational databases, which enforce data integrity through constraints such as primary keys, foreign keys, and unique indexes, NoSQL databases often lack built-in mechanisms for ensuring data consistency and enforcing relationships among data entities. This makes developers responsible for handling data integrity at the application level.
  • • Lack of mature tooling and ecosystem: Although NoSQL databases have been around for some time, they generally have a less-mature tooling and ecosystem compared to relational databases. This can result in smaller community support, limited development frameworks, and fewer third-party integrations.
  • • Learning curve and developer expertise: Working with NoSQL databases may require developers to learn new concepts, query languages, and data modeling techniques. This can increase the learning curve and the need for specialized expertise, especially when migrating from a relational database environment.
  • • Limited transactional consistency guarantees: Some NoSQL databases sacrifice strong consistency guarantees in favor of high availability and partition tolerance, following the CAP theorem. This means that in certain failure scenarios, trade-offs are made that can lead to eventual consistency or data staleness. There is also an increased risk of inconsistent data due to the eventual consistency model used by some NoSQL databases.

It’s important to note that the impact of these drawbacks can vary depending on the specific use case and requirements of the application. NoSQL databases excel in certain scenarios, such as handling large amounts of unstructured or semistructured data, real-time data processing, and highly scalable systems, but they may not be the optimal choice for all types of applications.

In conclusion, NoSQL databases offer a range of advantages that make them an attractive option for organizations dealing with large volumes of diverse data. Their flexibility, scalability, and high performance make them well-suited for big data applications, the Internet of Things (IoT), and real-time analytics. However, it’s essential to carefully consider the specific requirements of the organization and the application area before choosing a NoSQL database.

17.2 Key-Value Stores

Key-value data stores are a type of NoSQL database that is becoming increasingly popular due to flexibility and scalability. Unlike traditional relational databases, key-value stores do not use a fixed schema for most of the data. Instead, data is stored as a collection of key-value pairs, where the key is used to uniquely identify the data and the value is the actual data. This type of data store is particularly useful for applications that require fast, efficient data access and retrieval.

There are many commercial key-value data stores available in the market today, in addition to others that are not promoted as key-value stores but offer similar capabilities. Redis is an in-memory data structure store that is used for database caching, message brokering, and real-time analytics. It is known for its speed and versatility and is often used as a distributed cache. RiakKV is a high-availability distributed key-value data store that is designed to be fault-tolerant and scalable. Apache HBase is an open-source, distributed key-value store built on top of the Hadoop Distributed File System (HDFS). It is designed for large-scale, random read/write access to Big Data and is modeled after Google’s BigTable approach. Amazon DynamoDB is a fully managed key-value data store offered by Amazon Web Services (AWS). It offers features such as data replication, encryption at rest, and flexible indexing options.

The main feature of key-value stores is their conceptual simplicity. They build on the well-known technique of hashing to provide a consistent way of accessing data values that may not necessarily have a regular format. The values are held in a specialized structure, the internal details of which can be temporarily ignored by users. Values are associated with a unique key that provides a means of locating the values within the structure. A hash function is used that, given a key, provides access to the related value(s), either directly or indirectly using some form of pointer.

Such structures are supported in many programming languages. The terminology varies across different languages and such structures may be described as Hash Maps, Hash Tables, Dictionaries, Associative Arrays, and so on. The terminology is also not used consistently, so a precise definition is only relevant in the context of a specific language. For example, Python uses the term dictionary to refer to a structure containing key-value pairs. The items are ordered by key value in more recent versions of Python, but that’s not necessarily true of equivalent structures in other languages. JavaScript can simply use JSON-style Objects for the same purpose. Despite differences in syntax, all these programmatic approaches support a broadly equivalent range of operations, such as:

  • • Insert item (key, value)
  • • Update value (key, new value)
  • • Delete item (key)
  • • Retrieve value (key)
  • • Test for existence (key)

Most languages allow the types of values that can be stored to be anything expressible in that language, ranging from simple types (number, string, etc.) to items that may have their own internal structure, such as objects, lists, and perhaps even further dictionaries. Although such structures can be used within a program, they can’t be directly accessed from outside the program and must be exported in some form, such as JSON, if required externally.

Data within a program will obviously disappear when it terminates, and so key-value stores provide equivalent functionality in persistent storage. This also makes the data accessible from many different programs (assuming suitable language bindings).

We can approximate a key-value database using a relational database with a single table defined in a similar way to the following SQL fragment:

create table myKV (  theKey varchar(20) primary key,  theValue BLOB )

Here, the key is assumed to be a string of up to 20 characters, but any SQL data type could be used. The value here is a BLOB datatype that is used to contain undifferentiated binary data that is not parsed by the database. BLOB may be replaced by other types such as varbinary( ) in some SQL dialects.

Key-value stores differ from relational databases by focusing solely on the efficient storage and retrieval of complete units of data. The internal structure of a data unit can be ignored by the data store so it can be treated as a single item. This removes the need to support complex queries, as the only essential operations needed are writing and reading individual data units. The data store is no longer responsible for understanding the internal values, data types, and structure of the information. That responsibility is now devolved to applications that use it. Any changes to the internal data structure, adding or removing values, have no impact on the data store, though they obviously will within any associated application.

In addition to making storage and retrieval more efficient, this flat structure also greatly simplifies the design and implementation of a data store because its schema can be trivially simple. However, it’s important to remember that the need for a detailed schema has not gone away completely–it has simply been moved from the data store to the application.

Although key-value stores excel at rapid retrieval of data units, some also offer specific ways of operating on data values inside a unit, such as appending to a string, pushing an element to a list, and getting the member with the highest ranking in a sorted set. If the content of the data unit is encoded in some structured form such as JSON or XML, then facilities can be provided to query the content in the appropriate way.

Key-value stores are well suited to being distributed, and it’s probably not a coincidence that their rise in popularity has occurred alongside the emergence of cloud computing as a viable platform. A data store can be scaled almost indefinitely by partitioning horizontally across many servers, each of which handles its own subset of the keys and values. Resilience and performance can be improved by replication so that multiple copies can be held on different servers and accessed through an appropriate load-balancing mechanism.

Distribution does not apply in all situations; some key-value stores are designed to be held in memory to provide the fastest possible speed of retrieval. Solid-state disks are about 100 times faster than older hard disks, but RAM is orders of magnitude faster still. Distribution is much more problematic for an in-memory store, but hybrid solutions can be found. For example, an in-memory store can be used to provide a lookup between an application-based key and a server-based key that can then be used to access a distributed key-value store.

In all cases, some thought needs to be given to the design of the key. Obviously, this needs to provide unique values and must be generated consistently throughout the life of the data store. It’s a good idea to make the key as compact as possible, consistent with the need to fully identify the related data unit. Making the key somewhat human-readable can be useful for troubleshooting, providing it does not impact efficiency. In the case of distributed systems, the key must also indicate the partition to be accessed. This can be done by making the key more complex, in much the same way that a file can be uniquely identified on a computer through its file path. The key will almost certainly be indexed for rapid retrieval. In some situations, it may also be useful to provide a secondary index if values can be sought in different ways.

As already noted, there is a great deal of diversity among NoSQL databases, and this certainly applies to key-value stores. Individual systems have their own individual features, but there are some common characteristics associated with most popular key-value stores.

  • • Simplicity: Key-value stores typically offer a simple data model where data is stored as key-value pairs, making them easy to understand and use. They do not require a complex schema or complex table structures and can be easily integrated into existing applications.
  • • High performance: Key-value stores are designed for high-speed data access and low-latency operations. This is partly because they use simple data structures and avoid complex joins or indexing. They also tend to minimize disk I/O, using in-memory caching and optimizing data structures and algorithms for fast key-based lookups.
  • • Scalability: Key-value stores are easy to scale horizontally by distributing data across multiple nodes. They support sharding and partitioning techniques to handle large datasets and can grow gracefully as data volumes increase over time. This makes them a good choice for applications that need to handle a large volume of data and require high availability.
  • • Replication and fault tolerance: Key-value stores often provide replication mechanisms to ensure high availability and fault tolerance. They store redundant copies of data across multiple nodes or partitions and can provide automatic rebalancing of services in case of node failures.
  • • Flexible data models: Most key-value data stores can store a wide range of data types, including structured, semistructured, and unstructured data. This makes them useful for applications such as storing user profiles, sensor data, session data, and IoT applications that require a variety of types and formats.

Clearly, key-value stores offer some advantages that can be exploited in certain types of applications, but we must set these off against features that may make a key-value store less suitable in other circumstances.

  • • Ad hoc or complex queries are often not supported in the data store, such as searching for data with a specific feature or connections between data across different key-value pairs. Any such operations must be carried out in application code external to the data store.
  • • There are limited opportunities for operating on the data stored as the value of a key-value pair. Data retrieval is typically aimed at the efficient retrieval of the value as a unit. This also potentially makes modifications to some element within the data less efficient because the whole value must be handled as a complete data chunk.
  • • Unlike relational databases, there is no standard for the structure of key-value stores. There is little opportunity for the transfer of expertise from one key-value product to another because each uses its own proprietary functions and methodologies.
  • • Key-value stores are generally not well equipped to provide the kind of support for the ACID properties that are usually associated with relational systems. Transactions are generally limited to operations on a single data unit.
  • • There is limited scope for the validation of data or the application of constraints within the data store. Again, such operations must be carried out by the application code before the data is stored or after it is retrieved as a unit.

Identifying the right key-value store, or even deciding if a key-value store is appropriate, will depend heavily on the requirements of each individual case. Key-value stores are very well suited to applications that require rapid access to an individual unit of complex data from a very large pool of similar units. Some typical use cases include the following:

Caching. Data that is frequently accessed can be stored in a key-value data store for faster retrieval. This can help to improve application performance and reduce latency. For example, an e-commerce website may use a key-value data store to cache the product information for popular products so that the website can be served quickly without querying the traditional database every time.

Session management. A key-value data store can be useful in applications where a user’s session needs to be maintained across multiple requests or across multiple servers. Values such as log-in information and shopping cart contents can be held for quick retrieval of the information when needed.

Storing user preferences. User preferences can be stored as key-value pairs, allowing for easy retrieval and updating of user preferences. This can be useful in applications where users need to be able to customize their experience or where user preferences need to be shared across multiple devices.

Content management. Digital content is now commonplace. This includes text, images, videos, documents, and other multimedia assets. An application may need to collect diverse kinds of media into a collection that can be stored and retrieved as a single unit, which is ideally suited to a key-value store.

17.3 Column-Oriented Databases

The main difference between column-oriented databases and relational databases is how data is organized and stored rather than the logical structure of the data. A relational database stores information in tables, organized into rows and columns. A table can be thought of as information about a particular type of entity, with each row representing an individual entity of that type and the columns containing values that are relevant to that entity type. A row is often described as a record, and the related column values as fields of that record. The main focus is on managing records, so it is legitimate to describe this type of database as row-oriented.

If we need to query for specific data, the database must scan through all the rows in the table to find the relevant information. This can be aided by indexes but for large databases with millions of records, it can be slow and inefficient.

In contrast, column-oriented databases store data in columns, with each column representing a single attribute or field in a table. This means that the values for a particular attribute type are stored together in one column, regardless of which records they belong to.

When the database is queried for specific data, the database only needs to scan the relevant columns, rather than every row in the table. This can be much faster and more efficient, especially when dealing with large datasets and operations such as aggregation.

Several column-oriented database systems are available, including the following: Amazon Redshift has excellent integration with other AWS products. It provides dynamic scaling and automates many system management activities. Several open-source systems are available. PostgreSQL is a well-known row-based database, but it also has a column store option that is useful when you want to use only one database for both column and row store. MariaDB is another popular open-source database that supports both row and column storage. Apache Cassandra is a column-oriented database designed to handle large amounts of data across many commodity servers.

Fig. 17.6 shows a simple example. This does not represent any specific database product; it’s intended only to illustrate the concept. Assume that we have information about individuals and their dietary preferences. A relational table might look something like the following (with empty cells corresponding to NULL in relational terminology).

If we imagine this serialized into physical storage, it might look something like the following:

 1, Alice, glutenfree, 68, 2, Bob, NULL, 92, 3, Clare, NULL, NULL, 4, Dave, vegan, 66, 5, Edna, NULL, 78

Fig. 17.7 shows how the same information might look in a column-oriented database, assuming explicit identifiers.

The example in Fig. 17.7 is laid out in separate tabular form for comparison with the relational version, but it is also possible to visualize the name, diet, and weight “tables” as rows in a column-oriented database, as shown in Fig. 17.8. From this perspective, it’s possible to see that rows in this representation can contain a variable number of columns.

In this case, serializing the data into physical storage might look something like the following:

  1, Alice, 2, Bob, 3, Clare, 4, Dave, 5, Edna, 1, glutenfree, 4, vegan, 1, 68, 2, 92, 4, 66, 5, 78

At this simple level, we can’t see the specific detail of the data layout in persistent storage. This depends very much on the specific database being considered. Even so, it’s obvious that in one case, a retrieval will find colocated information for an entity and the other will find colocated information for an attribute. Another way of saying this might be that row-oriented retrieval gets values for the attributes of an entity, but column-oriented retrieval gets values for the entities of an attribute.

Consider a query to find the average person’s weight from this information. The relational case would require the retrieval of each row and the weight column value within the row before calculating the average value. In the column-oriented case, we simply need to retrieve the weight row in the table shown in Fig. 17.8 to get all the necessary values for the calculation. Because data retrieval from persistent storage is the most time-consuming part of the operation, this shows that the column-oriented approach has the potential for much better performance on certain types of queries. Performance is probably the greatest single motivator for this type of database, especially as the database becomes larger. In a column-oriented database, increasing amounts of data result in rows becoming bigger, not a bigger number of rows, so these are sometimes referred to as “wide tables”.

It’s important to remember that the distinctive feature of a column-oriented database is the way that the information is stored physically. From a conceptual viewpoint, we could still think of the database in the traditional manner, but we would find some types of operation more efficient and others less efficient than in a standard normalized relational database. In some cases, column-oriented databases can be queried using standard SQL, making the “NoSQL” label a little bit pointless.

The advantages of column orientation are only valid if queries operate on one column or a small number of columns. Queries involving several columns get less benefit from the localization of information from a single column. If multiple columns are frequently used together, it’s possible to add another level of organization by grouping columns into column families. For example, columns related to individual customer details (such as name, address, date of birth, etc.) could be grouped into a “Personal” column family. This can be used to ensure that the relevant columns are colocated in the database.

Column orientation provides additional opportunities for efficient storage of information. All the data from one row-oriented column (visualized as a row in a column-oriented database) is of the same type, opening possibilities for applying various types of compression to the values. An obvious instance of this is when the column contains many duplicate entries such as URLs or product names. In some cases, it may be possible to compress a column sufficiently to fit in memory for direct access, dramatically improving response time. Compression is useful because column-oriented databases are often used with very large datasets. There is also no need to allow for NULLs. An empty cell in a row-oriented database simply does not need to exist in its column-oriented equivalent.

The design of a column-oriented schema needs to consider not only the information to be stored but also how the database will be used and how it might evolve in the future. Adding a new column to the database is very easy–it can just be appended to the existing columns without impacting any existing queries. Other types of schema changes may be more problematic. Changes to query patterns can also reduce the effectiveness of the database if its design has been optimized for an anticipated scenario that no longer applies. It is also more difficult to design effective indexing schemes in the column-oriented case.

Column-oriented databases are very much skewed toward improving the efficiency of read operations (select in SQL). Operations such as insert (a new entity), update (an attribute of an existing entity), and delete (an existing entity) are generally slower because of the way the information is spread in physical storage. Also, read operations are improved only for certain types of queries. Consider the following two SQL queries:

select avg(weight) from Personselect * from Person

In a column-oriented database, the first of these will be faster but the second will be slower than the row-oriented equivalent (obviously, the differences will only be meaningful in large datasets). Generally, row-oriented operations or those involving many columns will be slower in a column-oriented database, making them unattractive for transactional applications.

Joins between tables in a column-oriented database are more complex than in the row-oriented case and are likely to have a lower performance. An alternative strategy is to consider the usage patterns of the database and define a schema that “prejoins” the relevant tables. This obviously requires additional controls to ensure the integrity of the duplicate data that will inevitably result, but the new table can then be treated in the same way as any other table with respect to a columnar arrangement. The risk here is that this optimization will make the database perform very badly if the usage patterns do not turn out to be as expected.

A major advantage of column-oriented databases is their ability to deal with very large datasets. Their structure lends itself very well to partitioning. An obvious first step is to partition the database vertically so that different columns (or perhaps column families) can be mounted on different servers. There is no need for each of these to be of the same type. Columns that are accessed less frequently can be mounted on less-powerful servers.

Within each vertical partition, there are options for further partitioning in the horizontal direction. A column can be split into shards, which, again, can be mounted on separate servers. Some additional effort is required to direct queries to the relevant shard, but this provides the potential for a huge expansion of capacity.

An additional measure to increase performance is replication: copies of the same data can be stored on multiple servers that can be accessed independently.
