This requires some kind of automated load-balancing mechanism to share queries evenly among the servers. A concern in replication is maintaining consistency between different copies of (what should be) the same data. However, as already noted, column-oriented databases are most applicable in situations with rare updates but frequent queries. Because updates are scarce in such cases, the consistency problem may be easily manageable in the right type of application.

The following characteristics summarize the features that are likely to be important in an application requiring a column-oriented database:

  • • Large amounts of data are involved, corresponding to millions of rows in more traditional row-oriented tables.
  • • Efficient use of storage is relevant, for example, in dealing with large amounts of sparse or repetitive data.
  • • Database operations are dominated by queries, with few (if any) changes to data once loaded.
  • • Queries typically use aggregation functions such as avg.(), count(), min(), max(), and sum().
  • • Each individual query involves only a small number of columns.

If we want to find a generic term to describe applications of column-oriented databases, the most appropriate is probably “analytic”, often referred to by the acronym OLAP (online analytic processing). Column orientation is not appropriate for transactional systems, often referred to by the acronym OLTP (online transactional processing). Examples of typical applications include the following:

Data warehouses and data marts: These are commonly used to extract insights from existing data. The input is usually created (or updated) by extracting data from transactional systems and reorganizing it into a more appropriate format. Information is added not on a row-by-row basis, but by bulk loading, which can be quite efficient.

Scientific research: Scientific research applications can involve complex queries across large datasets, making column-oriented databases a natural fit. Researchers can use these databases to analyze data quickly and efficiently, allowing them to focus on their research rather than on managing data.

Financial trading: Financial trading applications often require real-time access to large volumes of data. Column-oriented databases are specifically designed to handle data of this type, allowing traders to access information quickly and accurately.

Analysis of historical data: Stored data can be modeled and analyzed using various statistical and logical methods and techniques to gain insights of various types, such as descriptive, exploratory, predictive, diagnostic, and prescriptive viewpoints.

17.4 Document Databases

In Chapter 3, we discussed how reports and other documents can be analyzed and expressed in terms of elementary fact types. Modeling these fact types in ORM, along with the relevant constraints, leads to a model that can form the basis for a database schema. Document databases take a different approach by storing documents directly using their original structure, so, as the name suggests, a database of this type consists of collections of documents. Because no preanalysis of documents is necessary, it seems possible to add any kind of document to any collection without any kind of preparation. In principle, this promises a great deal of flexibility, but in practice, some degree of control is required to have any hope of making the database manageable over its lifetime.

Several document database systems are available, including the following: MongoDB is one of the most popular document databases. It stores data in flexible, JSON-like documents and allows for dynamic schemas. Couchbase is a distributed NoSQL database that offers high performance and scalability. It’s commonly used for applications requiring real-time data updates, caching, and mobile synchronization.

CouchDB is an open-source document database focused on ease of replication and conflict resolution. Document databases are available from cloud service providers such as Amazon DocumentDB and Google Firestore. Finally, MarkLogic is a NoSQL database that supports flexible schema design and stores data in XML or JSON documents. It’s commonly used for applications that require complex data modeling and querying. The examples in this chapter are based on MongoDB, though other document database systems have broadly similar capabilities to the ones we will discuss.

Documents are typically expressed using the structural capabilities of JSON, previously described in Chapter 16. Internally, the information storage may adopt BSON, a binary form of JSON that incorporates additional metadata to make data scans faster and can also reduce storage requirements, but we will ignore this detail.

A document database is formed from collections. Each collection contains documents of a similar kind: for example, Products, Orders, Customers, and so on. Each document can contain several fields, but the data in a field need not be single-valued as it would be in a normalized relational database–a field can contain a structure that, in turn, can contain other structures and so on. There is a rough correspondence between these concepts and their relational equivalents, as shown in Table 17.1.

Table 17.1

Comparison of RelationalDB and Document DB concepts.

To illustrate some features of this type of structure, the following example shows two documents from a hypothetical Contracts collection:

  •   Contracts: [
  •             {
  •                         _id: ObjectId("6481d941f682789c3b8d71ef"),
  •                         contractRef: 9876,
  •                         activeDate: "Jan 1 2024",
  •                         customerId: "DE876",
  •                         staffAllocation: [ { person: "Alice123", hours: 15 },{ person: "Bob456", hours: 35 } ]
  •             },
  •             {
  •                         _id: ObjectId("64820117f682789c3b8d71f0"),
  •                         contractRef: 8765,
  •                         startDate: "Jan 12 2024",
  •                         customerId: 2024002,
  •                         staffAllocation: {
  •                         marketing: [ { person: "Carol999", hours: 5 } ],
  •                operations: [ { person: "Bob456", hours: 5 }, { person: "Dave666", hours: 30 } ]
  •                         },
  •                         contractType: "FP"
  •             }
  •   ]

Six points to be noted for this example may be summarized as follows:

  1. 1. The _id field has been automatically generated to provide a unique identifier for each document. For simplicity, we’ll ignore this feature in subsequent examples.
  2. 2. The names of the same fields in different documents need not be consistent. The activeDate field in the first document and the startDate in the second document may refer to the same business concept, but they do not have the same field name.
  3. 3. The data types for the same field need not be the same in different documents. The customerId field is alphanumeric in the first document, but numeric in the second document.
  4. 4. Fields can be multivalued and can also contain other documents, as with staffAllocation in the two documents.
  5. 5. The internal structure of each document in a collection need not be the same. The staffAllocation field is a list in the first document, but an object (in the JSON sense) that contains multiple lists in the second document.
  6. 6. Different documents in the same collection need not contain the same fields. The contractType field appears in the second document but is absent in the first document.

This kind of flexibility is sometimes claimed as a great advantage of document databases over the relational alternative, where each row in a table (equivalent to each document in a collection) has a fixed structure with defined data types for each column (equivalent to each field in a document). While this flexibility makes it easy to add documents without worrying about any kind of schema, it makes other operations on such an uncontrolled database an almost impossible task to manage. Even something as simple as retrieving the value of a particular field could require an examination of the collection to determine all variants of the field name to write a sufficiently robust query. In the example above, listing all the dates when contracts began would need to query for both startDate and activeDate (and any other name variants that might have been used).

It is possible to add a validator to a collection to constrain the documents it contains to an acceptable structure. This can include checks for mandatory fields, data types, value ranges, and so on. In effect, a validator can provide something like a schema for an individual relational table.

Write operations for a document are atomic, as the document is either written in full or not at all. Writes involving multiple documents can be transactional, but this involves some additional effort. A session must be created for each update, and then the sessions must be combined so that all the updates are completed together or not at all. This is the same whether the collections are physically stored together on the same server or distributed over multiple servers. Such operations have a big impact on performance, and the general recommendation is to adjust the schema to avoid this situation if possible. For example, instead of a transactional update to collection A and to collection B, it may be possible to define a new AB collection so that the update can be handled by a single write operation.

Linking Data

Inserting, retrieving, and managing individual documents is relatively straightforward, but in any realistic database, there will almost certainly be a need to link different documents together. This can be seen as the equivalent of foreign key references in a relational database. There are two ways of achieving this in a document database. To provide some examples, assume that we have (highly simplified) documents relating to students and their grades in university courses.

The first approach to linking courses and students with customers is embedding. In general, if Document1 needs to be linked to Document2, this can be achieved by nesting one document within the other. In this example, we’ll assume that the Course document contains the Student details.

 {  "Courses": [     {"_id": "DB102",     "courseName": "Databases",     "creditValue": 15,     "Students": [         {"studentId": "12345", "name": "Abby Akbar", "grade": 3.4},         {"studentId": "67890", "name": "Bill Briggs", "grade": 3.2}         ]     },     {"_id": "SW101",     "courseName": "Python",     "creditValue": 10,     "Students": [         {"studentId": "12345", "name": "Abby Akbar", "grade": 3.8}         ]      }  ] }

It would also be possible to embed a list of Courses into a Student document, using the standard JSON structuring. Which of these would be preferable depends on the anticipated usage of the data. In this case, although we have two different kinds of information (Courses and Students), we end up with only one document collection: either Courses (as above) or Students, depending on how we decided to embed the documents.

It’s clear that embedding the data in this way will result in redundancy, corresponding to denormalization in a relational database. Given the falling cost of hardware, the need for additional storage space might be acceptable. More serious is the problem of maintaining consistency. In the example above, if we realize that Abby Akhbar’s name may have been misspelled, we must locate all the Course documents that may include her name to make the necessary changes. If this is not done rigorously, the result is an unreliable data store that is very difficult to manage. If, instead, we had embedded Courses into Students, an update to the Course details would entail accessing all Student documents.

The alternative approach to embedding is referencing. This concept is much closer to the way that foreign key references are used in a relational database. Using the same example as above, we could put Course documents and Student documents into different collections, as in the following example.

  •   {
  •        "Courses": [
  •              {"_id": "DB102",
  •                       "courseName": "Databases",
  •                       "creditValue": 15,},
  •                       {"_id": "SW101",
  •                       "courseName": "Python",
  •                       "creditValue": 10,}
  •        ]
  •   }
  •   {
  •        "Students": [
  •                       {"_id": "12345",
  •                       "name": "Abby Akbar",
  •                       "courses": [ {"courseId": "DB102", "grade": 3.4},
  •                                     "courseId": "SW101", "grade": 3.8} ]
  •                       },
  •                       {"_id": "67890",
  •                       "name": "Bill Briggs",
  •                       "courses": [ {"courseId": "DB102", "grade": 3.2} ]
  •                       }
  •        ]
  •   }

Here, the two collections contain a list of Course documents and a list of Student documents, respectively. The relationships between students and courses are recorded by references from Student documents to the identifiers of Course documents. This avoids the data redundancy of the previous example, but introduces other issues. For instance, if we want to obtain the total value of credits gained by a student, we have to read additional Course documents to get the necessary information. This is roughly the equivalent of a join in a relational system.

The relationship between Courses and Students is many-to-many (so in the example above, a Student document needs to contain references to multiple Course documents). We could resolve this by inventing a new Course-Student document, equivalent to a linking table in a relational system. However, this could be rejected as an unnatural artifice. Thinking of a paper-based equivalent in the real world, it’s quite plausible that there could be Course documents and Student documents, but a Course-Student document would be unlikely.

In designing a document database, the choice between embedding and referencing depends on finding the right balance between several competing factors.

First, we need to identify the significant document types. If we are starting from scratch, we can develop an object-role model (ORM) to clarify the information structure relevant to our concerns. From this, we can use relational mapping (as discussed in Chapter 11) to derive a set of candidate document types that could be represented in the appropriate JSON format. Alternatively, we may want to base our design on preexisting documents, respecifying these in JSON format if they have some other form (CSV, XML, …).

The next set of decisions is highly dependent on the expected usage of the documents. Broadly speaking, we want a document to be as big as it needs to be but not bigger. This may indicate that some candidate documents should be split to improve performance (there may be a database-imposed size limit on individual documents, but this is usually large enough not to be a concern). In thinking about relationships between documents, we need to know the relative frequency of the usual Create, Read, Update, Delete (CRUD) operations on the data. It’s quite common for Read operations to dominate, but that’s not always the case.

If we consider two document types, A and B, that are related in some way, here are some of the kinds of scenarios that might be relevant.

  • • If A and B are often queried together, consider embedding A in B, or B in A (whichever gives the optimum performance).
  • • Long lists are inefficient, so if embedding B in A results in long lists of Bs, consider referencing instead.
  • • If B is rarely queried in isolation, consider embedding B in A.
  • • If B is embedded in A, but B is associated with many other document types, consider referencing instead.
  • • If B is embedded in A, and B is updated much more frequently than A, consider referencing instead.

Partitioning

Partitioning in a document database usually refers to horizontal partitioning. Something akin to vertical partitioning could be achieved by splitting a document type to make two new document types, each containing a different subset of the original document fields, but this is an intrinsic part of the original database design. Horizontal partitioning can be based on any part of a document, but the choice is determined by the way that the database is expected to be used. Each partition, or “shard”, can hold a subset of the documents in a collection and is physically distinct from other shards. A crucial decision is the selection of the field or fields to be used as the basis for distribution. As with other aspects, this will depend on the expected pattern of usage of the database. For example, if queries often focus on data within a given year, it may be appropriate to assign a separate shard for each year and use a relevant date field as the basis for distribution.

Each document in a collection is assigned a shard key value based on the relevant field(s). The shard key should be chosen to distribute data evenly across the shards to prevent hotspots and ensure balanced performance. Each shard in the database maintains metadata that maps ranges of shard key values to specific shards. When an operation is performed, the database client includes the shard key value in the query or command sent to the cluster. This is handled by a specialized router that examines the shard key, determines which shards need to be involved in executing the operation, and then formulates a plan for executing the query across the relevant shards.

Assuming a query involving several shards, the router sends the parts of the query to the appropriate shards based on the shard key range for which the shard is responsible. Each shard locally executes its part of the query and returns partial results to the router containing the subset of the overall results specific to that particular shard. Once the router receives results from all shards, it combines them to form a complete result set. This may involve sorting, merging, and applying any additional query operations (e.g., filtering) to match the original query criteria. Finally, the router sends the merged result set back to the client application, providing a unified view of the query results as if it had been executed on a single nonsharded database.

The collection and merging of distributed results obviously impose a performance penalty, so the choice of shard key needs to be considered carefully. Ideally, the partitioning should be designed so that most queries can be addressed to a single shard within the cluster.

Indexing

As with Relational databases, document databases can use indexing to improve the performance of queries by creating data structures that allow for efficient data retrieval. As with other aspects of schema design, it’s important to have a clear strategy for indexing. Although indexing can improve query performance, it will also have an impact on write performance and will increase storage requirements.

The application(s) using the database should be examined for the type of queries used and their relative frequency. Based on the number and type of operations, the appropriate index types can be identified. Several types are available, including:

  • • Single Field Index: The most basic type of index where queries are based on a single field.
  • • Compound Index: Created on multiple fields, combining them into a single index.
  • • Multikey Index: Separately indexes elements of an array.

There are also other types of indexes for more specialized applications, such as Text, Geospatial, and Hashed indexes.

Indexes are created using an operation to specify the collection and fields to be indexed, along with any additional options that might be required, such as creating the index in the background to mimimize disruption. For example, we could create a Single Field index on a courseName field in a Courses collection as follows:

   db.Courses.createIndex( { courseName: 1 } )

Here, the digit 1 indicates that the index should be in ascending order; descending order would be indicated by a − 1 parameter.

It’s also important to handle updates and deletes carefully in document databases. Unlike relational databases, document databases do not enforce referential integrity or cascading deletes. It’s up to the developer to ensure that updates and deletes are performed correctly, without leaving orphaned data or breaking relationships.

Referential integrity is a concept commonly associated with relational databases, where relationships among tables are maintained and enforced using foreign keys. In a document database, which follows a NoSQL data model, referential integrity is not natively provided in the same way. However, referential integrity-like patterns and mechanisms can be employed to ensure data consistency and relationships among documents. Embedding and Referencing can provide some degree of integrity, as described above. Additional measures can include:

  • • Transactions, allowing multiple operations on different documents atomically to ensure data consistency across the affected documents. While transactions do not enforce referential integrity, they can help maintain data consistency among related documents.
  • • Triggers and Hooks, which allow custom logic to run before or after specific database operations, such as insert, update, or delete. These can be used to implement custom referential integrity checks and ensure that related documents remain consistent during data modification operations.
  • • Application code, external to the database, can be augmented with additional functionality to ensure that data modifications conform to the desired relationships and integrity constraints before persisting them to the database.

Database Queries

Because of their NoSQL status, document databases do not include the familiar select statement from SQL. However, they do provide equivalent facilities in their own query language. We will use MongoDB as an example (https://www.mongodb.com) and its MQL query language. The language allows similar functionality through functions that allow operations such as selection, projection, filtering, sorting and aggregation. Here, we will look at a few simple examples to give an impression of the scope available.

Selection is handled through a find( ) function, which contains the query criteria expressed as a JSON object. For example, we find relevant documents in a Courses collection as follows:

   db.Courses.find( { creditValue: { $gt: 12 } } )

In this example, $gt is a query operator used to specify “greater than”, so the function would return Courses with a credit value greater than 12. Other common query operators include $eq, $ne, $gt, $lt, $in, $exists, etc.

Projection allows fields to be included or excluded in the query results using projection. A parameter is used to specify the fields to be included (1) or excluded (0).

   db.Courses.find( { }, { courseName: 1,  _id: 0 } )

In this example, the names of courses would be returned, but the associated _id field would be suppressed.

Query results can be sorted based on one or more fields. The sort( ) method specifies the fields to sort and the sort order, either ascending (1) or descending (−1).

   db.Courses.find( ).sort( { creditValue: -1, courseName: 1 } )

Aggregation provides the ability to perform data transformations and calculations. The aggregation function can be applied in a simple way, as in the following.

   db.Courses.aggregate( [ $avg { "$creditValue" } ] )

This provides the average creditValue for all Courses. However, the aggregate function is much more powerful than this because it can contain a “pipeline”, a list of operations arranged so that the output of one operation becomes the input to the next operation. This allows complex operations combining grouping, summing, sorting, averaging, and so on. A typical sequence might be:

   $project −> $match −> $group −> $sort

nested within the aggregate( ) function.

In general, we can see that the functionality available is similar to that provided by relational systems, though realized differently. The attractions of the document model include flexibility in the representation of data and the possibilities for partitioning. Against this must be set issues such as the need to maintain the consistency of replicated data and the complexity of transactions involving multiple documents.

Document databases are an obvious choice where the data to be stored can be visualized in terms of groups of values that share a common theme or purpose. This is certainly the case where the database is being used to store the electronic equivalent of traditional business documents such as statements, application forms, specifications, and so on. Other application areas where document databases are popular include:

Content management systems (CMS), used to store and manage various types of material such as articles, images, videos, and metadata used in support of websites and other applications.

Management of catalogs, also directories or listings such as business directories, real estate listings, and online marketplaces, which can benefit from the ability to store diverse data structures within a single database.

Storing user profiles and preferences to enable personalized experiences in applications such as social networks, online forums, and streaming platforms.

Managing healthcare information such as patient records, medical histories, test results, and treatment plans that form well-bounded units of information.

E-commerce platforms, used to manage product catalogs, user profiles, customer reviews, and order histories while providing flexibility to accommodate changing product attributes and relationships.

17.5 Graph Databases

Graph databases use a property graph model to represent and store data. The basic graph structure consists of nodes and relationships (edges). Each node represents an entity, object, or data point, and each relationship represents a connection or association between two nodes.

Nodes are the fundamental units of a property graph. Each node can have one or more properties that store data attributes or characteristics associated with the node. For example, in a social network graph, a node could represent a person, and node properties could include attributes related to that person.

Relationships define the connections or associations between nodes. They represent the links or interactions between entities. Relationships can also have properties that provide additional information about the connection. For instance, in a social network graph, relationships might represent “friendship” connections between people, and relationship properties could include the date the friendship was established.

Properties are key-value pairs associated with both nodes and relationships. They store specific attributes or data values related to the corresponding node or relationship. For example, a node representing a person might have properties such as “name”, “age”, and “email”.

Graph databases offer several advantages over relational databases, especially when dealing with highly connected and complex data structures. In a relational database, it’s possible to imagine a connection between a pair of tables by following the relationships between intermediate tables. However, if the two tables are widely separated (i.e., there are many intermediate tables), then the query becomes complex, and the cost of the multiple joins can be significant. Traversing relationships in a graph is a direct operation, which makes querying for highly connected data very fast. As the size of the graph grows, graph databases maintain consistent performance, making them scalable solutions for applications with expanding relationships.

Graph databases typically have a flexible schema, allowing nodes and relationships to have different properties without strict constraints. This adaptability can be beneficial in scenarios where the data model evolves over time, as changes can be made without altering the entire schema, which can be cumbersome in a relational database. Relationships between data points are stored directly, making the data model more intuitive and easier to work with when the relationships are the primary focus of the application. They also represent hierarchical data structures (which are common in some domains) in an efficient way.

The schema flexibility in graph databases makes them well suited for scenarios where data models are subject to change, relationships are dynamic, and applications require adaptability and agility in data representation. However, a more flexible schema implies fewer constraints in the database, and so structure and constraints may need to be defined through the application logic, rather than through a centralized schema definition enforced by the database itself.

In terms of database products, Neo4j is often considered the market leader, partly due to its early adoption and strong ecosystem. Amazon Neptune also has a notable presence due to its integration with other AWS services. Other graph databases such as ArangoDB, JanusGraph, and Stardog have their own niches and user bases, and some are able to integrate with other types of NoSQL systems such as document and column-oriented databases.

To provide some concrete examples of graph database features, we’ll use Neo4j (www.neo4j.com). Its underlying graph processing engine is optimized for traversing and navigating graphs efficiently, making graph traversals and pattern-matching operations fast and scalable. It uses a language called Cipher to write graph queries and to carry out the usual CRUD types of operation. An Enterprise Edition provides advanced facilities for commercial operation, but we will focus on the facilities provided by the Community Edition.

Unlike other types of NoSQL databases, graph databases do not lend themselves to horizontal partitioning. The entire database resides on a single server, so as the database grows the server must be scaled vertically. Performance can be improved by providing a server cluster so that different read operations can be directed to different servers in the cluster to share the load, but updates are made through a master that then replicates changes to other servers in the cluster. Within a server, Neo4j supports ACID transactions to ensure data integrity and consistency.

Although there are some high-level similarities between relational and graph databases, the differences are considerable at the detail level. In the relational case, the most fundamental element is a table, whereas in the graph case, it is a node. However, these correspond to different kinds of concepts. A relational table relates to a particular type of object, but a graph node relates to an instance of a type. The notion of a node type certainly exists in graph databases; in Neo4j, it is referred to as a “label”.

All nodes with the same label can be assumed to have similar properties. If a property value is unknown (or not relevant), a relational database will hold a NULL in the corresponding cell of the table. In the graph database equivalent, the property will simply not exist (i.e., NULLs are not stored).

There is an equivalent dichotomy when we consider the relationships between objects. In the relational database case, this is defined at the table level with foreign key references, perhaps to “join” or “link” tables for many-to-many relationships. This cements the relationship at the type level. In a graph database, relationships are defined between nodes at the instance level, which does not depend on the multiplicity of types, so relationships between instances are simply relationships.

This has implications when we consider the kinds of relationships that can be accommodated in a database. In the relational case, all instances (rows in a table) must comply with the same relationship structure, but in the graph case, different nodes with the same label could have different relationships. Comparing this back to a relational system, it’s as though each row in a table could have its own individual foreign key references that differ from other rows in the table. The graph approach provides great flexibility to express complex relationships, but complicates the documentation needed to allow subsequent explorations of those relationships.

Another difference is the approach to data typing. SQL defines a range of data types, and all values in a table column are constrained to be of one specific type such as int, char, float, and so on (or perhaps null if a value is absent). In the community edition of Neo4j, the properties of nodes and relations are not preconstrained to a particular data type. Values have a type (string, integer, and so on) but properties do not, so, for example, a property may hold an integer value that later gets updated to a string value.

Graph Database Queries

Data querying in a graph database involves retrieving information from the graph by specifying patterns of nodes and relationships that match the desired data. Graph databases typically have their own query languages optimized for graph traversal and pattern matching, and Neo4j provides a language called Cypher.

Queries in a graph database often involve matching specific patterns of nodes and relationships. Cypher can be used to specify patterns, filter nodes based on properties, and include or exclude relationships based on certain criteria. Data can be retrieved using the match keyword, which is roughly the equivalent of select in SQL. The following query returns all the properties for a particular Customer node.

match ( c:Customer {customerID:"ABCDE"} ) return c

Indexing can be used to allow faster lookup of nodes and relationships based on specified properties, although this has the usual effect of slowing updates.

Cypher queries can include conditions based on node and relationship properties. This allows data to be filtered based on the values of attributes associated with nodes and relationships in a similar way to SQL, for example, by using a where clause. Results can also be organized in a similar way to SQL, for example, by using an order by clause. Aggregation functions are available to summarize data across nodes and relationships, again in a similar way to SQL using functions such as count( ), sum( ) and avg( ).

A particular strength of graph databases is the ease of graph traversal, which involves navigating from one node to another through relationships to find data that matches certain criteria or patterns. Paths between nodes can be specified as a fixed length or a variable length with specified limits. A library of functions is provided to implement many graph algorithms, such as breadth-first and depth-first search, shortest path, page rank, and others. Queries of this kind are much harder to implement in a relational database.

Before data can be entered into a relational database, it must first be populated with tables, which, in turn, will have been created in accordance with some schema. A graph database does not require this kind of preparation, as nodes and edges can simply be added as needed. In a sense, we could say that the schema of a graph database emerges from the create, update, and delete operations carried out on it.

This should not be taken too far. A completely ad hoc approach can lead to a database that does not give reliable results and is impossible to maintain. One of the important benefits of a schema is that it defines a vocabulary for a given application area so that all participants can communicate in a consistent way. For example, we could have the following facts in a graph database:

 Holmes – WATCHED -> Watson Holmes – OBSERVED -> Watson Holmes – NOTICED -> Watson Holmes – RECOGNIZED -> Watson

Each of these could be a plausible record of some event. Listed together in this way, the problem is obvious, but in practice, the individual entries could be made by different people at different times who may not be aware of other data that has been entered. Can we query the database to confirm that Holmes SAW Watson? Not according to this data!

Populating a Graph Database

In SQL, objects are created by an insert statement that adds the relevant values to a table. Relationships are created in the same way by inserting the destination key in the source table, so no separate insert is required. In a graph database, nodes and relations are separate items and so are created separately.

The following example shows the general style of node creation:

merge ( :Customer { customerId: "ABCDE" } )

This creates a node with a label (i.e., node type) of Customer with a given property. The individual node can be identified by using the customerId property in any subsequent queries. The keyword create can be used in place of merge, the difference being that if a matching node already exists (in this case, a Customer node with the same customerId), merge will do nothing but create will introduce a duplicate node. A constraint can be added to enforce uniqueness of a property value. Adding the constraint automatically creates an index on the unique property.

create constraint cust_id_uniq for (c:Customer)require c.customerID is unique

In a relational database, the absence of a value is indicated by a null in the relevant table cell. In a graph database, null has a slightly different interpretation. Properties do not have null as a value; null just indicates that the property doesn’t exist. This means that nonexistence and null are equivalent for properties of nodes and relationships. A property can be constrained to be not null, which in Neo4j is equivalent to saying that it must exist.

create constraint cust_existence for (c:Customer)require c.customerID is not null

The combination of uniqueness and existence constraints on a property provides something roughly equivalent to a primary key in a relational database.

The same merge or create keywords are used to insert relations. The Cypher notation allows the direction of the relation to be specified, as in the following example:

merge (:Customer {customerID:"ABCDE"}) -[:PURCHASED]-> (:Order {orderID:12345})

This will create the specified Customer and Order nodes together with a directed PURCHASED relationship between them. Adding a relationship between two existing nodes requires a slightly different strategy. We first find the relevant nodes by querying the database, and then use references to those nodes in creating the relationship, as in the following example.

match ( c:Customer { customerID:"ABCDE" } )match ( o:Order { orderID:12345 } )merge ( c ) - [ :PURCHASED ] -> ( o )

For large datasets, batch insertion methods can be used to insert multiple nodes and relationships in a single transaction. Utilities are also provided for the bulk import of data from external sources, such as CSV files or other databases.

Updating and Deleting

One of the most common update operations is modifying the properties of nodes and relationships. The relevant nodes or relationships can be found through a query, and the update applied to the results of the query. As with creation, batch update methods can be used to update multiple nodes and/or relationships in a single transaction. The following example shows a simple Cypher update data in a graph database:

match ( c:Customer { companyName: "Tamale Spice" } )set c.country = "Mexico"

Here, the variable c is bound to a specific Customer, and its country property is then set to the specified value. If the property value already exists, it will be replaced by the new value. If the property does not exist, it will be created. An existing property can be deleted completely by removing it. This is equivalent to setting the relevant table cell to null in a relational database.

match ( c:Customer { companyName: "Tamale Spice" } )remove c.country

A complete node (or set of nodes) can be deleted along with all associated properties using appropriate filter conditions.

match ( c:Customer )where c.country = "Mexico"delete c

This will have the effect of deleting all data for Customers located in Mexico, and of course:

match ( x ) delete x

could delete all nodes in the database, so it’s important to get the filtering conditions correct.

Comparison With Relational Databases

Table 17.2 lists some comparisons between the two database types (taking Neo4j as representative of graph databases).

Table 17.2

Comparison of relational and graph databases.

To illustrate the differences in structure between the two approaches, we can look at a typical customer-order-product scenario. This is similar to the well-known “Northwind” example database, but only a few properties are shown here to make the model more compact.

Fig. 17.9 shows a fragment of the table structure. The OrderDetails join table is used to resolve the many-to-many relationship that exists between Orders and Products.

The graph database equivalent of this structure that contains the same information is shown in Fig. 17.10. The properties associated with each element are shown for clarity. Note that there is no need for an OrderDetails node type between Orders and Products. In the graph model, each Order-Product combination is a separate relation, and the associated quantity value is simply a property of that relation.

Assume that we need to know the names of all customers who have ordered the product “Tofu”. In the relational case, we can express this in SQL using the following query:

select distinct customerName from Customersjoin Orders on Customers.customerId = Orders.customerIdjoin OrderDetails on Orders.orderId = OrderDetails.orderIdjoin Products on OrderDetails.productId = Products.productIdwhere Product.productName = "Tofu"

Here, the distinct keyword is used to avoid duplicates if the same customer has ordered the product more than once. The equivalent query in Neo4j can be expressed in the Cypher language as follows:

match ( c:Customer ) - [ :PURCHASED ] -> ( :Order ) - [ :ORDERS ] -> ( p:Product )where p.productName = "Tofu"return distinct c.companyName

In the Cypher query, the variables c and p are bound to nodes with labels Customers and Products, respectively. No bindings are required for Orders nodes or the two relationships.

Mapping ORM to a Graph Database

Chapter 11 discussed the mapping of an ORM model to a relational structure and presented a systematic procedure (Rmap) to produce a redundancy-free relational design. We’ll now consider the possibility of an equivalent approach for a graph database.

Fig. 17.11 shows a simple ORM model (constraints omitted, as discussed later) and a comparable graph model showing node labels. Leaving aside the obvious differences in graphical notation, it’s clear that the two models are very similar in structure.

At this simple level, it appears that an ORM model could potentially be taken as a direct definition of a graph schema. Unfortunately, things become more complicated when we get into the detail. The first difficulty is that graph databases can only represent binary relationships.

An ORM fact type of any other arity must be mapped to something structurally different in a graph model.

A unary fact type can be mapped to a graph property (normally a node property) or a binary relationship in a fairly straightforward way. Ternary or higher fact types must be remapped to binary relationships, perhaps involving multiple binary relationships for one ORM fact type. This may require additional constraints to preserve the intent of the original ORM model.

However, this raises the next difficulty, which is that graph databases generally provide very limited constraint options. In Neo4j, the only options are uniqueness and nonnull constraints (although a few more are available in the Enterprise Edition). It may be possible to work around these by taking care in the framing of create or update statements to preserve an appropriate structure, but for many ORM constraints, the only realistic solution is to implement the constraints in the application, not in the database.

A final difference in capability is the notion of subtypes. It is certainly possible to express subtyping notions in graph form, for example:

   ( :Species ) – [ :IS_MEMBER_OF ] -> ( :Genus ) – [ :IS_MEMBER_OF ] -> ( :Family ) ...

but the relationship is not distinguished in any way from other types of relationships. Similar considerations about absorption, separation, and partitioning arise when deciding if subtypes can be combined under one label or if different node labels are preferable. Any constraints involved in an ORM subtype relationship face the same issues as n-ary relationships and may need to be enforced in the related application code.

Despite these difficulties, the similarities between an ORM schema and a graph schema remain strong, and it’s possible to outline a systematic procedure for ORM-to-graph mapping, which we could call Gmap. This could run on similar lines to the Rmap procedure, following a series of steps to coerce the result into the appropriate form.

This is best illustrated with a concrete example. Chapter 11 discussed the application of the Rmap procedure to several models, including the TV channel model reproduced here as Fig. 17.12. This can provide the basis for a useful comparison between the two approaches. This model shows a number of features that must be accommodated in any possible Gmap procedure.

Any one-to-one fact type can be resolved by combining the two object types so that one becomes a property of the other. Which object type should be considered the “parent” is usually obvious from the model, but in some cases an arbitrary choice must be made. In this model, we can make Frequency a property of Channel and ProgramTitle a property of Program. This is essentially the same strategy as in the Rmap procedure.

The TimeSlot object type in the ORM model has a composite identifier: Day and Hour. Composite identifiers may be difficult to replicate in a graph database, so it might be necessary to introduce a surrogate identifier. In this case, we could form a timeSlotCode by concatenating Day and Hour, but it’s not necessary because the TimeSlot is only relevant in the context of a particular Program.

Fact types with spanning uniqueness constraints will become relations in the graph model. For ternary or higher constraints, a choice must be made as to the best labels to use as the two ends of the relation because relations can only be binary in the graph model. The other roles will become properties of the relation. For the quaternary fact type in this model, we can set a relationship between Survey and Channel, with Category and Rating as properties.

Objectified fact types also map to relations, with any functionally dependent fact types indicating properties of the relation. This will apply to “Office” and “Department” in this case. A functional dependency between two objectified fact types introduces a further complication, to be discussed shortly.

Fact types with functional roles attached to the same object type can be grouped into the same node type (label), becoming properties of the “parent”. In this model, the MoneyAmount object type can become a “worth” property of a Channel node and an “assets” property of a Company node.

The result so far is summarized in Fig. 17.13. In this figure, tentative node labels are shown in bold, and properties of nodes and relations are shown in italics to make the distinctions clearer.

We can immediately see a problem. A relation must be between two nodes and cannot be between a relation and a node. We can resolve the problem by moving the DepartmentKind relationship to Suburb. Recall that a graph schema is never created explicitly, as it is simply a high-level summary of labels for nodes and their relationships created in the database.

We can have multiple nodes with the same Suburb label but with different names. This allows a channel to be located in multiple suburbs, and multiple channels to be located in the same suburb. Similarly, a suburb can have multiple department kinds, and the same department kind can be in multiple suburbs. Fig. 17.14 shows a small example.

The final graph schema is shown in Fig. 17.15. All the data items from the original ORM model are recorded as properties of nodes or relations and all fact types are covered explicitly as relations or implicitly by structure.

We also need to consider the constraints specified in the ORM model. This is potentially problematic because of the very limited constraint options available in the graph database equivalent. Some workaround possibilities exist through careful framing of statements that modify the structure, but this may not always be possible.

Mandatory constraints can be enforced to some extent by requiring that, for example, a property of a label is not null, but this can be a nuisance if the property value is not known when the relevant node is created.

Uniqueness constraints are available in Neo4j and can be used where appropriate. In the model above, the identifying properties for Company, Channel, Survey, and Program can be defined as unique. This means that, for example, there will only be one node with the label “Channel” and a ChannelNumber property equal to “1”. However, this should not be done in the case of Suburb, Department, or TimeSlot because these labels can have multiple nodes with the same property, as can be seen in Fig. 17.14. These nodes can be distinguished from each other by having different instances of their relations with other nodes.

The external uniqueness constraint between the Channel role and the TimeSlot role is more difficult. We need to ensure that a TimeSlot can only relate to one Program for a given Channel, although the same TimeSlot can be used by other channels for their own programs. There is no constraint in Neo4j to express this, but we could specify the creation of the IS_SHOWN_IN relation between a specific Program and a specific TimeSlot using the following strategy:

  1. 1. Use a query to find the Channel that shows the specified Program.
  2. 2. Use a query to find any Program shown by that Channel in the specified TimeSlot.
  3. 3. If the result is null, create the IS_SHOWN_IN relation between Program and TimeSlot.

ORM has a very rich constraint language, and it may not be worthwhile to try to write complex Cipher code to capture the full intent of the ORM model. In such cases, it may be better to delegate the constraint to the application code instead of trying to enforce it in the database.

It’s clear from this example that there is a close affinity between ORM and graph databases, which is perhaps not surprising because an ORM model is itself a graph. Graph databases offer a useful alternative to relational systems in applications that are focused more on relationships than data processing. They share many of the same issues on scalability as relational systems, but can provide high availability by replicating servers.

Translating an ORM model into a graph database can be done in a systematic way that preserves most of the intent of the ORM model, though some creativity may be required in dealing with constraints. For a specific graph database system, it would be feasible to automate a Gmap procedure to generate a schema design, possibly including some code (in the appropriate language) to deal with issues such as constraints.

Probably the most important feature of graph databases is their ability to follow links through a connected network of data, perhaps extending over long chains of connections.

Many common problems can be expressed in terms of searches through data space, and there are well-known algorithms to perform this in an efficient way. These capabilities make graph databases a popular choice in application areas such as the following:

  • • Modeling and querying social network data and other interpersonal relationships.
  • • Creating recommendations for users of a system by analyzing their preferences and activities.
  • • Identifying patterns of fraudulent behavior by analyzing connections between entities.
  • • Building knowledge graphs that represent semantic relationships between entities.
  • • Analyzing connections between individuals, organizations, and events in criminal investigations.

17.6 Other Nonrelational Databases

A conceptual schema may be mapped to various logical data models. The Rmap procedure discussed in Chapter 11 assumes that the application platform is a centralized, relational DBMS. It is a fairly simple task to specify other procedures for mapping to other types of DBMSs, as we’ve seen earlier in this chapter.

Although relational DBMSs have long been dominant in the commercial marketplace, many alternatives exist. These include older systems based on the hierarchic or network data model as well as newer alternatives such as those discussed previously. While purely relational DBMSs suit most business applications, they may not be the ideal match for some specialized applications such as computer-aided software engineering (CASE) tools, computer-aided design tools (e.g., VLSI design, mechanical engineering, architecture), document processing, spatial databases, expert systems, scientific databases (e.g., genetic engineering), and communications management. Note that most of these applications involve complex objects and probably account for at most 10% of database applications.

Many reasons are cited for dissatisfaction with purely relational DBMSs for complex applications. They may be too slow–they don’t perform well with complex objects mainly because they require too many table joins. They often model objects in an unnatural way (e.g., information about a single object such as a person may be spread over several tables–this gets worse with complex objects). They are dependent on value-based identifiers. They don’t facilitate reuse (e.g., they have no direct support for subtyping). They require access to a procedural language for difficult tasks (e.g., special rules and behavior), which leads to an “impedance mismatch” with the declarative, set-based, relational query language. They might not support binary large objects (BLOBs) such as images (icons, pictures, maps etc.), sound tracks, video, and so on.

Object Orientation

An object database (ODB), or object-oriented database (OODB), incorporates various object-oriented features. Historically, ODB research drew upon related developments in four areas: programming languages, semantic data models, logical data models, and artificial intelligence.

With programming languages, the need was seen for user-definable abstract data types and for persistent data. The object-oriented programming paradigm began with Simula in 1962 and Smalltalk in 1972. Nowadays, many object-oriented programming languages exist (e.g., Eiffel), and many traditional programming languages have been given object-oriented extensions (e.g., C++ and C#).

Some object-oriented features were taken from semantic data modeling, which as we know models reality in terms of objects and their relationships and includes notions such as subtyping (e.g., ORM, UML, and extended entity-relationship (ER) modeling). Various ideas were also borrowed from work on logical data models (network, hierarchic, relational, and especially the nested relational model). Finally, some concepts were adapted from artificial intelligence, where structures such as frames are used for knowledge representation.

What features must a DBMS have to count as “object-oriented?” There is no commonly agreed-upon answer. A classic paper (“The OODBMS Manifesto”) on this issue was presented at the first international conference on object-oriented and deductive databases (Atkinson et al., 1990). To distinguish ODBMSs from OO programming languages, five essential features of a DBMS were identified, and then object-oriented features were added, of which eight were considered essential and five optional (see Table 17.3). Let’s look briefly at the essential object-oriented features in this proposal.

Table 17.3

Feature list in the “OODBMS manifesto” (Atkinson et al., 1990).

Complex objects are built from simpler ones by constructors. The manifesto proposed that these constructors should include at least set, list, and tuple, and be orthogonal (they can be applied in any order, recursively). For example, one object might be a list of sets of sets of tuples. Constructors are not orthogonal in the relational model (only sets of tuples of atomic values are allowed) or the nested relational models (e.g., the top-level construct must be a set). The notion of complex objects is considered important because it allows us to model a complex structure in a direct, natural way.

The basic idea behind object identity is that objects should be identified by system-generated object identifiers (OIDs) rather than by the values of their properties. This is in sharp contrast to the relational model, where for instance tuples are identified by the value of their primary key.

Among other things, OIDs can help keep track of objects whose external, value-based identification may change with time. This may occur because of simple renaming. For example, television channel 0 becomes channel 10, or a woman changes her family name upon marriage. More drastically, the reference scheme itself may change (e.g., a student identified by a student number becomes an employee identified by an employee number).

Object identifiers in the OO sense partly overcome this problem because they are rigid identifiers (i.e., they refer to the same object throughout time). They are system generated, nonreusable, immutable, and typically hidden. In ODB systems, they might be implemented as surrogates (logical identifiers or autoincremented counters, mapped by indexes to physical addresses), as typed surrogates (which makes migration between types awkward), or as structured addresses.

Encapsulation involves bundling the operations and data of an object together, with normal access to the object being through its operational interface, with implementation details hidden. For example, hiring, firing, and promoting employees are regarded as operations on Employee and are encapsulated with it. Implementations of operations are often called “methods”.

Encapsulation includes the idea that, as in a conceptual schema, objects should be classified in terms of types or classes. Moreover, some form of inheritance mechanism should be provided (e.g., so that a subtype may inherit the data and operations of its supertype(s)). A subtype may have a specialized version of a function with the same name as one of its supertype functions. In this case, the specialized version will typically override the more general version when the operation on the subtype is invoked.

For example, the display procedure for a colored, equilateral triangle may differ from the general display procedure for a polygon. Various overriding options are possible.

The requirement for computational completeness means that any computable function can be expressed in the data manipulation language (if necessary, by calling programming languages). The extensibility requirement means that users may define their own types, and the system should support them just like its built-in types.

Partly in response to the OODB manifesto, a group of academic and industrial researchers proposed an alternative “third-generation DBMS manifesto” (Stonebraker et al., 1990). Here, they referred to hierarchic and network systems as first generation, and relational systems as second generation. Under this scheme, third-generation DBMSs were seen as the next generation.

The manifesto specified three basic tenets and 13 detailed propositions to be adhered to by the next-generation DBMSs (see Table 17.4). This proposal essentially argued for extending existing relational systems with object-oriented features and effectively laid the groundwork for today’s object-relational database systems, which we’ll discuss shortly.

Table 17.4

Next-generation DBMS features proposed by Stonebraker et al. (1990).

Although supporting several of the object-oriented features, the group argued against implementing them in such a way as to negate key advances made by the relational approach. For example, all facts in a relational system are stored in tables. In contrast, some facts in hierarchic, network, and object database systems may be specified as links between structures, requiring navigation paths to be specified when the data is accessed.

Hence, OO queries typically require specification of access paths. Although path expressions are often more compact than relational queries, their reliance on existing navigation links can make it difficult to perform ad hoc queries efficiently.

As an example, consider the UoD schematized in Fig. 17.16. Students either hold a degree or are currently seeking one (or both). The exclusion constraint forbids students from reenrolling in a degree that they already hold. Subjects are recorded only for current students, as shown by the subset constraint. Because this is not an equality constraint, students may enroll in a degree before choosing subjects.

This aspect of the schema may alternatively be modeled by introducing the subtype CurrentStudent, to which the optional takes role is attached, using the definition Each CurrentStudent is a Student who seeks some Degree.

Each subject is identified by its subject code, but also has a unique title. For some subjects, a lecture plan may be available. This lists the topics discussed in the various lectures. For example, lecture 10 for CS114 might discuss relational projection, relational selection, and natural joins. The footnoted textual constraint qualifies (and implies) the external uniqueness constraint, requiring lectures to be numbered from 1 within each subject.

The conceptual schema of Fig. 17.16 (minus some constraints) might be specified in an ODB schema roughly as follows, using a syntax based on the Object Definition Language (ODL), as specified in Cattell and Barry (2000).

class Student {attribute unsigned long studentNr;attribute string studentName;attribute set<string> degreesHeld;attribute string currentDegree; };class CurrentStudent extends Student {relationship set<Subject> takesinverse Subject::is_taken_by; };class Subject {attribute string subjectCode;attribute string title;attribute unsigned short credit;relationship set<CurrentStudent> is_taken_byinverse CurrentStudent::takes;relationship list<Lecture> hasinverse Lecture::is_for; };
class Lecture {attribute unsigned short lectureNr;relationship Subject is_forinverse Subject::has;attribute set<string> topics; };

Although readable, this OO schema is incomplete and needs additional code for the extra constraints in the conceptual schema. We could display this on a UML class diagram, with the extra constraints in notes (e.g., exclusive-or, pair exclusion, and subset constraints). In general, OO schemas are best developed as abstractions of ORM schemas.

Notice that the OO classes correspond to the major object types abstracted from the conceptual schema. Hence, they provide a useful basis for building screen forms for the application. Encapsulation involves adding generic operations as well as type-specific operations (e.g., a graduate operation might be added to Student).

One problem of the ODB approach is that it mixes too many levels together–an OO schema includes conceptual, logical, and physical elements. It also involves redundant specification of associations. For example, consider the fact type Student takes Subject. In the OO schema, this is specified twice: once on CurrentStudent and again on Subject.

In specifying the OO schema, inverses were used to declare bidirectional object links between CurrentStudent and Subject as well as between Subject and Lecture. This enables queries in either direction to be specified using path expressions. This versatility is lost if the link is made unidirectional. Notice that no such navigational problem can exist in the relational model, although of course many queries will require joins. While joins might slow things down, there is no restriction on their use because they do not require links to be set up beforehand. In contrast, the ODB approach obtains its efficiency by “hardwiring” in the links to be used in queries. This makes it difficult to optimize ad hoc queries.

The problem of relying on predeclared access paths in the schema itself to achieve efficiency is exacerbated when the schema evolves. We may then have to reset navigation pathways to optimize them for the new situation rather than simply relying on the system optimizer to do the job, as in current relational systems.

This is not to say that ODBs are a bad idea, or that complex objects should not be modeled as such at the implementation level. Many complex structures are awkward to model in relational terms. However, we should be able to specify such structures in a clean way, without resorting to low-level mechanisms.

Unlike ODBs, relational databases are based on a single data model formally based on predicate logic. Moreover, relational DBMSs are now dominant, and many are being extended to address several of the deficiencies mentioned earlier. Such extended relational database systems are usually called object-relational database (ORDB) systems. These are essentially relational DBMSs extended by adding support for many OO features, such as extra data types (spatial, image, video, text …), constructors (arrays, sets, …), and inheritance. Some of the major commercial systems support extended data types by allowing modules to be plugged in. Such modules may be developed by the vendor or a third party. These modules are variously called “relational extenders”, “datablades”, or “data cartridges”.

The SQL standard has been progressively extended significantly to include several object-oriented features (e.g., user-defined types and functions, encapsulation, support for oids, subtyping, triggered actions, and computational completeness) as well as deductive features (e.g., recursive union).

Given the massive installed base of relational DBMSs, the ongoing extensions to these products, the cost of porting applications to a new data model, and the widespread adoption of the SQL standard, it may well be that the next generation of DBMSs will evolve out of current relational products. Just as Hinduism absorbed features from other religions that threatened its existence, the relational model can probably absorb the interesting features of the object-oriented faith without being replaced by it.

It’s debatable whether all the transformations taking place in SQL-based DBMSs are actually desirable. While the use of extended data types (spatial, video, etc.) is clearly a step forward, the use of constructors (arrays, multisets, etc.) is questionable in many cases because they can make it harder to design efficient databases for ad hoc queries and updates, and they complicate the task of writing good optimizers.

For a detailed critique of the way in which many OO features have been grafted onto the relational model, see Date (2000) and Date and Darwen (1998). At any rate, relational and object-relational systems currently dominate commercially, and other contenders such as object database systems are struggling to gain any significant market share.

SQL includes arrays, row types, and multisets. One challenge then is to model such collections and provide mapping algorithms to implement them efficiently. Various constructors (e.g., for sets, bags, sequences, and schemas) have been added to some versions of ORM and ER. In addition, both ORM and UML allow some kinds of collections to be expressed as mapping annotations on the conceptual schema. Although the use of collection types in conceptual models can facilitate mapping to equivalent implementation structures, it is typically much harder to model complex objects directly at the conceptual level, and they are extremely awkward to validate by verbalization and population. Complex objects also tend to be overused, and simpler solutions are overlooked. For further discussion on collection types, see Chapter 10.

Nowadays, many applications are built using a third-generation language (3GL) such as C# or Java to specify an object model for the transient, in-memory storage, and using SQL to specify a relational or object-relational database for the persistent storage. As data must be moved between the object model and the relational model, considerable effort is spent on the object-relational mapping. Using a tool such as NORMA to generate both object and relational models from ORM models simplifies the task of creating an object-relational mapping process.

Deductive Database Systems

Logic programming languages such as Prolog are declarative languages based on first-order predicate logic. Facts and derivation rules (including recursive rules) may be declared concisely, with built-in backtracking support.

Datalog combines features from relational database systems and a safe subset of logic programming languages. Unlike Prolog, queries in Datalog are guaranteed to execute in a finite time. Datalog has been used for natural language processing and as a query language for deductive database systems.

Deductive databases offer elegant and powerful ways of managing complex data in a declarative way, especially for information that is derived by use of recursion. This gives them a strong rule enforcement mechanism with built-in backtracking and excellent support for recursive rules. For example, the isanAncestorOf relation can be derived from a base parent relation and the following two rules in Horn clause notation:

  •      X isanAncestorOf Y :- X isaParentOf Y.                                  (basis clause)
  •      X isanAncestorOf Y :- X isaParentOf Z, Z isanAncestorOf Y. (recursive clause).

Here, the “:-” between the head and body of the rule means “if”, and the comma “,” in the body of the rule means “and”. Individual variables in the head of the rule are assumed to be universally quantified, and variables introduced in the body are assumed to be existentially quantified, so the rules are equivalent to the following formulae in predicate logic:

  •      ∀x,y ( x isanAncestorOf y  if  x isaParentOf y )
  •      ∀x,y [ x isanAncestorOf y  if  ∃z(x isaParentOf z and z isanAncestor of y) ]

In contrast, SQL-92 cannot express recursive queries at all. SQL:1999 introduced a recursive union operator, but its syntax is more complex and its execution does not enjoy built-in backtracking.

Various deductive database systems based on or influenced by Prolog or Datalog have been developed, such as LogiQL (Halpin and Rugaber, 2015) and Soufflé (https://github.com/souffle-lang). LogiQL was developed by LogicBlox, but is no longer available since the acquisition of LogicBlox by Predictix in December 2014. Soufflé is an open-source, parallel, logic programming language that includes both an interpreter and a compiler that targets parallel C++.

An extremely powerful programming language that supports deductive database features as well as knowledge graphs is under development by RelationalAI (https://relational.ai), with a likely release date around mid-2024. The system, called RAI, is cloud-based, and its language is called Rel, as its data structures are centered on relations (sets of ordered tuples).

The recursive rule for ancestorhood ∀x,y [ x isanAncestorOf y if ∃z(x isaParentOf z and z isanAncestor of y) ] may be expressed in Rel by means of the following definition: def isanAncestorOf (x, y): exists((z) | isaParentOf(x, z) and isanAncestorOf(z, y)).

As an indication of the power of Rel, a team of RelationalAI programmers has written a program in Rel that automatically transforms ORM models captured in the free, public-domain version of the NORMA tool into structures in Rel. This transformation is able to map extremely complex ORM models, and can capture essentially all alethic constraints in ORM. At the time of writing, deontic constraints are not supported.

The rest of this section provides a brief overview of the main logical features of the Rel language, and uses examples to illustrate how constraints may be formulated. Table 17.5 summarizes the basic logical operators between propositions supported in the Rel language. Multiple syntaxes are supported for each operator. Here, “implies” is used for the material implication operator of propositional logic, so “p implies q” is equivalent to “not p or q”.

Table 17.5

Summary of basic logical operators in the Rel language.

This differs significantly from the English meaning of “if p then q” because a false proposition materially implies any proposition whatsoever, and a true proposition is materially implied by any proposition. For example, the proposition “Earth is a star” materially implies the proposition “Earth has 10 moons”, and the proposition “Mars is a star” materially implies the proposition “Mars is a planet”.

We’ll use the ORM schema in Fig. 17.17 to illustrate how mandatory role and uniqueness constraints may be formulated in Rel. Constraint formulations start with “ic” (for “integrity constraint”), followed by a parenthesized list of the individual variables involved and then the detailed constraint expression in braces “{}”.

Assuming the ORM fact type Country has CountryName has been declared in Rel using the binary predicate hasCountryName, the ORM mandatory role constraint Each Country has some CountryName may be expressed as follows:

   ic (c) { Country(c) implies hasCountryName(c, _) }

The head variable c is universally quantified, and the underscore character “_” denotes the anonymous variable, so the constraint expression is equivalent to the following predicate logic formula:

  •    ∀x [Country(x) → ∃y(x hasCountryName y)].

The internal uniqueness constraint on Country’s role in Country has CountryName may be declared by declaring the predicate to be functional as follows:

   ic () requires function(hasCountryName)

The uniqueness constraint on CountryNames’s role in Country has CountryName may be declared thus:

   ic (c1, c2, n) requires (hasCountryName(c1,n) and hasCountryName(c2,n) implies c1 = c2

Assuming the ternary fact type has been declared, its composite uniqueness constraint may be declared as follows:

 ic (c, y, p1, p2) requires (inYearHadPopulation(c, y, p1) and inYearHadPopulation(c, y, p2)) implies p1 = p2

The external uniqueness constraint in the composite reference scheme for State may be declared thus:

 ic (s1, s2, c, sc) requires (isInCountry(s1,c) and hasStateName(s1,sc) and isInCountry(s2,c) and hasStateName(s2,sc)) implies s1 = s2

The ORM schema in Fig. 17.18 includes several other kinds of constraints. The inclusive-or constraint in example (a) ensures that each job applicant is either qualified or has a reference (or both). This may be expressed in Rel thus:

   ic (p) requires JobApplicant(p) implies (isQualified(p) or hasaReference(p))

The exclusive-or constraint in example (b) ensures that each planet in our solar system is an inner planet or an outer planet but not both. This may be expressed in Rel thus:

   ic (p) requires Planet(p) implies (isAnInnerPlanet(p) xor isAnOuterPlanet(p))

The value constraint in example (c) restricts the value of GenderCode in the underlying reference type Gender has GenderCode. The value constraint in example (d) restricts IQ values to the range 0..300. These constraints may be formulated thus:

 ic (g, gc) requires hasGenderCode(g,gc) implies (gc = “M” or gc = “F”) ic (x, y) requires hasIQNr(x,y) implies (x >= 0 and x <=300)

The exclusion constraints in examples (e) and (f) say that nobody can author and review the same book, and that nobody can review a paper authored by someone who lectures at the same university where he/she lectures. The diagram in (f) for the exclusion constraint over a join path is a screenshot from the NORMA tool. The constraints may be formulated thus:

 ic (p, b) requires reviews(p, b) implies not authors(p, b) ic (p1, p2, u, pr) requires       (authors(p1, pr) and lecturesAt(p1, u) and reviews(p2, pr)) implies not lecturesAt(p2,u)

The ORM schema in Fig. 17.19 includes some more constraints. The equality constraint in example (a) ensures that a patient has a diastolic blood pressure reading if and only if the patient has a systolic blood pressure reading. This may be expressed in Rel using an anonymous variable as follows:

   ic (p) requires hasDiastolicBP(p, _) iff hasSystolicBP(p,_)

The internal frequency constraint in example (b) ensures that each reviewer is assigned at most three papers to review. It may be formulated thus:

   ic (r, n) requires isAssignedNrPapers(r, n) implies n <= 3

The composite frequency constraint in example (c) ensures that no student may enroll more than twice in the same course. This may be formulated as follows. Here, “def” prepends the definition or derivation rule for the inCourseHasNrEnrollments relation, which uses the built-in count function. The constraint makes use of the derived ternary relation.

def inCourseHasNrEnrollments(s, c, n):n = count[(e): isanEnrollmentByStudent(s, e) and isanEnrollmentInCourse(e, c)]ic (s, c, n) requires inCourseHasNrEnrollments(s, c, n) implies n <=2

The external frequency constraint in example (d) ensures that for each country, at most two politicians are both in its government and are a coregent. This constraint may be formulated using the count function or instead simply thus:

ic (p1, p2, p3 c) requires(isaCoregent(p1) and servesOnGovtOf(p1, c) and isaCoregent(p2)and servesOnGovtOf(p2, c) and isaCoregent(p3) and servesOnGovtOf(p3, c))implies p1 = p2 or p1 = p3 or p1 = p3

Ring constraints are easy to specify in Rel. The reflexive ring constraint that people know themselves may be expressed as: ic(p) requires Person(p) implies knows(p,p). The irreflexive ring constraint that nobody a parent of himself/herself may be expressed as: ic (p) requires not isaParentOf(p, p). The symmetric constraint on siblinghood may be specified thus: ic (p1,p2) requires isaSiblingOf(p1, p2) implies isaSiblingOf(p2, p1). The asymmetric ring constraint that nobody is a parent of himself/herself may be expressed thus: ic (p1,p2) requires isaParentOf(p1, p2) implies not isaParentOf(p2, p1).

The transitive nature of the isOlderThan relation may be formulated as follows: ic (p1, p2, p3) requires (isOlderThan(p1, p2) and isOlderThan(p2, p3)) implies isOlderThan(p1, p3). The intransitive constraint on the direct precedence relation may be formulated as follows: ic (e1,e2,e3) requires (directlyPrecedes(e1, e2) and directlyPrecedes(e2, e3)) implies not directlyPrecedes(e1, e3).

The ancestorhood relation may be defined as follows: def isanAncestorOf(p1, p2): isaParentOf(p1, p2) or isaParentOf(p1, p3) and isanAncestorOf(p3, p2). The acyclic constraint on ancestorhood may be specified thus: ic (p) requires not isanAncestorOf(p, p).

The pair-subset constraint in Figure 17.20(a) ensures that each student who passed a course also enrolled in that course. This may be expressed in Rel thus: ic (s, c) requires passedCourse(s, c) implies enrolledInCourse(s, c).
