Starting with the overall objectives, the main functions and processes of the application may be specified systematically using a variety of diagrams. This kind of analysis helps us divide the domain into coherent modules of manageable size and facilitates the task of specifying information examples where none exist. At this point, CSDP step 1 may be applied to each module.

Functional requirements may be laid out in top-down form using a function tree. For example, Fig. 18.15 lists functions of a hospital information system. The four main functions are numbered 1..4. Each of these is refined or decomposed into a number of lower-level functions, numbered 1.1, and so on.

For example, function 3 is refined to functions 3.1 and 3.2. This may be refined further, for example, function 3.1 is refined to functions 3.1.1, 3.1.2, and 3.1.3. To help fit the tree on a single sheet, this third level has been laid out vertically rather than horizontally. Tools such as the Org-Chart solution in Microsoft Visio allow a very flexible layout of such diagrams. The other three main functions may be refined in a similar way. Other kinds of diagrams may be used to show dependencies between functions, which can help in deciding how to group functions into processes.

One common way of specifying information flows between processes is by means of data flow diagrams. Although invented long before UML use case diagrams, which have a somewhat similar purpose, data flow diagrams tend to be more useful in practice (Jeyaraj and Sauter, 2007) and are still popular.

By decomposing the processes, a data flow diagram at one level may be refined into several lower-level diagrams, and so on. As a precursor to this refinement, we might specify a very higher-level view in the form of a context diagram.

A context diagram provides an overview of the interaction between the information system and the environment, treats the system as a single process, and ignores any data stores. A context diagram for the pharmacy module of our hospital application is shown in Fig. 18.16. External agents appear as shadowed boxes. Material flows are not shown, but some data flows may be associated with material flows (e.g., drug supply details).

At a lower level of detail, Fig. 18.17 shows a data flow diagram for a fragment of the pharmacy system. This could be further refined (e.g., decompose the order placement process into processes for computing totals, printing order forms, etc.).

However, because such refinements are time consuming, somewhat arbitrary, and lack the safeguards of population checks, there is usually little point in specifying low-level data flows. In general, then, once the requirements of the application are clear and modules of manageable size are identified, modeling efforts are best focused on obtaining a set of information examples and applying the CSDP. Once the conceptual schema is specified, the logical schema is obtained by applying a mapping procedure, such as Rmap.

The external schemas may now be developed for the various categories of user. It is through the interaction of users with the external interface that the original functions specified in the requirements analysis phase are ultimately executed. Hence, it is important to design the external interface in a way that naturally reflects these functions.

Fundamentally, all that happens when users interact with an information system is that elementary facts are added, deleted, retrieved, or derived. In principle, we could specify the process perspective in terms of these two update and two query operations. But this is too fine a level of granularity for humans to work with efficiently.

We need a way of grouping these elementary operations into larger units. It is often natural to think of operations being performed on significant objects, such as patients and stock items. The major object types abstracted from an ORM schema (see previous section) correspond closely to these object types, and hence provide a good basis for defining operations. The more important classes or entity types in UML class diagrams or ER diagrams provide another good choice for this.

A generic set of external update operations may now be generated with three varieties: add object, delete object, and modify object. Some generic query operations may be generated (e.g., list all facts about an object), but specific queries require an appropriate selection of the relevant fact types (stored or derived).

Users perform such operations through an external interface, typically screen forms or menus. For each screen, we need to consider content (which fact types and operations to include), format (how the screen is displayed), and use (how the operations are invoked by the user). As discussed, default decisions about screen content may be based on operations on the major object types. For example, if Patient is a major object type for the hospital system, a screen is required for it with at least the operations add Patient, modify Patient, delete Patient, show Patient.

Unlike conceptual and logical tables, forms may overlap in their content. This redundancy at the external level conveniently allows users to perform an operation whenever relevant, without having to switch screens. For example, consider the m:n fact type Doctor treated Patient. When working with a Doctor screen, we might query which patients were treated by that doctor. When at a Patient screen, we might query which doctors treated that patient. In the conceptual and logical schemas, facts of this type are stored only once. As long as the external screens have been properly related to the underlying data structures, this overlap is safe. For a discussion on the use of ORM schemas to generate screen forms and transactions, see Campbell and Halpin (1993).

Although there is only one (global) conceptual schema for an application, there may be many external schemas. Different user groups might have different authorization levels that can be specified in access rights tables. This may be done at the conceptual level (e.g., for each fact type, which groups have read, add, delete rights) or at the logical level (e.g., for each table or column, which groups have read, insert, delete, update rights).

Regarding access to options on screen forms, it is generally best to display to users only those options that they are authorized to select. As usual, access rights to screen options may be soft coded as data in tables rather than hard coded in procedures. This avoids having to recompile the forms when access rights are changed, and simplifies reuse of common code. As part of the overall security, passwords are required, and users are given the power to change their passwords.

Apart from access rights, users might also differ in their ability level. Designing application screens to optimize the way various users can perform their tasks is an important aspect of human-computer interface (HCI) design.

Many kinds of interfaces can be used. For example, dialog with the user may use natural language, short questions, command lines, menus, forms, tables, diagrams, images, or sound. Input devices include keyboard, mouse, joystick, pen, and microphone.

In general, the user interface should be easy to learn and easy to use. To achieve this, the interface should be consistent, simple, structured, efficient, and adapted to the user. Let’s examine each of these in turn.

Consistency of interface implies that all the components use the same basic conventions for display format and operations. This promotes positive transfer (learning how to use one screen helps you with the others) and avoids negative transfer. Consistency may be achieved at different levels, such as within the one screen, within the application, among applications from the same company, and with external standards. For example, many Windows applications are being developed nowadays in conformity with Microsoft’s user interface guidelines.

Simplicity of interface implies it is intuitive to use, with minimal effort for users. Each screen should provide the right amount of relevant information (e.g., limit the number of menu options seen at once). Don’t clutter the screen. To allow many operations directly from the one screen, remove all but the main options from the permanent screen display, allowing the user to toggle extra options on as required. For example, use pull-down menus, pop-up windows (e.g., for look-up codes), and status-line help (and pop-up detailed help). To facilitate navigation within and between screens, consider the use of arrow keys for movement, and allow windows and menus to be cascaded or tiled.

Efficiency of interface entails that options may be selected quickly and intuitively. A graphical user interface (GUI) provides a more intuitive means of operation, especially where graphics or sophisticated layouts are involved; here, it is important that “what you see is what you get” (WYSIWYG). However, key-based shortcuts (e.g., hot keys) are sometimes faster and should be provided for the experienced user.

Menu design has a major impact on efficiency. Menus come in various shapes and sizes (full-screen, pull-down, pop-up, ring, button bars, etc.). They provide most, if not all, of the application’s operations. Options on the same menu should be semantically related.

Navigation between menus or screens requires planning (state charts can help here), especially for web-based applications that use hyperlinks to navigate from one place to another. Some navigation patterns are shown in Fig. 18.18. Hyperlink access is typically cyclic.

In addition, the following principles should be observed; Order menu options in decreasing frequency of use. Vary color and fonts, but don’t overdo it. For options, use either intuitive icons or terse, clear textual descriptions that are mostly in lowercase. Allow selection of options by mouse clicks or hot keys, and support undo operations.

Adapt the interface to the user as follows. Show only what is relevant to the user. Provide simple procedures for casual users and shortcuts for experienced users. Let users configure the environment to their own taste. Provide levels of context-sensitive help: short messages on status lines, detailed help in pop-up windows. Trap errors as soon as possible and give short and long error messages. Provide online tutorials, user manuals, technical support, and training courses.

If you use some software packages that you find particularly intuitive, have a close look at the interface design and see if you can adapt its good features to your own (as long as you don’t violate any copyright in doing so!). Once you develop your prototype interface, test it on typical users and use their feedback to finesse it.

That’s a quick run through several topics that could easily fill a book on their own. Indeed, whole books are devoted to interface design; many refinements exist for modeling processes, including some very technical approaches that attempt to formally integrate these models with data models. Some interesting work in this regard is referenced in the chapter notes. Various methods and tools are also in common use for associated tasks such as project management (e.g., Gantt charts and PERT charts), testing, performance measures, documentation, and versioning.

18.6 Ontologies and the Semantic Web

Etymologically, the term “ontology” means the study of existence. In philosophy, ontology is the branch of metaphysics concerned with the fundamental nature of being, addressing deep questions such as “Do nonphysical things exist?”, “Does an object remain identical to itself when it changes?”, and so on. The informatics community later adopted the term “ontology”, typically using it to mean a conceptual model about some business domain where the model facilitates sharing information about that domain by conforming to some standard set of constructs.

With the rise of the Internet, millions of documents are now readily accessible over the World Wide Web. In 2001, to simplify sharing or combining information in different web documents, Sir Tim Berners-Lee, the founder of the Internet, proposed a new vision for a semantic web as an extension of the current web “in which information is given well-defined meaning, better enabling computers and people to work in cooperation” (Berners-Lee et al., 2001). The main idea is to add global identifiers and structure to the documents (e.g., using uniform resource identifiers and embedded tags) to reveal the underlying semantics of what is to be shared in a way that is accessible to automated agents.

In 1999, the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) produced the first version of the Resource Description Framework (RDF) language as a standard on top of XML to capture metadata for web resources (e.g., who authored a web document). Other work on adding automatically accessible meaning to language via markup tags was conducted in the United States by the Defense Advanced Research Products Agency (DARPA), which produced the DARPA Agent Markup Language (DAML). With similar objectives, researchers in the European Union (EU) developed the Ontology Inference Layer (OIL). In 2001, joint work between the United States and the EU incorporated many concepts from OIL into DAML, resulting in the DAML+OIL language, which was submitted in late 2002 to the W3C.

In 2004, the W3C adopted RDF Schema (RDFS), which extended RDF to a simple ontology language, and also recommended the Web Ontology Language (OWL), which incorporates many aspects from DAML+OIL and RDFS, has a cleaner formal semantics based mainly on description logics, and is now the most popular language for developing ontologies on the semantic web. Fig. 18.19 summarizes the dependencies between layers, where upper layers depend on lower layers.

RDF and RDFS

RDF models are basically directed graphs, where each node is either a resource or a literal, and each directed arc represents a binary relationship between the nodes. A resource is basically an entity instance or a logical predicate.

RDF 1.0 identifies resources by Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) references. A URI is a Uniform Resource Locator (URL) or a Uniform Resource Name (URN). A URL (e.g., http://www.orm.net) includes a network access type (e.g., http for hypertext transfer protocol) plus a network address to locate the resource. A URN (e.g., urn:isbn:1-55860-672-6) includes a name space (e.g., ISBN for International Standard Book Number) plus a name that identifies that resource within that name space. Unlike a URL, a URN does not provide a way to locate the resource on the web. Both URLs and URNs are global identifiers, so when used in different documents they refer to the same resource.

A URI reference (or URIref) is a URI, optionally followed by a fragment identifier, for example, the URI reference https://ww.w3.org/TR/rdf-primer/#basicconcepts consists of the URI https://www.w3.org/TR/rdf-primer/, a “#” separator, and the fragment identifier basicconcepts. Character strings used for URIrefs are composed of Unicode characters.

Fig. 18.20 shows a simple RDF 1.0 model depicted as a graph. Here, we show resource nodes as named, soft rectangles; literals as named, hard rectangles; and relationships as named arrows from the subject node to the object node. The graph is intended to convey the semantics that there is a book identified by the ISBN 1-55860-672-6 that is authored by a person named “Terry Halpin”.

RDF captures the information as simple statements, each represented as a triple (subject, predicate, object). The subject and predicate are resources, so are identified by a URIref. The object is either a resource or a literal. Literals may be untyped (as here) or typed (by pairing the value with a data type that itself is identified by a URIref to a standard XML Schema data type). Each predicate includes a predicate reading, for example, authored_by. Because the same predicate reading means different things in different contexts, a URIref is required to assign a unique meaning to a predicate.

The resource nodes on the left of Fig. 18.20 denote an individual book and an individual person. However, the resource nodes on the right denote the types Book and Person. The type predicate relates an instance to a type, and means “is an instance of”. RDF also allows descriptions of resource collections (e.g., sets and lists), and RDF graphs can be serialized into XML format using RDF/XML.

As the example in Fig. 18.20 shows, RDF graphs allow nodes that are instances or types, and allow arcs that represent relationships between instances, or relationships between instances and types. RDF also allows relationships between types and types (e.g., Woman is_a Person). RDF even allows you to state that a type is an instance of itself (e.g., Class is_of_type Class), which can lead to formal problems such as Russell’s paradox. Moreover, no special semantics is assigned to any predicate, so the is_an_instance:of relationship and the is_a_subtype_of relationships are treated the same as the has_name relationship (apart from different strings used for the URIrefs). So, there is no ability to perform inferences based on knowledge of special properties for certain predicates (e.g., transitivity of is_a_subtype_of).

RDFS builds on RDF by providing inbuilt support for classes and subclassing. For example, resources can be typed as classes (using rdfs:Class) and the predefined predicate rdfs:subClassOf is defined to be transitive. For a given predicate, the sets of instances playing the subject and object roles are called the domain and range, respectively. RDFS allows predicates to be typed by restricting their domain (using rdfs:domain) and range (using rdfs:range), respectively. Membership in a collection can also be specified using the rdfs:member property.

Despite these improvements, RDFS is still both too inexpressive (e.g., it cannot constrain associations to be other than m:n, and it cannot express complex properties by conjoining existing properties) and too expressive (e.g., like RDF, it allows you to state that Class is an instance of itself, and its underlying logic is undecidable).

In 2014, RDF was upgraded to RDF 1.1, and RDFS was upgraded to RDFS 1.1. Both these standards identify resources by Internationalized Resource Identifiers (IRIs). While URIs use ASCII characters, IRIs use the Universal Coded Character Set (Unicode/ISO/IEC 10646) to cater for non-English characters.

For a detailed primer on RDF 1.1, see https://www.w3.org/TR/rdf11-primer/. The RDFS 1.1 standard is accessible at http://www.w3.org/TR/2014/REC-rdf-schema-20140225/. In 2023, the W3C published a working draft of RDFS 1.2 (see https://www.w3.org/TR/rdf-schema/.

OWL and Its Sublanguages

Like RDFS, OWL is restricted to binary fact types (no n-aries or unaries). OWL has a simpler formal semantics than RDFS, disallowing some freedoms in RDFS while at the same time adding the ability to capture further constraints. OWL is used to specify the ontology schema (called a terminological box or Tbox) for a business domain, and RDF/XML is used to mark-up conforming instance data (the fact population is called an assertional box or Abox).

Because information on the web is often incomplete, OWL adopts the open world assumption (the failure to find or infer some proposition does not imply that proposition is false). OWL was endorsed as a W3C recommendation in February 2004. In October 2009, a major upgrade to the language, known as OWL 2, was recommended by the W3C, and the previous version was renamed OWL 1. In December 2012, a second edition of OWL 2 was recommended, and is still the current version (see https://www.w3.org/TR/owl-overview/).

OWL 1 has three flavors: OWL Lite, OWL DL, and OWL Full. OWL Lite is a subset of OWL DL, which itself is a subset of OWL Full. OWL Lite is used for basic classification hierarchies where all the constraints are simple. It is based on the description logic SHIF(D), has a low formal complexity, and is decidable. OWL Lite can express only simple constraints, and supports only simple inferences (e.g., those based on transitivity). OWL DL is much more expressive while still being decidable, and it is based on the description logic SHOIN(D). OWL DL includes all the constructs of OWL Full but restricts their use. OWL DL is a fragment of first-order logic, so does not allow a class to be declared an instance of another class in the same model. OWL Full is more expressive, allowing all RDF expressions, including allowing a class to be an instance of itself. OWL Full is undecidable, going beyond even first-order logic. In spite of its undecidable nature, OWL Full still cannot express some important constraints that are expressible in ORM (e.g., acyclicity).

OWL 2 introduced three new sublanguages as subsets of OWL DL: OWL 2 EL, OWL 2 QL, and OWL 2 RL. OWL 2 EL is designed to provide good performance for basic reasoning tasks on large ontologies and is based on the EL family of description logics that provides existential quantification but not universal quantification. OWL 2 QL is designed to provide good performance with basic queries on large ontologies, where those queries can be implemented by rewriting them into queries in a standard relational query language such as SQL. OWL 2 RL is designed to provide good performance for managing ontologies with rule languages such as rule-extended database technologies operating directly on RDF triples.

Cardinality Restrictions in OWL 1

By default, all relationship types are optional and m:n. OWL Lite allows fact roles to be declared mandatory and fact types to specified as n:1, 1:n, or 1:1 using minCardinality and maxCardinality restrictions. Fig. 18.21 explains the meaning of these restrictions by relating them to an equivalent representation in ORM. The ORM fact type A R B is diagrammed as an RDF graph, where the subject and object nodes are assumed to be classes. The predicate R is directed from A to B.

OWL itself has no graphic notation, so the fact type and its restrictions are declared textually (see example later). Restricting R with a minCardinality of 1 means that each instance of A plays in that relationship type with at least one instance of B. In ORM terms, the first role of R is mandatory. In OWL DL and OWL Full, a minCardinality above 1 may be specified (in ORM this adds a frequency constraint to the mandatory constraint).

Assigning a minCardinality of 0 means that the role is optional. Restricting the maxCardinality to 1 means that each instance of A plays in that relationship type with at most one instance of B. In ORM terms, the first role of R has a simple uniqueness constraint. In OWL DL and OWL Full, a maxCardinalty above 1 may be specified (in ORM this replaces the uniqueness constraint by a frequency constraint).

Restricting the maxCardinality to 0 means that each instance of the class (let’s call this class C) being discussed (perhaps in a query) plays in that relationship type with no instance of B. In ORM terms, this could be handled explicitly by a subtype definition as shown, or simply included as a condition in an ORM query. For example, we might define a teetotaller as a person who does not drink alcohol.

As an example of some cardinality declarations, the following OWL code declares that the hasFaxNr predicate is optional and n:1.

 <owl:Restriction>  <owl:onProperty rdf:resource=“#hasFaxNr”/>  <owl:minCardinality rdf:datatype=“&xsd;nonNegativeInteger”>0</owl:minCardinality> </owl:Restriction> <owl:Restriction>  <owl:onProperty rdf:resource=“#hasFaxNr”/>  <owl:maxCardinality rdf:datatype=“&xsd;nonNegativeInteger”>1</owl:maxCardinality> </owl:Restriction>

As a shortcut when the minimum and maximum cardinalities are the same, the value may be assigned to the cardinality property. So, setting owl:cardinality to 0 means forbidden, and setting it to 1 means exactly one.

OWL Syntaxes

From now on, our discussion of OWL relates to OWL 2, Table 18.2 lists the five concrete syntaxes proposed for expressing an OWL 2 ontology in textual form. RDF/XML is the only syntax that is required to be supported by OWL 2 conformant tools, but it is awkward to read and onerous to write. OWL/XML is also designed for processing by XML tools, so it too is painful to read and write. The Functional Syntax is designed to expose the formal structure of an OWL ontology, and is readable by technical users.

Table 18.2

Concrete syntaxes for OWL 2.

For general readability purposes, the Manchester syntax (see https://www.w3.org/TR/owl2-manchester-syntax) and the Turtle (Terse RDF Triple Language) syntax (see https://www.w3.org/TeamSubmission/turtle/) are far easier for non-technical people to use than the other three syntaxes. Though popular, Turtle is not a product of the OWL working group. The Manchester syntax is typically a little easier to read than Turtle syntax, and is structured in a way to facilitate specifying a large list of OWL statements in one go.

As a simple example of all five syntaxes, the statements in Table 18.3 can be used to assert that Biden is a politician (i.e., the individual thing referenced in the current document as Biden is an instance of the class referenced in the current document as Politician) and that each politician is a person (i.e., the Politician class is a subclass of the Person class).

Table 18.3

Example statements in OWL 2 syntaxes.

Overall, we consider the Manchester Syntax to be the most convenient of the five syntaxes for communicating typical ontologies to nontechnical people. From now on, we’ll typically phrase the OWL examples in terms of Manchester syntax. We now discuss some basic features of OWL 2 using Manchester syntax.

Namespace prefixes may be declared as abbreviations, using a prefix command of the form Prefix: namespacePrefix: IRI. The prefixes “rdf:”, “rdfs:”, “owl:”, and “xsd:” are predefined. Each user-defined prefix used in an ontology document must have exactly one prefix declaration in the ontology document, such as Prefix: owl: Prefix: gup: https://www.galacticUni.edu/programs#. If no prefix is supplied, the current document is assumed to be the namespace.

Literals are delimited by double quotes (e.g., “64”), and may be typed (e.g., “64”ˆˆxsd:integer). An individual may be declared by prepending “Individual:” to its name, optionally followed by a declaration of properties that apply to it. For example, the classes to which the individual belongs may be listed after “Types:”. An individual may belong to many classes at once, such as Individual: Biden Types: Politician, MalePerson.

A class may be declared after “Class:”, and declared as a subclass of some (typically other) class using “SubClassOf”, such as Class: Politician SubClassOf: Person. In OWL, subclassing is reflexive (so each class is a subclass of itself) and transitive (so if A is a subclass of B, and B is a subclass of C, then A is a subclass of C). This differs from the subtyping relationship in ORM, which for efficiency reasons is used only for proper subtyping (and hence is irreflexive) that is direct (and hence intransitive).

A binary fact that relates individuals may be specified by declaring the subject as an individual and then listing the predicate and object of that statement after “Facts:”. One or more facts may be listed using comma separators. For example, we could state that Terry is the husband of Norma and that Terry is the father of Selena as follows: Individual: Terry Facts: isHusbandOf Norma, isFatherOf Selena. Manchester syntax allows you to use “some” for the existential quantifier. So, we can state that Terry is father of somebody thus: Terry isFatherOf some Person.

A domain of a binary predicate is a class to which its subject must belong, and a range of a binary predicate is a class to which its object must belong. In Manchester syntax, a predicate may be declared as an ObjectProperty, and its domain(s) and ranges(s) specified after “Domain:” and “Range:” respectively. For example:

 ObjectProperty: isFatherOf     Domain: MalePerson     Range: Person

A predicate may be assigned multiple domains and ranges, in which case the subject must belong to the intersection of the predicate’s domains and the object must belong to the intersection of the predicate’s ranges.

Some OWL 2 Taxonomy

Fig. 18.22 shows a UML class diagram for several concepts in OWL 2. This diagram is based on https://www.w3.org/TR/owl2-syntax/. What we called “resources” in our discussion of RDF are called “entities” in OWL. OWL entities may be named individuals, classes, properties (binary predicates), or data types. This differs from the use of the term “entity” in ORM and ER, where all entities are nonlexical individuals (not types or classes).

In OWL, entities are identified by IRIs, but unlike some approaches, OWL does not adopt the Unique Name Assumption (UNA). So, in OWL the same entity may be assigned different IRIs, even within the same document. Hence, the multiplicity constraint of 1 on entityIRI in Fig. 18.22 should instead be 1..* (1 or more). As discussed earlier, OWL includes the SameAs predicate to indicate when two different IRIs denote the same entity (e.g., DownUnder SameAs Australia).

Literals (data values such as names or numerals) are not treated as individuals. This practice differs from formal logic, where literals do count as individuals. Only OWL individuals (not literals) may be members of OWL classes.

OWL predicates are directed, binary relationship types that map subject individuals (instances) to object individuals. OWL includes a predefined, universal class called owl:Thing that includes all individuals. It also predefines the empty class owl:Nothing, which has no members. By default, all OWL predicates have an unrestricted domain and range (equal to owl:Thing).

Object properties are binary predicates that relate entities to entities. Data properties are binary predicates that relate entities to literals. For example:

 ObjectProperty: wasBornIn DataProperty: hasName Individual: Einstein   Facts: wasBornIn Germany, hasName “Albert Einstein”ˆˆxsd:string

The following extreme OWL predicates (“properties”) are predefined. The owl:topObjectProperty is the class of all object properties, and hence is a binary predicate relating all individuals in the model to all individuals in the model (its population is the Cartesian product owl:Thing × owl:Thing). Every object property is a subproperty of this property. The owl:topDataProperty is the class of all data properties, and hence is a binary predicate relating all individuals to all literals. Every data property is a subproperty of this property. The owl:bottomObjectProperty is the empty object property, and hence is a subproperty of every object property. The owl:bottomDataProperty is the empty data property, and hence is a subproperty of every data property.

Annotation properties are binary predicates that provide informal documentation annotations about ontologies, statements, or IRIs. For instance, the rdfs:comment annotation property is used to provide a comment, as in this example:

 Class: Moon Annotations: rdfs:comment "Natural satellite of a planet or other celestial body."

Other predefined annotation properties are shown below:

  • • The rdfs:label annotation property is used to provide a human-readable label.
  • • The rdfs:seeAlso annotation property is used to provide an IRI with another IRI such that the latter provides additional information about the former.
  • • The rdfs:isDefinedBy annotation property is used to provide an IRI with another IRI where the latter provides a definition of the former.
  • • An annotation with the owl:deprecated annotation property and the value equal to “true”ˆˆxsd:boolean is used to specify that an IRI is deprecated.
  • • The owl:versionInfo annotation property is used to provide an IRI with a string that describes the IRI’s version.
  • • The owl:priorVersion annotation property specifies the IRI of a prior version of the containing ontology.
  • • The owl:backwardCompatibleWith annotation property specifies the IRI of a prior version of the containing ontology that is compatible with the current version of the containing ontology.
  • • The owl:incompatibleWith annotation property specifies the IRI of a prior version of the containing ontology that is incompatible with the current version of the containing ontology.

OWL tools typically support ontology parsing—the process of converting an ontology document written in a particular syntax into an OWL ontology. Depending on the syntax used, the ontology parser may need to know which IRIs are used for which kinds of entity (e.g., is a predicate an object property, data property, or annotation property?). For example, is wasBornIn an object property or a data property? This typing information can be extracted from declarations—axioms that associate IRIs with entity types (e.g., ObjectProperty: wasBornIn).

Comparing Individuals, Classes, Datatypes, and Predicates

OWL predefines the owl:sameAs and owl:differentFrom predicates for “=” and “≠” respectively, when they apply between individuals (so their range and domain is owl:Thing). These predicates are used to declare whether two IRIs in the same or different documents refer to the same individual or to different individuals, for example,

 Individual: Elvis SameAs: TheKing    DifferentFrom: Donovan

OWL predefines the owl:equivalentClass predicate to equate two classes or class expressions. In Manchester syntax, this is called “EquivalentTo”, for example,

  Class: Human  Class: Person EquivalentTo: Human.

In Manchester syntax, EquivalentTo may also be used to define a data range. For example, the datatype RatingNr may be confined to {1..7}, thus Datatype: RatingNr EquivalentTo: integer[> = 1, <=7].

In Manchester syntax, the DisjointWith predicate is used to declare that two classes (or class expressions) are mutually exclusive, for example,

       Class: Cat DisjointWith Dog.

The predefined class DisjointClasses is a class whose members are pairwise exclusive (i.e., each pair of member classes is disjoint). In Manchester syntax, “DisjointClasses:” prepended before two or more class descriptions indicates they are mutually exclusive (so have no instances in common). This provides an efficient way to declare that many classes are pairwise disjoint.

In ORM, top-level entity types are assumed to be mutually exclusive. For example, in the ORM schema in Fig. 18.23(a), if Person, Car, and Dog are not subtypes, then they are assumed to be disjoint. In OWL, however, this disjointness needs to be explicitly stated, as shown in the first statement of Fig. 18.23(b).

The single statement using DisjointClasses is equivalent to the lengthier approach of using DisjointWith to declare disjointness between each pair. The Domain and Range specifications restrict the predicates to the object types indicated.

Given the following statements:

 Individual: Adam Types: Man Individual: Eve Types: Woman DisjointClasses: Man, Woman

we may infer:

   Individual: Adam  DifferentFrom: Eve

In Manchester syntax, the SubPropertyOf predicate may be used to declare that all (subject, object) instances of one predicate must be instances of another. Once a resource is declared, you can list all its properties in one go. For example, you could declare the fatherhood predicate along with its superproperty, domain, and range together, thus:

 ObjectProperty: isFatherOf    SubPropertyOf: isaParentOf    Domain: MalePerson    Range: Person

In Manchester syntax, the DisjointWith predicate may be used to indicate that the populations of binary predicates must be mutually exclusive. This is equivalent to a pair-exclusion constraint in ORM. For example, the exclusion constraint that no person authored and reviewed the same book may be specified as follows:

 ObjectProperty: authored  Domain: Person  Range: Book ObjectProperty: reviewed  Domain: Person  Range: Book  DisjointWith: authored

If more than two predicates are mutually exclusive, it’s more efficient to simply list them after the DisjointProperties header, for example,

 ObjectProperty: gotFirstPlaceIn ObjectProperty: gotSecondPlaceIn ObjectProperty: gotThirdPlaceIn DisjointProperties: gotFirstPlaceIn, gotSecondPlaceIn, gotThirdPlaceIn

If two predicates must always have the same instance populations, they are said to be (materially) equivalent. This is the same as declaring a subPropertyOf relationship in both directions. In Manchester syntax, equivalence between predicates is declared by listing the predicates after the EquivalentProperties header.

For example, an ORM pair-equality constraint to ensure that people drive a car if and only if they own the car (this constraint actually applies in some taxi companies) may be specified thus: EquivalentProperties: owns, drives.

Another use of equivalent properties is to support synonyms for predicate readings in the same document (or different documents), for example, EquivalentProperties: worksFor, isEmployedBy. A third use of equivalent properties is to specify derivation rules for derived predicates.

Functional, Inverse, Mandatory, and Key Relationships

By default, all OWL predicates are optional and many-to-many (m:n). Although the predefined predicates for equating and distinguishing individuals have unrestricted domains and ranges, user-defined predicates typically have at least one domain and at least one range explicitly declared. This is always the case for relationships declared in information modeling approaches such as ORM, ER, and UML.

Fig. 18.24(a) depicts two ORM fact types. The fact type Politician was born in Country is a many-to-one (n:1) association (each politician was born in at most one country, and many politicians may be born in the same country). Both roles are optional as our knowledge might be incomplete. The fact type Politician heads/is headed by Country is 1:1 (each politician heads at most one country, and each country is headed by at most one politician).

Fig. 18.24(b) depicts the ORM schema in OWL using Manchester syntax. OWL confusingly uses the term “property” to mean predicate. Hence, an n:1 predicate is called a functional property. A functional predicate is declared as an object property, and then its functional nature is declared by including Functional as one of its characteristics. Knowledge of functional properties enables OWL tools to make useful inferences. For example, given:

 Individual: Terry     Facts: wasBornIn TheLuckyCountry, wasBornIn Australia

we may deduce:

   TheLuckyCountry  SameAs  Australia.

ORM treats an elementary fact type as a set of one or more typed predicates. In Fig. 18.24(a), the head of government fact type has a forward predicate reading “heads” as well as an inverse predicate reading “is headed by” directed from Country to Politician (a slash “/” separates forward and inverse readings).

OWL allows you to declare one predicate to be the inverse of another using the owl:inverseOf predicate. In Manchester syntax, you prepend “InverseOf:” to the inverse predicate, for example, ObjectProperty: isaChildOf InverseOf: isaParentOf.

Functional and inverse functional declarations apply globally to the predicate in all contexts. OWL cardinality constraints, however, apply only locally to the domain classes being introduced in a local context. This local nature of cardinality restrictions differs markedly from the usual approach in information modeling.

OWL does not allow an inverse to be declared for a data property, partly because it never allows a literal to be the subject of a predicate. This is unfortunate because we may wish to talk about literals.

Consider the data property Person misspelt Word. OWL does not allow us to declare its inverse Word wasMisspeltBy Person. Moreover, OWL does not let us assert the fact type Word is a synonym for Word. To work around such problems in OWL, you have to cheat, for example by treating Word as an entity type rather than as a value type (literal type).

Consider the fact types Person is in Country and City is in Country. In information modeling approaches such as ORM, ER, and UML, the two is in predicates would be treated as different predicates/relationships/associations. However, in OWL we may treat these instead as different occurrences of the same predicate, simply by assigning them the same IRI.

OWL does not allow a data property to be declared inverse functional. In practice, many data properties are either 1:1 or 1:n, thus requiring a uniqueness constraint on the role played by the literal. Although we can’t declare uniqueness constraints on roles played by literals as inverse functional characteristics, we can specify such constraints in OWL 2 using HasKey declarations.

In Fig. 18.24(a), politicians are identified by their name and countries by their country codes. The ORM diagram depicts this compactly using parenthesized reference modes, but internally these are expanded to the injective (mandatory, 1:1) reference relationships Politician has PoliticianName and Country has CountryCode.

Unfortunately, the HasKey feature only partly addresses the need to specify identification schemes (simple or compound) for entity types because HasKey captures only the inverse functional nature of the data property.

The name choice “HasKey” for this feature is somewhat misleading, as it is weaker than the notion of “key” in relational databases. To fully capture the identification scheme, we need to explicitly declare the data property to be both functional and mandatory.

In Manchester syntax, the mandatory role constraint that each Politician has a name is expressed by using the SubClassOf property to declare that Politician is a subclass of those things that play the subject role in the hasPoliticianName predicate with a minCardinality of 1 (or more), as follows:

  Class: Politician   SubClassOf: hasPoliticianName min 1.

A maxCardinality of 1 may be declared in a similar way using max 1, which is another way to declare that the predicate is functional. If minCardinality = maxCardinality, you can set both at once using exactCardinality. For example, the 1:1 reference scheme for Politician may be declared in OWL 2 as follows:

 Class: Politician   SubClassOf: hasPoliticianName exactly 1.   HasKey: hasPoliticanName DataProperty: hasPoliticianName   Domain: Politician   Range: PoliticianName

As a composite identification scheme example, consider the ORM schema in Fig. 18.25(a). Here, each building is identified by its building number, and each room is identified by combining its local room number with its building.

Now, consider the ORM schema in Fig. 18.26(a). In the fact type Employee drives Car, the drives predicate is optional and m:n. The two textual constraints in FORML add a restricted mandatory role constraint (see constraint footnote 1) and a restricted uniqueness constraint (see constraint footnote 2). Here, the drives predicate is functional only with respect to NonExecutive, not Employee. We should not declare drives as a FunctionalProperty because that would then apply to all employees (and any other subjects of the drives predicate in an OWL version of the model). These restricted constraints may be declared in OWL using qualified cardinality restrictions, as shown in Fig. 18.26(a) using Manchester syntax.

In practice, it is very rare to encounter explicit declarations for minCardinality = 0 and minQualifiedCardinality = 0 because these apply by default, so they may be ignored. However, setting the maximum cardinality to zero does have some use. The setting maxCardinality = 0 means that each instance of the subject class expression A is related via the predicate R to no object instance.

The setting maxQualifiedCardinality = 0 means that each instance of the subject class expression A is related via R to no instance of the specified range B. These restrictions are used mainly in defining subclasses, and the qualified version is typically used in such cases. Fig. 18.27(a) and Fig. 18.27(b) summarize the corresponding ORM patterns. Fig. 18.27(c) provides a concrete example, and Fig. 18.27(d) shows the OWL code.

ExactCardinality restrictions other than 1 are allowed. For example, the following OWL 2 code may be used to state that Asimov authored exactly 506 books.

 ObjectProperty: authored  Domain: Person  Range: Book Individual: Asimov  Types: Person     authored exactly 506 Book

Database systems typically identify countries by country codes or country names. Many country names contain embedded spaces (e.g., “Czech Republic”) so can’t be used directly as IRIs (though modified names using underscores or hyphens for spaces could be).

In practice, many OWL ontologies use meaningless, automatically generated identifiers as IRIs just as some relational database designers prefer artificial, surrogate keys for their table schemes. Human-readable labels can be associated with IRIs using rdfs:label annotation properties, and OWL software tools such as Protégé (http://protege.stanford.edu/) can be configured to display labels instead of IRIs to make the ontologies more readable.

Constraints specified in data models are not translated into actual constraints in OWL, but rather logical propositions that are understood in terms of open world semantics where some individuals may be unnamed. For example, the subclass restriction “hasPoliticianName min 1” for Politician simply says that each politician has a politician name—it doesn’t require the system to know what that code is.

Union, Intersection, and Complement

Recall that the union of sets A and B is the set of all elements in A or B or both. The union operator is supported in all versions of OWL, except for OWL Lite, and may be applied to classes or data ranges (e.g., datatypes or other collections of literals). The complex class expression or data range expression resulting from a union may be used anywhere a simple class or data range may be used. The union of two or more classes contains all the individuals that occur in at least one of those classes. In Manchester syntax, the union operator appears as “or”, placed in infix position. This is an inclusive-or operator. For example, we may define a promising student as a student who is either bright or industrious (or both) as follows:

   Class: PromisingStudent EquivalentTo: BrightStudent or IndustriousStudent

This implies that BrightStudent and IndustriousStudent are subclasses of PromisingStudent. Inferences may be drawn about membership in the superclass. For example, given Individual: Hermione Types: BrightStudent, IndustriousStudent, we may infer Individual: Hermione Types: PromisingStudent.

A class partition may be declared in OWL by adding a disjoint classes declaration to the union operation. In Manchester syntax, to declare two or more classes that are disjoint (i.e., mutually exclusive), simply prepend “DisjointClasses:”. Adding this to an inclusive-or operator results in an exclusive-or operator. For example, we may define a Party as either a person or an organization but not both, thus:

 DisjointClasses: Person, PrivateCompany, PublicOrganization Class: Party EquivalentTo: Person or Organization

A partition of more than two classes may be specified in a similar way, for example,

 DisjointClasses: Person, PrivateCompany, Organization Class: Party EquivalentTo: Person or PrivateCompany or PublicOrganization

As an alternative for declaring partitions, OWL supports the disjoint union operator. In Manchester syntax, this is rendered by using “DisjointUnionOf:”. For instance, the partition just discussed may be declared more concisely thus:

Class: Party DisjointUnionOf: Person, PrivateCompany, PublicOrganization

Recall that the intersection of sets A and B is the set of all elements that occurs in both A and B. In OWL, the intersection operator may be applied to classes or data ranges, and the complex class expression or data range expression resulting from an intersection may be used anywhere a simple class or data range may be used. In Manchester syntax, the intersection operator appears as “and”, placed in infix position. For example, the final line of the following OWL code defines the class StudentEmployee as the intersection of Student and Employee, which are themselves subclasses of Person.

 Class: Person Class: Student SubClassOf: Person Class: Employee SubClassOf: Person Class StudentEmployee EquivalentTo: Student and Employee

Contrast this example with the following declaration, which is based on an example from the official OWL 2 Primer. Here, the class Grandfather is simply asserted, not defined. Instead, it is simply constrained to be included in (rather than being identical to) the intersection of the Man and Parent classes. Not all men who are parents are grandparents.

   Class: Grandfather  SubClassOf:  Man and Parent

Recall that the complement of set A is the set of all elements in the universal set but not in the set A. In OWL, the complement operator may be applied to classes or data ranges, and the complex class expression or data range expression resulting may be used anywhere a simple class or data range may be used.

The complement of a class contains each individual that is not a member of that class. In Manchester syntax, the complement operator appears as “not”. For example, the class NonHuman may be defined as the complement of the class Human as follows:

 Class: Human Class: NonHuman EquivalentTo: not Human

The definition below of the class NonDriver is another example:

 Class: Person Class: Driver EquivalentTo: Person and drives min 1 Car Class: NonDriver EquivalentTo: Person and not Driver

All the examples so far have used classes. In OWL 2, the union, intersection, and complement operations may also be applied to data ranges. For example:

 Datatype: StringOrInteger EquivalentTo: xsd:string or xsd:integer Datatype: PassGradeNr EquivalentTo: GradeNr and not FailGradeNr

Reflexive, Irreflexive, Symmetric, Asymmetric, and Transitive Predicates

In OWL, all properties are binary predicates. If the domain and range are the same or compatible, one may compare subject and object instances. In ORM, such predicates are called ring predicates, and constraints that apply specifically to them (or more generally, pairs of compatible roles) are called ring constraints.

ORM includes graphical notation for several kinds of ring constraints, some of which are simply defined (e.g., irreflexive, asymmetric) while others are recursively defined (e.g., acyclic, strongly intransitive). OWL 2 supports only the following five kinds of restrictions on ring predicates: reflexive, irreflexive, symmetric, asymmetric, and transitive. Of these, OWL 1 supported only symmetric and transitive. Unlike ORM, OWL allows restrictions on ring predicates to be applied only to object property expressions, not data property expressions.

A relation R is reflexive if and only if every individual thing in the domain of R bears the relation R to itself. If the domain is owl:Thing, the only predicate likely to be reflexive is the identity relation “=”.

OWL allows object property expressions to be declared reflexive by characterizing them as reflexive properties. In Manchester syntax, we declare “Reflexive” as a characteristic. For example, if each person knows himself/herself, the “knows” predicate may be declared to be reflexive as follows:

 ObjectProperty: knows  Domain: Person  Range: Person  Characteristics: Reflexive

Given this, the following inferences may be made:

  •    Individual: Einstein
  •      Types: Person”                 →     Individual: Einstein Facts: knows Einstein.
  •    Individual: Terry
  •          Facts: knows Tony”     →     Individual: Terry Types: Person
  •                                                                                Individual: Tony Types: Person

As an example with a union domain, the following declaration of the isAsOldAs predicate asserts that each Person, each Cat, and each Dog is as old as itself.

 ObjectProperty: isAsOldAs  Domain: Person or Cat or Dog  Characteristics: Reflexive

A ring predicate R is irreflexive if and only if no individual can bear the relation R to itself. For example, the parenthood relation is irreflexive because nothing can be a parent of itself. OWL object property expressions are declared irreflexive by characterizing them as irreflexive properties. To do this in Manchester syntax, we declare “Irreflexive” as a characteristic. For example, the isaParentOf predicate is declared irreflexive as follows. Any assertion that someone is his/her own parent would then render the OWL ontology inconsistent.

 Class: Person ObjectProperty: isaParentOf  Domain: Person  Range: Person  Characteristics: Irreflexive

A ring predicate R is symmetric if and only if ∀x∀y(xRy → yRx); that is, for each individual x and y (not necessarily distinct), if xRy then it is also the case that yRx. For example, the siblinghood relation is symmetric because if one person is a sibling (brother or sister) of another, then the second person is a sibling of the first.

OWL object property expressions are declared symmetric by characterizing them as symmetric properties. In Manchester syntax, we declare “Symmetric” as a characteristic, for example, isaSiblingOf may be declared to be symmetric in OWL as shown below. For completeness, the irreflexive nature of the predicate is also declared.

 Class: Person ObjectProperty: isaSiblingOf  Domain: Person  Range: Person  Characteristics: Symmetric, Irreflexive

In OWL, if a predicate is declared to be symmetric, and we assert a fact instance of it, then its converse may be inferred. For example, if we now add the declaration.

       Individual: Romulus  Facts: isaSiblingOf Remus

we may infer

  •      Individual: Remus Facts: isaSiblingOf Romulus.

In ORM, constraining a predicate to be symmetric means that the asserted fact population must be symmetric. For example, if we assert that Romulus is a sibling of Remus, then we must also assert that Remus is a sibling of Romulus (both facts are stored). In OWL, however, you can assert just one of these facts and have the other fact inferred. To do that in ORM, you would provide a derivation rule for inferring the converse rather than constraining the fact type to be symmetric.

For example, in ORM you could declare the fact type Person is a sibling of Person to be semiderived, meaning that some of its instances may be asserted and some may be derived, and use the following rule to derive the converse facts: Person1 is a sibling of Person2 if Person2 is a sibling of Person1. In this case, you would constrain the siblinghood fact type to be irreflexive, but not symmetric.

A ring predicate R is asymmetric if and only if, for each individual x and y (not necessarily distinct), if xRy then it is not the case that yRx. In other words, if the relationship applies, then its converse cannot apply. For example, the parenthood relation is asymmetric because if one person is a parent of another, then the second person cannot be a parent of the first.

OWL object property expressions are declared asymmetric by characterizing them as asymmetric. To do this in Manchester syntax, we declare “Asymmetric” as a characteristic. For example, isaParentOf predicate may be declared to be asymmetric in OWL, as shown below.

 Class: Person ObjectProperty: isaParentOf  Domain: Person  Range: Person  Characteristics: Asymmetric

Note that if a predicate is asymmetric, it is automatically irreflexive as well (consider the definition of asymmetry for the case where x = y). Although asymmetry implies irreflexivity, the converse does not apply. For example, isaSiblingOf is irreflexive but not asymmetric.

If the above asymmetric constraint has been declared and we assert that Ann is a parent of Bill, then any attempt to add the fact that Bill is a parent of Ann would render the OWL ontology inconsistent.

A ring predicate R is transitive if and only if, for each individual x, y, and z (not necessarily distinct), if xRy and yRz then it is also the case that xRz. For example, the ancestorhood relation is transitive because if one person is an ancestor of another, and the second person is an ancestor of a third person, then the first person is an ancestor of the third person.

Ignoring reincarnation, the ancestorhood predicate is actually acyclic (an object can never cycle back to itself by applying one or more ancestorhood facts). Unlike ORM, OWL does not support acyclicity constraints. However, OWL does allow object property expressions to be declared transitive by characterizing them as transitive. To do this in Manchester syntax, we declare “Transitive” as a characteristic. For example, isanAncestorOf predicate may be declared to be transitive, as shown below. For completeness, the asymmetric nature of the predicate is also declared.

 Class: Person ObjectProperty: isanAncestorOf  Domain: Person  Range: Person  Characteristics: Transitive, Asymmetric

In OWL, declaring the ancestorhood predicate to be transitive does not require that all its instances must be asserted. For example, if you declare the predicate to be transitive, and assert that Ann is an ancestor of Bill and that Bill is an ancestor of Chris, then the OWL engine can infer that Ann is an ancestor of Chris.

Enumerated Types in OWL 2

Recall that OWL allows you to define a new class or datatype by specifying its intension (i.e., meaning) in terms of operations on classes or datatypes that are already declared. A type definition that specifies the necessary and sufficient conditions for an item to be a member of the type is said to be an intensional definition of the type. For example, intensional definitions for StudentEmployee and PassGradeNr may be declared in Manchester syntax as shown below, assuming that the types referenced (Student, Employee, GradeNr, FailGradeNr) have been previously declared.

 Class: StudentEmployee  EquivalentTo: Student and Employee Datatype: PassGradeNr  EquivalentTo: GradeNr and not FailGradeNr

The set of all possible instances of a type is said to be the extension of the type. If a class or data range is composed of a known, finite set of items, it may be defined by enumerating (i.e., listing) those items. For example, while EvenDigit could be defined intensionally as {x | x is a digit that is divisible by 2}, it could also be defined extensionally as a member of {0, 2, 4, 6, 8}. A type that is defined by enumerating its extension is said to be an enumerated type, and its definition is said to be an extensional definition. In Manchester syntax, the usual set notation is used to specify the extension, using braces as set delimiters and commas as element separators, such as.

 Class: Weekday EquivalentTo: { Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday } Datatype: EvenDigit EquivalentTo: {0, 2, 4, 6, 8}

“Value” Restrictions on Predicates

OWL uses the term “value” loosely to mean either an individual entity or a literal. Given this understanding, a named class or (unnamed) class expression may be defined as the subject of a predicate whose range is restricted to include one of the following three options: (1) some specific value; (2) some value from a specified class or data range; (3) only values from a specified class or data range. We consider these cases in turn.

In Manchester syntax, the set of all elements that relates via a binary relation R to the value v is expressed simply as “R value v”. As an example of option (1), if we treat Gender as an enumerated class of two individuals (male and female), the following OWL code defines MalePerson as the class of people who have male gender.

 ObjectProperty: Person hasGender  Domain: Person  Range: Gender Class: Gender  EquivalentTo: { male, female } Class: MalePerson  EquivalentTo: Person and hasGender value male

In Manchester syntax, the set of all elements that relates via R to some value in a specified subrange D is expressed simply as “R some D”. As an example of option (2), the following OWL code defines CarDriver as the class of people who drive a car.

 ObjectProperty: drives  Domain: Person  Range: Vehicle Class: Car  SubclassOf: Vehicle Class: Driver  EquivalentTo: Person and drives some Car

In Manchester syntax, the set of all elements that relate via R to some value in a specified subrange D only (if at all) is expressed simply as “R only D”. As an example of option (3), given the previous declarations for the drives predicate and Car subclass, the following OWL code defines CarOnlyDriver as the class of people who drive only vehicles that are cars. This subtype includes those people who drive no vehicles at all.

   Class: CarOnlyDriver  EquivalentTo: Person and drives only Car

Property Chains in OWL 2

OWL 2 allows you to derive a new object property fact by composing two or more object property facts together in a chain, where the entity in the object position of one fact (other than the last fact) is also the subject of the following fact. In relational database work, this corresponds to performing an equijoin between two elementary relations and then projecting on the first and last attribute in the chain. In OWL, the equijoin operation is known as a composition operation, and an expression that composes two or more predicates is called a property chain.

To illustrate this notion, consider a business domain in which each person is born in at most one city (e.g., some people might instead be born in a village), and each city is located in exactly one country. One way of specifying this schema in OWL using Manchester syntax is as follows:

 ObjectProperty: wasBornInCity  Domain: Person  Range: City  Characteristics: Functional ObjectProperty: isLocatedInCountry  Domain: City  Range: Country Class: Person SubClassOf: wasBornInCity max 1 Class: City SubClassOf: isLocatedInCountry exactly 1

Now, suppose we are also interested in knowing which countries people are born in. In ORM, we could add the semiderived fact type Person was born in Country, allowing some instances to be asserted and others derived using the derivation rule Person was born in Country if Person was born in some Country that is located in that Country.

In OWL 2, we can specify the derivation rule by declaring the wasBornInCountry predicate to be a subproperty of the predicate formed by projecting on the start and end of the property chain that composes the wasBornCountry and isLocatedInCity predicates. In Manchester syntax, the property chain is specified using the symbol “o” as the composition operator placed between adjacent predicates in the chain, and listed after the header “SubPropertyChain:”. Our current example may be specified in Manchester syntax by adding the following OWL code:

 ObjectProperty: wasBornInCountry  Domain: Person  Range: Country   SubPropertyChain: wasBornInCity o isLocatedInCountry

The subproperty declaration is just a simple implication that applies to any satisfying models. OWL is not concerned with choices about how to actually implement implications. A property chain may compose multiple occurrences of the same predicate. For example, grandparenthood facts may be derived by composing two parenthood facts, as shown.

 ObjectProperty: isaGrandparentOf   SubPropertyChain: isaParentOf o isaParentOf

If knowledge of parenthood facts is incomplete, we may wish to allow some grandparenthood facts to be simply asserted by adding the following declarations.

 ObjectProperty: isaGrandparentOf   Domain: Person   Range: Person.

Property chains composed from more than two predicate occurrences are also allowed. For example, the following declaration enables great-grandparenthood facts to be inferred from three relevant parenthood facts. For instance, given the facts that Edward VII is a parent of George V, George V is a parent of George VI, and George VI is a parent of Elizabeth II, we may derive the fact that Edward VII is a great-grandparent of Elizabeth II.

 ObjectProperty: isaGreatGrandparentOf   SubPropertyChain: isaParentOf o isaParentOf o isaParentOf

As an example of a property chain with three different predicates, the following declarations capture the derivation that a person drives a car made by a specific company if that person drives a car that is of a carmodel made by that company.

 ObjectProperty: drives   Domain: Person   Range: Car ObjectProperty: isOfCarModel   Domain: Car   Range: CarModel ObjectProperty: isMadeBy   Domain: Car   Range: CarModel ObjectProperty: drivesCarMadeBy   SubPropertyChain: drives o isOfCarModel o isMadeBy

In dealing with property chain axioms, OWL includes formal restrictions to avoid circular reasoning that could lead to problems of decidability. We now consider an example. In general, an uncle is either a brother of a parent or the husband of an aunt. Unclehood by birth may be defined as follows: given persons x and y, x is a birth uncle of y if x is a brother of a parent of y. Now, suppose we also define brotherhood as follows: given persons x and y, x is a brother of y if x is a birth uncle of a child of y. These derivation rules may be specified in OWL as follows.

 ObjectProperty: isaBirthUncleOf     SubPropertyChain: isaBrotherOf o isaParentOf ObjectProperty: isaBrotherOf     SubPropertyChain: isaBirthUncleOf o isaChildOf

Note that the derivation rule for brotherhood calls the birth unclehood predicate, which itself depends on brotherhood. So, the derivation rules in combination involve a vicious circle. In OWL, this property chain combination is illegal.

Some Differences Between OWL Ontologies and Typical Databases

In OWL 2, a named individual is identified by an IRI. OWL 2 also allows unnamed or anonymous individuals (corresponding to blank nodes in RDF), which may be referenced within a given ontology by a local nodeID that starts with an underscore, for example, _:x or _:p1. The following example asserts the existence of a woman president of Taiwan, using the nodeID _:p1 to denote this person.

 Individual: _:p1  Types: Woman  Facts: isPresidentOf Taiwan

In relational databases, individuals are normally identified by simple or compound names, so existential assertions like those above are typically not supported, although we can store specific facts that imply them, such as Tsai Ing-wen is a woman and president of Taiwan.

From a logical perspective, IRIs correspond to individual constants rather than names in the usual sense they have in relational databases. To illustrate how OWL’s treatment of IRI-based identification schemes differs from the value-based identification schemes used in database systems, consider the following declarations:

 DataProperty: hasCountryCode  Domain: Country  Range: xsd:string Class: Country  SubClassOf: hasCountryCode exactly 1 Individual: Australia  Types: Country  Facts: hasCountryCode "AU" Individual: Germany  Types: Country

Here, we asserted that Germany is a country without explicitly providing a country code for it. This would not be allowed in an information model or relational database because our declaration that each country has a country code is implemented as an integrity constraint, forbidding a country without a country code.

In contrast, OWL allows this because the declaration that each country has a country code is interpreted simply as a proposition, not as a constraint. This proposition may be formalized in logic as ∀x(Country x → ∃y x hasCountryCode y). Because we asserted that Germany is a country, the system infers that Germany has a country code, which is currently unknown. This is allowed in OWL, which adopts open world semantics and permits unnamed individuals.

Note also that if we add the data property hasCountryName, OWL has no way to choose one of the hasCountryCode or hasCountryName relationships for the preferred reference scheme, as any distinction between primary and alternate keys is lost.

InverseFunctional declarations apply to any kind of individual (named individuals, anonymous individuals, and individuals whose existence is implied by existential quantification). However, the uniqueness aspect of HasKey declarations applies only to named individuals (individuals that are explicitly named by an IRI). Suppose we declare the object property wasBornInCountry and the data property hasCountryCode in the usual way and then add the following declarations.

 Class: Country  SubClassOf: hasCountryCode exactly 1  HasKey: hasCountryCode

We can now assert that Julia Gillard (a former prime minister of Australia) was born in some country that has the country code “GB” without knowing the name of that country, as follows:

 Individual: JuliaGillard  Facts: wasBornInCountry _:c1 Individual: _:c1    Facts: hasCountryCode “GB”

Now, suppose we discover that the United Kingdom has the country code “GB” (chosen by ISO based on the long name “The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland”). Using TheUK as an intuitive IRI for the United Kingdom, we can now assert that the UK has the country code “GB” as follows:

 Individual: TheUK    Facts: hasCountryCode "GB"

One might expect that it is correct to infer the fact that Julia Gillard was born in the United Kingdom, which may be expressed thus:

 Individual: JuliaGillard  Facts: wasBornInCountry TheUK

However, this fact does not follow! This is because the HasKey declaration for Country applies only to named individuals (those with IRIs explicitly asserted) while allowing that Julia Gillard may be born in many unnamed countries.

Negated Facts and Unary Facts in OWL

Similar to the way OWL uses “not” as a complement operator for classes and data ranges, OWL enables you to explicitly assert the negation of a proposition by declaring a NegativePropertyAssertion. Manchester syntax uses the logical not operator before the relevant predicate object pair in the Facts slot for the individual. Consider the ORM fact type Scientist was born in Country. This is used purely to record which scientists are born in which country. Suppose we know that Newton was born in England, and that although we don’t know where Einstein was born, we do know he wasn’t born in England. OWL allows us to assert both the positive and negated facts as follows:

 ObjectProperty; wasBornIn  Domain: Scientist  Range: Country  Characteristics: Functional Individual: Newton  Facts: wasBornIn England Individual: Einstein  Facts: not wasBornIn England

Contrast this approach with the closed world approach of typical databases where any fact that is neither asserted nor derived is assumed to be false. The previous example negates an object property. Data properties may be negated in a similar way. For example, treating IQs as numbers, we may assert that Einstein’s IQ is not equal to 100 as follows:

 DataProperty: hasIQ  Domain: Scientist  Range: xsd:nonNegativeInteger  Characteristics: Functional Individual: Einstein  Facts: not hasIQ 100

OWL adopts the open world assumption, so if a fact is neither asserted nor implied, it is unknown. Hercule Poirot, Captain Hastings, and Inspector Japp are characters from Agatha Christie novels. Unary facts (e.g., Poirot smokes) and their negations (e.g., Hastings does not smoke) have to be remodeled in OWL as binary relationships that relate the subject to an object that is either a Boolean value (true or false) or a status value with two possibilities (e.g., “Smoker”, “NonSmoker”).

For example, the following OWL declarations assert that Poirot smokes, Hastings doesn’t smoke, and leave it unknown whether Japp smokes. In ORM, this example would be modeled using the unary fact type Person smokes under open world with negation semantics.

 DataProperty: isaSmoker  Domain: Person  Range: xsd:boolean
  Characteristics: Functional Individual: Poirot  Facts: isaSmoker true Individual: Hastings  Facts: isaSmoker false Individual: Japp  Types: Person

Join Semantics of External Uniqueness Constraints

External uniqueness constraints with inner join semantics may be declared in OWL simply by using compound HasKey properties on the referenced class. Recall Fig. 18.25, where each room was identified by combining its local room number with its building, and this OWL code was used for the composite reference scheme.

 Class: Room  SubClassOf: isInBuilding exactly 1  SubClassOf: hasRoomNr exactly 1  HasKey: isInBuilding, hasRoomNr

Capturing external uniqueness constraints with outer join semantics in OWL requires more work. Typically, this will involve introducing a subclass for the instances that don’t play the relevant optional role and then declaring a HasKey property for that subclass. To ensure that the HasKey declarations are affective, IRIs must be included for the referenced instances.

Fig. 18.28 reproduces an example from Section 10.1. The external uniqueness constraint has outer join semantics, with the added proviso that nulls produced in the outer join are treated as actual values. Hence, in addition to being identified by its course code, each course that is offered by a department may be referenced by the combination of its course title and its department, for example, (Mechanics, PY) and (Mechanics, MA). Each course offered by no department may be identified either by its code or its title.

Adding course NDC4 with the same title “Mechanics” as course ND3 would violate the external uniqueness constraint. Assuming the object properties and data properties are declared in the usual way, the outer join semantics of the external uniqueness constraint may be captured in Manchester syntax as shown below. The subclass NonDepartmentalCourse is added for courses offered by no department, and hasCourseTitle is declared as a HasKey property for it.

 Class: Course  SubClassOf: hasCourseTitle exactly 1 xsd:string, hasCourseCode exactly 1 xsd:string  HasKey: hasCourseCode Class: Department  SubClassOf: hasDepartmentCode exactly 1 xsd:string  HasKey: hasDepartmentCode Class: NonDepartmentalCourse  EquivalentTo: Course and (isOfferedBy max 0 Department)  HasKey: hasCourseTitle

If we add the test data shown in Fig. 18.28, this will violate the HasKey condition that nondepartmental courses can be identified by their titles because two nondepartmental courses, NDC3 and NDC4, would have the same title “Mechanics”.

Mapping ORM to OWL

Recent research efforts have investigated mapping from conceptual models in ORM, UML, and ER to OWL as well as other description logic-based languages. The direct formal semantics of OWL 2 is based on the description logic SROIQ (D). Much of ORM can be mapped cleanly to these description logics, facilitating the use of efficient DL-based theorem provers for consistency checking of ORM schemas, and interoperability with other semantic web applications. Unlike OWL 2, ORM has a clean, first-order formalization, so problems about types being instances are avoided. However, some ORM structures and constraints cannot be captured in OWL. This has both good and bad consequences.

On the plus side, ORM is capable of capturing, in a natural fashion, several complex aspects of reality that commonly occur in business domains but cannot be captured in popular description logics. Hence, ORM enables higher-fidelity models of typical business domains.

On the negative side, ORM is so expressive that its underlying logic extends a little beyond decidable fragments of first-order logic. This makes it difficult to achieve efficient automated checking of aspects such as schema satisfiability (e.g., in very large schemas with millions of constraints, checking that none of the constraints contradict one another).

This is yet another example of the trade-off between expressibility and tractability. The more expressive the language, the harder it is to efficiently verify the logical consistency of models expressed in it. Because we ought to ensure that our models accurately reflect the business domains they are intended to model, it seems reasonable to capture the intended semantics in a language such as ORM, apply efficient automated checking where possible, and use heuristic techniques for the rest.

Examples of ORM features that can’t be translated into SROIQ (D), and hence OWL DL, include uniqueness and frequency constraints spanning multiple roles (of the same or different relationships), set-comparison constraints involving multirole arguments, acyclic ring constraints, and deontic constraints. The 𝒟ℒℛifd description logic adds support for identifier and functional dependency constraints, so it can capture internal uniqueness constraints spanning multiple roles as well as external uniqueness constraints.

Unlike ER and UML, ORM is attribute-free and hence is easier to relate to RDF, RDFS, OWL, and description logics, which also represent all facts in the form of relationships. Although RDF and OWL use binary relationships only, it is a trivial matter to transform unary and n-ary fact types into binary form, as discussed in earlier chapters. So, there is a fairly obvious mapping of facts and fact types in binary ORM to these semantic web languages.

The only aspects lost in the mapping are those ORM constraints and derivation rules that have no counterpart in the logic underlying the target language. These can be mapped over as unambiguous verbalizations in ancillary notes.

An atomic fact type in ORM offers an ideal semantic unit for sharing semantics between different models. Such a unit is constraint-free, allowing different models to apply different constraints without altering the semantics of the fact type. For example, the fact type Person drives Car might be optional and m:n in one model, but mandatory and n:1 in another model. Using a fact-based approach instead of an attribute-based approach facilitates this kind of exchange. This is one reason why the OMG’s SBVR approach for exchanging semantics of business rules is also fact-oriented.

18.7 Metamodeling

Modeling involves making models of business domains. Metamodeling involves making models of models—this time the things being modeled are themselves models. Just as recursion is one of the most elegant and powerful concepts in logic, metamodeling is one of the most beautiful and powerful notions in conceptual modeling. This section uses a simple example to convey the basic idea.

A database holds fact instances from a business domain while its conceptual schema models the structure of the domain. Fig. 18.29 recalls our basic view of an information system where the database conforms to the rules laid down in the conceptual schema. Essentially, a DBMS is a system for managing various databases; for each database that models some UoD, it checks that each database state agrees with the structure specified in the conceptual schema for that UoD.

Among other things, a conceptual modeling tool is a system for managing conceptual schemas. Each valid schema diagram in this book may be thought of as an output report from this system. The trick then is to treat a schema as an instance of this higher-level system. As long as we can verbalize the diagrams into atomic facts, we can use the CSDP to develop a conceptual schema for such conceptual schemas. We would then have a conceptual metaschema (schema about schemas).

Suppose that Table 18.4 is part of an output report from a movie database. Other reports from the database provide further information (e.g., people’s birth places).

Table 18.4

One report extracted from a movie database.
